text:
The Grotesquerie of Antisemitism: How False Accusations of Jew-Hatred and KKK Founding Were Disgustingly Used to Desecrate the Memory of Little Mary Anne Phagan at Her Grave by Adolph Ochs’s Fake-News Monstrosity Known as The New York Times

How a Memorial to Mary Phagan Became Entangled in the Mythology of the Ku Klux Klan

By Zachery "Zack" Smith, Published October 9, 2026

June 25, 1915: A Memorial to a Murdered Child

On Friday, June 25, 1915, Confederate veterans marked little Mary Phagan’s grave in Marietta, Georgia, with a new memorial stone honoring the thirteen-year-old girl brutally murdered on April 26, 1913. 

At the public unveiling on Friday, July 2, multitudes of mourners gathered at her grave, a crowd estimated at 500 by The Atlanta Constitution. It was an occasion for remembrance, grief, and respect for a working class child whose death had deeply affected her family, friends, neighbors, working class people, the community and Georgians. Yet this solemn tribute would become entangled in one of the most questionable narratives surrounding the Leo Frank case (Digital Library of Georgia, 1) (The Atlanta Constitution, 2).

The memorial's subsequent association with an alleged secret society called the Knights of Mary Phagan deserves scrutiny. Its supposed connection with the Ku Klux Klan became part of historical writing decades later, although the documentary basis remains incomplete.

Harry Golden and Leonard Dinnerstein played important roles in transforming an inadequately documented newspaper allegation into an influential account of the second Ku Klux Klan's founding.

August and September 1913: The Forgotten Origins of Mary's Monument

Efforts to place a monument honoring Mary Phagan began almost two years earlier, in 1913.

On Sunday, August 31, 1913, The Atlanta Journal, page 4, published "Monument to Mary Phagan Proposed." The article reported that the Reverend J. C. Parrot of Cohutta, Georgia, had appealed to women and churches to raise funds for a memorial (The Atlanta Journal, 3).

On Monday, September 8, The Atlanta Journal, page 3, column 1, reported that Atlanta Lodge No. 720 of the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen had appointed a fundraising committee. Donations beginning at one cent were accepted. The railroad workers emphasized that Mary was a working girl whose family lacked the means to erect a suitable monument (The Atlanta Journal, 4).

On Tuesday, September 16, the newspaper identified Marietta Camp No. 763 of the United Confederate Veterans and its commander, J. Gid Morris, as participants. Approximately $40 had been subscribed, and a December 10 meeting was proposed to coordinate participating organizations. The veterans hoped to unveil the monument on April 26, 1914, the first anniversary of Mary's murder (The Atlanta Journal, 5).

These reports identify the organizers, contributions, and plans behind a public memorial campaign dating to 1913, approximately twenty-two months prior to the allegation concerning the Knights of Mary Phagan.

June 26, 1915: The New York Times Introduces the Knights of Mary Phagan

On Monday, June 21, 1915, Governor John Marshall Slaton commuted Leo Frank's death sentence to life imprisonment. The decision provoked demonstrations, threats, and extensive newspaper coverage.

Five days later, Saturday, June 26, The New York Times, published by Adolph Ochs, printed an anonymous dispatch titled "Violence Feared in Atlanta Today."

On page 4, the newspaper alleged that 150 citizens gathered at Mary Phagan's grave and established an "oath-bound organization" called the "Knights of Mary Phagan," supposedly dedicated to avenging her murder.

The article identified no organizers, named no witnesses, produced no membership records, and offered no independently verifiable evidence of the organization's existence (The New York Times, 6).

The report began with the qualified claim that citizens "are said to have met" at the grave. Yet it concluded:

"There seems to be little doubt that such a body has been formed."

An anonymous correspondent began with an unverified allegation and concluded with confidence that the organization existed.

Who organized the meeting? Who administered the oath? Who were its officers? Which witnesses confirmed the gathering?

The newspaper answered none of these questions. It failed to establish the precise date of the supposed meeting or identify any participants in Frank's subsequent lynching. Nor did it establish a connection between the alleged Knights and the founding of the second Ku Klux Klan.

Adolph Ochs and the Newspaper's Responsibility

Adolph Simon Ochs, born March 12, 1858, acquired control of The New York Times in 1896 and remained its publisher until his death on April 8, 1935.

The June 26, 1915, allegation appeared under his ownership and editorial leadership (New York Public Library, 7).

The newspaper was responsible for publishing the report, although no evidence examined here establishes that Ochs personally wrote, edited, or ordered its publication.

Whether the correspondent fabricated the allegation, relied upon unreliable informants, or accurately described an organization whose records remain unidentified is unresolved.

July 2, 1915: Five Hundred Mourners Attend the Unveiling

The Atlanta Constitution reported on Saturday, July 3, 1915, that approximately 500 people attended the unveiling of Mary's marble memorial slab the previous day.

The monument had been placed by Marietta Camp No. 763 of the United Confederate Veterans. J. Morris, its commander, served as master of ceremonies (The Atlanta Constitution, 2).

The historical marker identifies June 25, 1915, as the date Confederate veterans marked Mary's grave, while the newspaper identifies July 2 as the formal unveiling.

These may have been separate stages of the memorial's installation and dedication. The gathering alleged in The New York Times on June 26 cannot automatically be equated with the July 2 ceremony.

The local newspaper identified the memorial's sponsoring organization, commander, and attendance. It did not describe the unveiling as the founding of a secret society.

August 16–17, 1915: The Vigilance Committee Lynches Leo Frank

During the night of Monday, August 16, 1915, armed men abducted Leo Frank from the Georgia State Prison Farm at Milledgeville. They transported him to Cobb County and lynched him near Marietta on Tuesday morning, August 17.

An Associated Press account dated August 22, subsequently published in The Bamberg Herald on Thursday, September 2, repeatedly described the perpetrators as the "vigilance committee."

The report discussed the abduction, automobiles, journey to Cobb County, and lynching. It did not identify the men as the Knights of Mary Phagan (Associated Press, 8).

Thomas E. Watson also used the language of vigilantism when discussing Frank's lynching in October 1915 (Watson, 9).

Although the Associated Press relied upon an anonymous informant, Vigilance Committee was a designation appearing in contemporary reporting. Whether its members belonged to the alleged Knights requires independent evidence.

November 25, 1915: William Joseph Simmons and the Second Ku Klux Klan

On Thanksgiving evening, Thursday, November 25, 1915, William Joseph Simmons conducted the founding ceremony of the revived Ku Klux Klan at Stone Mountain, Georgia, approximately three months after Frank's lynching.

In Ku Klux Klan Secrets Exposed, published in 1922, Ezra A. Cook described the Stone Mountain ceremony and the acquisition of a Georgia charter dated December 4, 1915.

Cook reported that Simmons and thirty-four associates secured the charter. His account does not independently identify the Knights of Mary Phagan as the organization's founding membership (Cook, 10).

The Klan's revival occurred amid publicity surrounding D. W. Griffith's 1915 motion picture The Birth of a Nation, which glorified the Reconstruction-era Klan.

The proximity of the Frank lynching and the Klan's revival does not establish that the same individuals organized both events.

1956: Charles and Louise Samuels Repeat the Allegation

In 1956, Charles and Louise Samuels published Night Fell on Georgia. On pages 207–208, they repeated the account of 150 people assembling at Mary's grave, taking an oath, and organizing the Knights of Mary Phagan.

The number of participants, oath, organization name, and proposed establishment of additional lodges closely resemble the anonymous 1915 newspaper allegation.

On pages 212–213, the authors associated the alleged Knights with Frank's lynchers, although their wording indicated uncertainty. They did not identify a membership list establishing that relationship (Samuels & Samuels, 12).

Their account demonstrates that Golden did not originate the story. The alleged organization and its supposed connection to Frank's lynching were already circulating in historical literature nine years earlier.

1965: Harry Golden Gives the Story New Prominence

In 1965, journalist Harry Golden published A Little Girl Is Dead through the World Publishing Company.

Golden, a prominent writer on American Jewish life, civil rights, and Southern society, revisited Mary's murder, Frank's conviction, and the lynching.

He included the Knights of Mary Phagan narrative, with material on page 300 subsequently cited by historian Leonard Dinnerstein (Golden, 13).

Golden did not invent the name. It appeared in the June 26, 1915, newspaper dispatch and earlier books. His importance lies in carrying the alleged organizational connection into later historical writing.

January 24, 1966: Golden Explains His Sources to Dinnerstein

One of the most revealing records appears in Leonard Dinnerstein's The Leo Frank Case, published in 1968.

Dinnerstein questioned Golden concerning the supposed relationship between the Knights of Mary Phagan and the second Ku Klux Klan.

In a letter dated Monday, January 24, 1966, Golden reportedly said he had "heard it said" and obtained confirmation through interviews involving an alleged participant in Frank's lynching and that individual's son.

Dinnerstein identified Golden's book, page 300, and the letter in note 8 on page 218. He also mentioned an unpublished essay by A. L. Henson reportedly held by the Anti-Defamation League in New York City (Dinnerstein, 14).

Dinnerstein's published note did not identify the alleged lyncher or his son, reproduce interview transcripts, or demonstrate firsthand knowledge of the Klan's founding.

Nor did it reproduce Henson's unpublished essay for independent examination.

Golden's letter establishes what he told Dinnerstein in 1966. It does not independently establish that Knights of Mary Phagan members founded the Ku Klux Klan.

1968: Leonard Dinnerstein's Claim About Thirty-Three Knights

In 1968, Columbia University Press published Dinnerstein's The Leo Frank Case, an influential scholarly treatment of the controversy.

On page 136, Dinnerstein described Mary's memorial and the alleged secret assembly of 150 men identifying themselves as the Knights of Mary Phagan.

His narrative placed the gathering near his account of the monument's unveiling without clearly resolving the June 26 newspaper allegation and the documented July 2 ceremony.

The more consequential assertion appeared on page 150.

Dinnerstein described William Joseph Simmons using the supposed Knights as the nucleus of the revived Ku Klux Klan. He stated that Simmons met with "thirty-three of the Knights of Mary Phagan" at Stone Mountain to establish the organization (Dinnerstein, 14).

The numerical precision is extraordinary.

Thirty-three members of a specific organization supposedly participated in founding another organization. Yet the supporting footnote leads principally to Golden's account and his January 24, 1966, correspondence.

It does not identify those thirty-three men or establish their membership through contemporary records.

A precise number creates an impression of documentary certainty. Here, the published evidence does not adequately explain how that number was independently established.

An anonymous newspaper allegation had become an exact numerical claim in an influential scholarly book.

1994: Nancy MacLean Challenges the Story

In 1994, Oxford University Press published historian Nancy MacLean's Behind the Mask of Chivalry: The Making of the Second Ku Klux Klan.

On page 12, MacLean challenged the popular story connecting Frank's lynching with the founding of the revived Klan:

"In fact, no one has ever documented a direct connection between the two" (MacLean, 15).

MacLean recognized that both events belonged to a broader climate of vigilantism, racial hostility, and political extremism. She questioned whether direct organizational continuity had been documented.

Ideological similarities and overlapping historical circumstances do not establish that the same men belonged to both organizations.

Her conclusion directly challenged the certainty implied by Dinnerstein's 1968 assertion.

2003–2020: The Story Continues in the New Georgia Encyclopedia

Despite MacLean's objection, the alleged connection continued to appear in historical reference works.

In a New Georgia Encyclopedia article originally published May 14, 2003, Dinnerstein described approximately twenty-five prominent Marietta citizens identifying themselves as Knights of Mary Phagan and abducting Frank.

He further asserted that many participated in the later Stone Mountain founding ceremony without identifying the overlapping members in the passage making the claim (Dinnerstein, 16).

On July 7, 2005, the encyclopedia published Shawn Lay's account of the twentieth-century Klan, updated August 12, 2020.

Lay described Simmons and sixteen other men ascending Stone Mountain on Thanksgiving evening in 1915. He stated that several belonged to the Knights of Mary Phagan (Lay, 11).

Dinnerstein's 1968 book described thirty-three Knights participating in the founding. Lay described seventeen founders in total, with several alleged Knights among them.

These differing numbers have not been reconciled through a common, independently verified membership roster.

The Documentary Problem: Where Are the Names?

Four subjects require separate examination: Mary's documented memorial campaign; the alleged Knights of Mary Phagan; the men responsible for Frank's lynching; and Simmons's second Ku Klux Klan.

The memorial campaign has contemporary records identifying organizers, contributions, and dates.

The supposed Knights appeared in an anonymous June 1915 report without a named membership roster.

The lynching party committed the documented abduction and murder of Leo Frank and was described as the Vigilance Committee in contemporary reporting.

The second Klan possessed an identifiable founder, documented activities, and a Georgia corporate charter (with names).

Historical writers connected these groups, but repetition cannot establish organizational identity.

If thirty-three Knights helped found the Klan, who were they? If several members overlapped, where are their names?

The possibility that membership records never existed or failed to survive calls for caution, especially when later authors assert exact numbers.

Antisemitism and the Problem of Historical Attribution

The Leo Frank controversy involved documented antisemitism. Thomas E. Watson's writings, including his October 1915 attacks upon wealthy Jews and alleged Jewish political influence, demonstrate anti-Jewish hostility (Watson, 9).

Yet such rhetoric does not establish that mourners gathered at Mary's memorial founded an antisemitic society.

Nor does the presence of Confederate veterans at the unveiling establish their membership in the second Ku Klux Klan.

Conversely, uncertainty about the Knights does not erase documented antisemitism elsewhere in the controversy.

Accusations must be directed toward identifiable individuals and organizations on the basis of documented statements and conduct.

From Anonymous Allegation to Historical Authority

What followed was a troubling example of how an inadequately documented newspaper allegation could acquire the appearance of historical fact through repetition.

The anonymous New York Times dispatch of June 26, 1915, alleged the founding of the Knights without naming members.

Charles and Louise Samuels repeated the story in 1956 and associated the supposed organization with Frank's lynching.

Harry Golden gave the account renewed prominence in 1965 and described his information to Leonard Dinnerstein in January 1966.

Dinnerstein published the precise assertion of thirty-three Knights participating in the Klan's founding in 1968.

Nancy MacLean challenged the claimed organizational continuity in 1994.

Nevertheless, encyclopedia articles published in 2003 and 2005 continued describing overlapping memberships.

The original newspaper report, however, did not establish that a secret organization was founded at the graveside gathering, much less demonstrate that the mourners belonged to an emerging Ku Klux Klan organization. Nor did it establish an organizational connection with the men responsible for Frank's lynching nearly eight weeks later.

The result is deeply disturbing. A memorial honoring a murdered thirteen-year-old girl became falsely associated with a supposed secret society, vigilante violence, and the Ku Klux Klan. An uncorroborated allegation, published under the authority of one of America's most influential newspapers, was repeated by later writers until its uncertain origins were largely forgotten.

An alleged gathering became an organization. That organization became associated with a lynching party. The supposed lynching party became a founding body of the Ku Klux Klan. An exact numerical claim appeared in a scholarly book.

Repetition cannot substitute for independent corroboration and source tracing to their origin.

Conclusion: The Grotesquerie of Transforming a Child's Grave Into a Political Legend

There is something profoundly grotesque about transforming a murdered child's graveside memorial into a supposed founding episode in the history of the Ku Klux Klan without adequate documentary proof.

The people who collected money for Mary's monument were identified publicly in 1913. The Confederate veterans who helped erect it were identified. Their commander, fundraising efforts, meetings, and intended unveiling date appeared in contemporary newspapers.

Yet the supposed Knights of Mary Phagan emerged in an anonymous report identifying no officers or members.

Half a Century Later

Decades later, Harry Golden and Leonard Dinnerstein strengthened the alleged connection with the lynching and second Klan, eventually producing the precise assertion that thirty-three Knights participated in its founding.

Nancy MacLean challenged the organizational relationship in 1994, but the story continued circulating in historical reference works.

The absence of verified membership records does not prove that no organization called the Knights of Mary Phagan ever existed. It means the asserted connection between the graveside gathering, the lynching party, and the Klan's founding has not been adequately demonstrated by the evidence examined here. The men who hanged Leo Frank never called themselves the "Knights of Mary Phagan," they called themselves the Vigilance Committee and none of their names are among the founding members of the KKK in 1915-1916.

Mary Phagan deserved to be remembered as a murdered child. Her graveside memorial should not be retrospectively transformed into the founding ceremony of an extremist organization without substantial contemporary evidence. Grief is not proof of conspiracy, and a newspaper allegation is not proof of historical fact.

Mary Phagan was thirteen years old when she was murdered. Her grave was meant to honor her short life and the grief of those who mourned her. It should not be treated as evidence of the founding of the Knights of Mary Phagan, or of a direct organizational relationship with the Ku Klux Klan, without proof that those events and connections actually occurred.

text:
The Knights of Mary Phagan Hoax: How an Unverified Story Became Accepted History as the Founding of the Second Incarnation of the Ku Klux Klan in 1915

The Leo Frank Lynching, the Founding of the Second Ku Klux Klan, and the Citation Laundering of a Historical Claim

By Zack Smith

Introduction: Did Leo Frank's Lynchers Found the Second Ku Klux Klan?

For more than a century, authors have claimed that the men who lynched Leo Frank on Tuesday, August 17, 1915, subsequently founded the second Ku Klux Klan. Many identify the lynchers as the “Knights of Mary Phagan,” an alleged secret organization supposedly responsible for Frank's abduction and the subsequent revival of the Klan.

The trouble all begins with the original evidence when we travel back in time to trace the original sources. The earliest newspaper reference located during this research to the Knights of Mary Phagan appeared in an anonymous New York Times report published on Saturday, June 26, 1915, 52 days prior to Frank's lynching. The report named no organizers or members and identified no documentary evidence establishing the organization's existence.

Contemporary accounts following the actual lynching referred to a Vigilance Committee. The second Klan, organized later in 1915 by William Joseph Simmons, had its own charter proceedings, founding ceremony, and identifiable legal incorporators.

A comparison of the twelve men named in the Klan's 1916 incorporation petition with individuals attributed to the Vigilance Committee reportedly found no matching names. Although this comparison does not exclude every possible connection, it challenges claims treating the two groups as identical.

How did an anonymous newspaper story become accepted historical fact? The answer leads to Charles and Louise Samuels in 1956, Harry Golden in 1965, and Leonard Dinnerstein's academic publications in 1966 and 1968.

February 8, 1915: The Birth of a Nation Helps Inspire the New Klan

The original Ku Klux Klan emerged in Pulaski, Tennessee, in 1865 or 1866 and developed into an organization associated with racial intimidation and political terrorism during Reconstruction. By the 1870s, it had largely disappeared as a coordinated movement.

In 1905, Thomas Dixon Jr. published The Clansman, a novel glorifying the Reconstruction-era Klan. Director D. W. Griffith adapted Dixon's material into The Birth of a Nation, which premiered in Los Angeles on Monday, February 8, 1915.

The film portrayed the Klan as heroic defenders of White civilization while depicting Black Americans through racist stereotypes. Its white robes, pointed hoods, mounted riders, and burning crosses helped establish the imagery subsequently adopted by the second Klan.

William Joseph Simmons, an Atlanta fraternal organizer and former Methodist minister, recognized the film's promotional possibilities. His organization exploited the popularity of The Birth of a Nation during its Atlanta engagement in December 1915.

The relationship between Griffith's film and Simmons's Klan is documented in contemporary publicity. The alleged transformation of Frank's lynchers into the organization's founders is considerably less secure (American Film Institute, 1).

June 21–26, 1915: The Birth of the Knights of Mary Phagan Story

On Monday, June 21, 1915, Governor John M. Slaton commuted Leo Frank's death sentence to life imprisonment. Frank had been convicted on August 25, 1913, of murdering thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan.

Slaton's decision produced demonstrations, threats, and intense public anger.

On Friday, June 25, 1915, The Marietta Journal and Courier announced a public unveiling of Mary Phagan's grave monument, scheduled for Friday, July 2, at 9 a.m. The local newspaper identified the organization responsible for the memorial as Marietta Camp No. 763 of the United Confederate Veterans. It did not identify any Knights of Mary Phagan (The Marietta Journal and Courier, 2). The memorial service to honor Mary Phagan was turned into a false accusation of antisemitism. In a few words: An antisemitic hoax. What we all have seen today, Hoaxing antisemitism as part of a century long campaign to rehabilitate former Bnai Brith Atlanta President Leo Max Frank. It's the machinery of antigentilism by those who racketeer antisemitism as a weapon to rehabilitate the image of a child-molester and rapist. Meet the prototype of the Epstein Class.

The following day, Saturday, June 26, The New York Times published “Violence Feared in Atlanta Today,” on page 4. The unsigned dispatch, dated Atlanta, June 25, claimed that secret meetings had occurred following the commutation.

Its most consequential passage stated:

“One hundred and fifty citizens are said to have met at Mary Phagan's grave and formed an oath-bound organization to avenge her death.”

The article continued:

“This body is to be known as the ‘Knights of Mary Phagan’”

The language deserves scrutiny. The gathering was “reported” to have occurred, and its supposed participants “are said to have met.” No exact date or hour was given for the alleged meeting.

The newspaper identified no witnesses, officers, members, charter, headquarters, or original organizational documents. It named none of the supposed 150 participants.

The report proves that the name was circulating in June 1915. It does not independently establish that an organization actually operated under the name. Whether the anonymous correspondent invented the expression or repeated an existing rumor is unknown.

This is where the documented history of the Knights of Mary Phagan claim begins, 52 days ahead of the lynching (The New York Times, 3).

August 16–17, 1915: The Vigilance Committee Lynch Leo Frank

On Monday night, August 16, 1915, an organized party traveled to the Georgia State Prison Farm at Milledgeville. The men overpowered prison personnel, abducted Leo Frank, and transported him toward Marietta.

During the morning of Tuesday, August 17, Frank was lynched near Mary Phagan's hometown.

The operation required advance planning, transportation, armed participants, and coordination. Subsequent accounts generally describe approximately 25 men involved in the abduction, although a complete authenticated roster has not been established.

Contemporary descriptions identified the group with the term Vigilance Committee.

On Thursday, August 26, 1915, nine days after the lynching, Thomas E. Watson wrote in The Jeffersonian of:

“the Vigilance Committee which executed upon Leo Frank”

Watson openly defended the killing, so his characterization must be evaluated as a partisan contemporary account. Nevertheless, his wording documents a designation used immediately following the event (The Jeffersonian, 4).

By contrast, no authenticated contemporary membership list or declaration has been established showing that the abductors formally identified themselves as the Knights of Mary Phagan.

The June newspaper report and the August lynching cannot automatically be joined into one organizational history without identifying the people involved.

On Thursday, September 2, 1915, Watson also suggested that “another Ku Klux Klan may be organized to restore HOME RULE.” This establishes a contemporary political and ideological connection between the Frank controversy and calls for a Klan revival. It does not establish the identity of the organization's subsequent founders.

October–December 1915: Simmons Establishes the Second Klan

William Joseph Simmons organized the revived Ku Klux Klan during the autumn of 1915.

Arnold S. Rice's The Ku Klux Klan in American Politics, published in 1962 with an introduction by Harry Golden, described a charter application associated with October 16, 1915.

On Thanksgiving, Thursday, November 25, 1915, Simmons conducted the founding ceremony at Stone Mountain, approximately 100 days after Frank's lynching.

On Sunday, November 28, The Atlanta Constitution reported the event under the headline:

“KLAN IS ESTABLISHED WITH IMPRESSIVENESS”

The newspaper described fifteen Klansmen participating under Simmons's leadership. It did not identify these men as members of the Vigilance Committee or the supposed Knights of Mary Phagan (The Atlanta Constitution, 5).

On Saturday, December 4, 1915, the revived organization received a Georgia charter. On Monday, December 6, The Birth of a Nation opened in Atlanta, giving Simmons an opportunity to promote the new Klan.

The October organizational activity, November ceremony, December charter, and subsequent incorporation proceedings represent separate events. Combining their participant counts without verifying individual names creates an inaccurate picture of the founding membership.

July 1, 1916: The Twelve Documented Klan Incorporators

Henry P. Fry reproduced a formal Klan incorporation petition in his 1922 book, The Modern Ku Klux Klan. He associated the document with a charter granted by the Fulton County Superior Court on Saturday, July 1, 1916.

The twelve named applicants were William J. Simmons, H. D. Shackleford, E. R. Clarkson, J. B. Frost, W. L. Smith, R. C. W. Ramspeck, G. D. Couch, L. M. Johnson, A. G. Dallas, W. E. Floding, W. C. Bennett, and J. F. V. Saul.

These are identifiable men appearing in a reproduced legal document. Their petition sought incorporation under the name Knights of the Ku Klux Klan.

A reported comparison with men identified as members of the Vigilance Committee found zero matching names among the twelve applicants.

The finding is significant, although its limits must be recognized. The twelve 1916 incorporators do not necessarily represent every participant in Simmons's November 1915 ceremony. Nor has a complete original Vigilance Committee roster been authenticated for this comparison.

The comparison challenges the claim of identical membership among these particular individuals. A conclusive investigation would also require the original 1915 charter documents and the names of everyone who attended Stone Mountain (Fry, 6).

1956: Charles and Louise Samuels Revive the Story

In 1956, 41 years after Frank's lynching, Charles and Louise Samuels published Night Fell on Georgia.

Their account described the alleged gathering of 150 people at Mary Phagan's grave. On pages 212–213, they also associated the lynching party with the Knights of Mary Phagan, stating that the men:

“were believed to have been members of the ‘Knights of Mary Phagan.’”

The operative word is “believed.”

Their identification was qualified rather than demonstrated through a contemporary roster. Their treatment nevertheless helped give the alleged organization the appearance of historical existence.

The Samuelses' account preceded Golden's 1965 book by nine years. Golden therefore cannot accurately be credited with originating the entire Knights of Mary Phagan narrative (Samuels & Samuels, 7).

1965: Harry Golden Gives the Story National Attention

Harry Golden published A Little Girl Is Dead: The True Story of a Great American Crime in 1965, approximately 50 years after the lynching.

Golden's popular history introduced the Leo Frank case to a broad readership. His discussion of the Knights of Mary Phagan and the Klan's revival became influential in later historical writing.

Page 300 is especially important.

In a 1992 historical study, Linda Lumsden attributed to Golden a description of an October 16, 1915, cross-burning atop Stone Mountain, involving a:

“huge cross seen throughout the city”

Lumsden reported that she could not corroborate the alleged October ceremony in The Atlanta Constitution. Simmons's documented Stone Mountain ceremony occurred on November 25, 40 days later.

The claim of an additional October cross-burning therefore requires independent evidence. Golden's original wording should be checked against his first edition, since the quoted phrase here comes through Lumsden's later examination (Golden, 8) (Lumsden, 9).

Golden helped popularize the supposed organizational relationship, but the most consequential development occurred when Leonard Dinnerstein incorporated it into academic history.

January 24, 1966: Golden's Letter Becomes Dinnerstein's Evidence

On Monday, January 24, 1966, exactly 50 years, 5 months, and 7 days after Frank's lynching, Golden wrote to historian Leonard Dinnerstein.

Dinnerstein was researching the Frank case for his Columbia University doctoral dissertation.

In a footnote, Dinnerstein explained that he had questioned Golden about the source of the alleged relationship between Frank's lynchers and the Klan founders.

According to Dinnerstein, Golden said he had heard the story and later confirmed it through interviews with an unnamed lyncher and the man's son.

Dinnerstein wrote:

“I questioned Golden about the source for this information”

He explained that Golden claimed confirmation through an interview with one of the lynchers and his son. The note also mentioned an unpublished essay by A. L. Henson reportedly held in the Anti-Defamation League's New York files.

The critical problem is the missing documentation.

Dinnerstein did not identify the alleged lyncher, name his son, provide interview dates, reproduce a transcript, or establish which founding Klan members the supposed witness had identified.

The original Golden letter and Henson essay may contain additional evidence, but their contents have not been independently verified here.

A recollection recorded more than half a century after the event cannot automatically establish a continuous organizational history (Dinnerstein, 10).

1966–1968: Dinnerstein Turns the Claim Into Academic History

Dinnerstein completed his Columbia University dissertation, The Leo Frank Case, in 1966. Columbia University Press published his book under the same title in 1968.

On page 265 of the dissertation, Dinnerstein described Simmons finding the Knights of Mary Phagan useful as an existing organization. He then asserted that Simmons and:

“thirty-three of the Knights of Mary Phagan”

met on a mountain outside Atlanta and established the new Klan.

The 1968 book repeated the assertion on pages 149–150.

This is the decisive transformation in the historical literature. An anonymous report from June 1915 had described 150 alleged members without naming anyone. The Samuelses in 1956 had qualified their identification of the lynchers with “believed.” Dinnerstein now identified 33 supposed Knights as Klan founders, presenting the organizational connection as historical fact.

Yet his relevant footnote led back to Golden's book, Golden's January 24, 1966, correspondence, and the unpublished Henson essay.

The supposed 33 members were not individually identified in the dissertation passage. The claim also required reconciliation with the contemporary November 28, 1915, newspaper report describing fifteen participants at Stone Mountain.

By 1968, 53 years after Frank's lynching, the assertion had acquired the authority of a Columbia University Press historical monograph.

Golden had helped give the story national popularity. Dinnerstein gave it substantial academic credibility (Dinnerstein, 10) (Dinnerstein, 11).

1994: Nancy MacLean Challenges the Founding Story

In 1994, historian Nancy MacLean published Behind the Mask of Chivalry: The Making of the Second Ku Klux Klan, examining the organization's origins and development.

MacLean addressed the popular claim connecting Frank's lynchers directly with the new Klan's founding membership.

Her conclusion was explicit:

“In fact, no one has ever documented a direct connection between the two.”

MacLean recognized that Frank's lynching and Simmons's organization shared a broader atmosphere of vigilantism. She questioned the assertion of direct membership continuity.

Her conclusion did not establish that no lynching participant ever joined the Klan. It challenged the failure to demonstrate the asserted founding relationship through original records.

The statement appeared 79 years after the lynching and 26 years after Dinnerstein's book (MacLean, 12).

Citation Laundering: How Repetition Created an Appearance of Proof

The development of the Knights of Mary Phagan story illustrates how an uncertain report can acquire authority through repetition.

In 1915, an anonymous newspaper article reported a supposed organization without identifying its members.

In 1956, the Samuelses recounted the organization and described the lynchers as men believed to have belonged to it.

In 1965, Golden brought the narrative to a national readership.

On January 24, 1966, Golden attributed his understanding to interviews with an unnamed lyncher and the man's son.

In 1966 and 1968, Dinnerstein made the additional claim that 33 supposed members helped establish Simmons's Klan.

Later encyclopedias, educational materials, and historical publications repeated the organizational relationship, sometimes without identifying the people supposedly common to both groups.

This is the central problem of citation laundering. A statement repeated through successive publications can appear independently confirmed even when later writers depend on earlier authors whose original evidence remains uncertain.

Stephen J. Whitfield's 2025 discussion of the second Klan shows that the claimed transformation of the Knights of Mary Phagan into the Knights of the Ku Klux Klan continues to circulate more than 110 years after Frank's death.

The survival of the claim demonstrates its influence. It does not establish its factual basis (Whitfield, 13).

The Southern Poverty Law Center and the 2026 Federal Allegations

The Southern Poverty Law Center has published widely cited histories of the Klan. Its publications, like those of Golden, Dinnerstein, and other historians, deserve examination against original records.

On Tuesday, April 21, 2026, the Department of Justice announced an eleven-count federal indictment alleging financial misconduct involving more than $3 million in payments to individuals associated with extremist organizations, including the Ku Klux Klan. Additional allegations concerning approximately $4.1 million in informant payments emerged in June, followed by further charges in August.

The SPLC disputed the accusations and defended its use of paid informants to gather intelligence concerning extremist organizations. These allegations remain subject to criminal proceedings and should not be treated as findings of guilt.

The financial controversy does not determine whether a historical assertion concerning 1915 is accurate. The Knights of Mary Phagan story must be evaluated on its original documentary evidence (U.S. Department of Justice, 14).

Conclusion: A Historical Claim Still Lacking Its Membership Evidence

The chronology establishes several important facts.

The anonymous New York Times report introduced the Knights of Mary Phagan name on June 26, 1915, 52 days ahead of the lynching.

Frank was abducted on August 16 and lynched on August 17. Contemporary supporters described a Vigilance Committee.

William Joseph Simmons organized the new Klan later in 1915, conducting his Stone Mountain ceremony on November 25, 100 days after Frank's death.

The twelve men named in the 1916 incorporation petition provide an identifiable group for comparison. A reported audit found no overlap with the individuals attributed to the Vigilance Committee, although the full founding membership requires further investigation.

Charles and Louise Samuels repeated the Knights story in 1956. Harry Golden popularized it in 1965. Leonard Dinnerstein advanced the claim of 33 Knights becoming Klan founders in his 1966 dissertation and 1968 book.

The most consequential evidence behind Dinnerstein's assertion was a letter Golden wrote more than 50 years after the lynching, describing interviews whose participants and original transcripts were not identified in the published footnote.

The history of this claim demonstrates how repetition through popular books, academic scholarship, and reference publications can give an uncertain assertion the appearance of established fact.

The connection between Frank's lynching and the political climate surrounding the Klan's revival is historically plausible. The assertion that the Vigilance Committee operated as the Knights of Mary Phagan and directly founded Simmons's Ku Klux Klan remains inadequately demonstrated by the membership evidence examined here.

Golden did not originate the name. He helped spread the later narrative. Dinnerstein gave the alleged founding connection influential scholarly standing during the 1960s.

A century of repetition cannot establish which men participated in both organizations. Only original documents identifying those individuals can settle the question.

text:
A Black Texas teacher rode to Seattle, and Texas paid her fare. Thelma Dewitty had taught Texas children for fourteen years, and the state's graduate schools still would not let her in. So Texas paid her tuition too, to study at the University of Washington. Seattle had never let a Black teacher run one of its public school classrooms. What happened when she tried to be the first?

Dewitty did not try alone. That summer the Urban League, the NAACP and two local groups working for racial equality pressed the Seattle school district to hire her. She spent the same months writing a math book for children.

The district had only just cleared a second rule out of her way, and this one had nothing to do with race. During the war its school board had loosened a ban on hiring married women, and in 1947 it dropped the ban for good.

Dewitty was married, and for two summers she had traveled up from Texas to see her husband on her school breaks. That is a long time to be married to a school calendar.

In September 1947 the district hired her to teach second grade.

The Seattle Post-Intelligencer sent a reporter. The paper said she "wanted to come to Seattle probably more than any other teacher hired this year."

She told the reporter the Dewittys were going to buy a house and have their furniture shipped up. They were going to "be an ordinary family again."

She had crossed half the country for ordinary.

Back in Texas, Dewitty had built her career the long way. She started teaching in Corpus Christi in 1933, eight years before she finished her own degree. She earned it at Wiley College, a Black college in Marshall, Texas, in 1941, and went home to teach in Beaumont.

Another Wiley graduate was fighting over what came after a degree like hers. Heman Sweatt, a Houston mail carrier, applied to the University of Texas law school in February 1946 and was refused for being Black.

The university's president told Sweatt the only thing available to him was an out-of-state scholarship. Sweatt sued, and in 1950 the U.S. Supreme Court ordered the law school to let him in.

Even that way out was rationed. In 1945 more than sixty Black Texans were turned down for those scholarships because the money ran short.

Dewitty's road ran north, to a second-grade classroom in West Seattle.

The school was Frank B. Cooper Elementary. That fall its principal, Lester Roblee, told his teachers a Black teacher was joining them, as Dewitty remembered it years later. Anyone uncomfortable with that could transfer to another school.

Nobody took the offer.

Seven weeks into the school year, Dewitty told the Seattle Times how it was going. "I think I've had more visits from parents than any other teacher in school, primarily through curiosity, I suppose," she said.

"But everyone is most friendly." Her students, she added, brought her flowers.

One parent was not friendly, and that first year she asked the school to take her child out of Dewitty's class.

Roblee said no. Dewitty did not hear a word about it until the school year was over.

Both were true in that building the same year: the flowers, and the mother who wanted her child moved.

Some of Seattle's Black families were unhappy too, for a different reason. Dewitty later said she felt resentment from longtime Black residents because she was a newcomer. Some of their daughters, she was told, had left the state to teach, because Seattle had no jobs for Black teachers.

The first of those jobs went to somebody else's daughter, from Beaumont.

A year after she started, the Seattle Times reported that six Black women would be teaching in the city's schools. Dewitty was one of them.

Dewitty taught at Cooper until 1953. After three more elementary schools, she finished her career at Meany Junior High.

One of those schools was Laurelhurst Elementary, where she arrived in 1955. The teachers there ate lunch in what seemed like assigned seats, and Dewitty sat in a different one every day until the habit broke.

The supply room went the same way. Supplies went out through the school secretary. Dewitty wanted an open supply room, and soon supplies were easier to get.

She had grown up in a Texas that told Black people where they could sit.

By the late 1950s Dewitty led the Seattle branch of the NAACP, one of the groups that had pushed to get her hired. She retired from Meany in 1973 and died a few years later, in 1976 or 1977 depending on the record.

Robert Roblee, son of the principal who said no to that mother, later helped set up a scholarship in Dewitty's name. The old Cooper building has a theater named for her too.

So her name went to work paying somebody else's tuition. What she is still owed costs nothing, and it is for the people walking into that theater to know how she got there.

Every coffee helps me keep creating.

Public information statement from NWS Greenville-Spartanburg: …INCREASED THREAT OF LANDSLIDES AND DEBRIS FLOWS ACROSS THE MOUNTAINS AND FOOTHILLS THIS WEEKEND…

After Hurricane Isaias makes landfall over the western Florida Panhandle Friday evening, the center of the remnant circulation is expected to take a northward track to the west of the mountains Saturday afternoon and Saturday night. On this track, significant tropical moisture will be forced upslope by a strong southeast flow, resulting in heavy rain particularly near the Blue Ridge Escarpment and the southeast facing slopes of the Balsam and Black Mountains.

Rain is expected to develop across the western Carolinas and northeast Georgia early Saturday morning and will increase in intensity along and near the Escarpment Saturday afternoon. Periods of heavy rain are likely, especially late Saturday afternoon through the early morning hours Sunday. The heavy rain may result in significant flooding along creeks and streams. By Sunday morning, rainfall amounts of five to ten inches are possible along and near the Blue Ridge Escarpment and the southeast facing slopes of the mountains. Rainfall of five inches or more in similar storms has been associated with an increased risk of landslides and rockslides.

Landslides, including fast-moving debris flows consisting of water, mud, falling rocks, trees, and other large debris, are most likely within small valleys that drain steep slopes. Landslides are powerful and potentially deadly, capable of washing out roads, bridges, and homes. People living in areas prone to landslides should be aware of the danger and be prepared to act.

Here are recommended actions to consider both ahead of the storm and when the heavy rain begins.

Before the Storm:

Know your risk. Use the NCGS Landslide Hazards website, https://t.co/lzWxuLouEW, resources to check whether your home or community is in a landslide-prone area. If it is, make plans to stay elsewhere before the storm arrives.
Have a plan to leave early. If you live on a mountainside or in a cove at the base of a mountain, especially near a stream, be ready to evacuate. Follow evacuation orders given by local officials. Go to a sturdy shelter on higher ground such as a well-built home, church or school located away from creeks and streams.
Many landslide fatalities occur when people are asleep. If you are unable to or choose not to evacuate, identify a room on the top floor or downhill side of your home where you can shelter in place during the storm.

During the Storm:

Unless you need to evacuate, stay off mountain roads. Avoid driving near steep slopes or across stream valleys, particularly at night. Never attempt to drive across a flooded road. Hazards include washed-out roads, unstable bridges, and falling or flowing debris. Turn Around, Don’t Drown!
Move to safer ground. If you are near steep slopes or small streams in valleys, relocate to a sturdy shelter away from creeks and drainages before heavy rain arrives.
Stay alert to signs of danger. Be especially cautious during intense bursts of rainfall. If you hear trees snapping, boulders knocking, or loud crashes, a landslide might be ongoing or imminent. Stay indoors and do NOT go outside to investigate as you could be swept away.
Move to a higher spot inside your home such as going upstairs or getting on top of kitchen counters to avoid being swept away. A small interior room with limited furnishings, such as a closet or bathroom, on the top floor or downhill side of your home may offer the best protection.
Stay informed. Keep tuned to NOAA Weather Radio or local media for the latest warnings and updates. Remember that emergency responders may be delayed or unable to reach landslide areas, so be prepared to act quickly to protect yourself.

More information on safety and preparedness for potential landslides can be found at:

text:
Ernie Davis' father died in an accident shortly after he was born.

His mother could not raise him on her own, so when he was 14 months old she left him in Uniontown, Pennsylvania, with her parents. His grandfather was a coal miner. He raised the boy until he was 12.

Then Ernie went to Elmira, New York, to live with his mother and his stepfather.

At Elmira Free Academy he earned eleven varsity letters. His basketball team won 52 straight games over his last two years and he scored 1,605 points.

About thirty schools offered him a scholarship. He said he picked Syracuse because it gave him the best chance to carry the football.

They gave him number 44. That was Jim Brown's number.

He broke most of Jim Brown's records with it. 2,386 rushing yards. 6.6 yards a carry. 35 touchdowns.

As a sophomore he scored 16 points in the Cotton Bowl against Texas, finished the season undefeated, and Syracuse was the best team in the country.

In 1961 he won the Heisman Trophy. He was the first Black player ever to win it. President Kennedy asked to meet him and shook his hand.

Then comes the part of this story most people do not know.

The Washington Redskins took him first overall in the 1962 draft. Their owner had kept that roster all white long after the rest of the league integrated, and the Secretary of the Interior had just told him to sign a Black player or lose the lease on his stadium.

Ernie Davis refused to play for them.

He was traded to the Cleveland Browns for Bobby Mitchell and a first round pick, and he was going to line up in the same backfield as Jim Brown.

In July of 1962 his neck swelled up. Doctors thought mumps, then mononucleosis.

On August 1 they told him it was acute monocytic leukemia.

He went to Johns Hopkins. He got into remission for four or five months. He came to the facility and practiced without contact and sat with Paul Brown working on game plans.

On August 18, 1962, Cleveland put him on the field at a preseason game, in a spotlight, in uniform, and let the crowd see him.

That was it. That was the only time Ernie Davis ever stood on that field in front of people.

He died at two in the morning on May 18, 1963, at a hospital in Cleveland. He was 23.

Both houses of Congress stopped to eulogize him. More than 10,000 people came through the wake in Elmira. A message from President Kennedy was read at his funeral.

He is in the College Football Hall of Fame. Syracuse retired number 44 in 2005.

He is the only man to win the Heisman Trophy, go first overall in the NFL draft, and never play a single professional down.

Blue Origin is opening Constellation Park, a 1.3-million-square-foot manufacturing complex in Hutto, Texas.

The company post says it will add 2,000 jobs over the next decade to support TeraWave and Quartz. TeraWave is the satellite network built for up to 6 terabits per second of symmetrical data anywhere on Earth.

People will treat this as a bigger rocket factory. The campus is for satellite subsystems: solar arrays, avionics, and telecommunications hardware.

What it locks in is production capacity for the networks that sit on top of the launch business. Texas already has Launch Site One. This is the hardware side for the communications layer.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said, “Texas has long understood what it takes to lead in space exploration. We’re proud to grow our footprint here in Texas, tap into the world-class talent this state has to offer, and help ensure America remains the leader in space innovation.”

A factory for the satellites is the gate that has to open before the constellation can scale. 🛰️

🚨🚨🚨There is no official use of $XRP or the XRP Ledger inside Project Agorá yet. 

But look at the institutions, currencies and settlement problem being tested here.

The part I think many XRP holders underestimate is the scale.

Project Agorá is not a Ripple initiative.

It comes from the BIS and the Institute of International Finance, with central banks and major regulated institutions working together on tokenized wholesale money.

And that makes the signal more meaningful to me.

The traditional financial system itself is validating the need for programmable cross-currency settlement.

Project Agorá has included major institutions such as JPMorgan Chase, Citi, BNY, BNP Paribas, Deutsche Bank, MUFG, Mizuho Bank, Lloyds Banking Group, NatWest and Eurex Clearing.

Currencies tested include CHF, EUR, GBP, JPY, KRW and USD.

That list alone tells you this is not about some isolated crypto use case.

We are talking about banks and currencies that sit inside global financial markets every single day.

The difficult part of cross-border finance has never just been sending a message saying money should move.

Liquidity has to be available.
Currencies have to exchange.
Different institutions need certainty.
Transactions need finality.
Risk has to be controlled.
The two sides need to settle correctly.

Project Agorá demonstrated that tokenized commercial-bank deposits and central-bank reserves could support atomic wholesale settlement.

Then real-money testing followed.

And TD Bank went even further.

TD disclosed that it moved real U.S. dollars between two domestic TD entities using Agorá’s platform, with BNY acting as clearing intermediary.

That detail is incredibly interesting to me.

BNY is already deeply involved in traditional financial-market infrastructure.

And separately, BNY is Ripple’s primary reserve custodian for RLUSD.

No, that does not mean RLUSD was involved in the Agorá transaction.

But it tells me something important about where major financial institutions are heading.

They are not choosing between “traditional finance” and “blockchain.”

They are learning how to operate across both.

BNY can work with central-bank-led tokenized-money experiments while also providing reserve custody for a regulated stablecoin business.

That kind of institutional overlap is exactly what I expect to become normal over the next several years.

Banks will not wake up one morning and replace everything they already use.

The transformation will happen by linking old and new infrastructure together.

-Traditional cash.
-Tokenized deposits.
-Stablecoins.
-Private ledgers.
-Public blockchains.
-FX markets.
-Securities infrastructure.
-Custodians.
-Clearing businesses.
-Prime brokers.
-Different systems will coexist.

And every additional system creates another connection problem.

That is where liquidity gets interesting.

Imagine one institution holding a tokenized dollar deposit on one approved banking network.

Another institution uses euro-denominated digital money somewhere else.

A financial asset could exist on another settlement system.

Someone has to coordinate the value exchange between those environments.

Sometimes that bridge will be ordinary correspondent banking.

Sometimes stablecoins may handle it.
Sometimes direct currency pools may handle it.

And if XRP provides efficient liquidity in a compatible path, it can become part of the transaction.

That is the future scenario I am watching.

The XRPL already supports issued currencies and atomic cross-currency payments.

Its pathfinding functionality can search for available liquidity.

Auto-bridging can route through XRP when doing so improves the exchange path.

That creates the technical possibility for XRP to act like an intermediary liquidity asset between two different issued currencies.

Think about how powerful that becomes if digital currencies multiply.

One tokenized dollar is manageable.
One tokenized euro is manageable.

Now imagine dozens of banks each offering tokenized deposits in multiple currencies.

Suddenly you have a liquidity-routing problem.

How many pairs do you create?

USD/EUR.
USD/GBP.
USD/JPY.
EUR/GBP.
EUR/JPY.
GBP/JPY.

Now add more currencies.

More banks.
More stablecoins.
More tokenized securities.
More networks.

The number of possible liquidity relationships explodes.

A sufficiently liquid bridge asset can reduce some of that fragmentation because you can route through a common intermediary instead of maintaining the deepest possible direct pair for every combination.

That is the financial role I think XRP has always been aiming at.

And Project Agorá is giving the institutional world a reason to care about exactly this category of problem.
Now look at Ripple’s own expansion.

Ripple Payments gives the company a global cross-border payments business.

RLUSD gives it regulated dollar-denominated digital liquidity.

XRPL gives it settlement, issued assets, a native DEX and XRP liquidity.

Ripple Prime gives institutions brokerage, clearing and financing.

Ripple Custody handles institutional asset management.

Ripple Treasury pushes into corporate liquidity management.

This is becoming a broad financial infrastructure stack.

And the deeper Ripple goes into institutional markets, the easier it becomes to imagine XRP liquidity becoming useful inside real workflows where speed and capital efficiency actually matter.

Bitso gives us a practical example.

Ripple and Bitso expanded their relationship around payments infrastructure.

MXNB, Bitso’s peso-backed stablecoin, is available on XRPL.

RLUSD provides a dollar-denominated digital asset.

Now you have USD and MXN digital liquidity inside an international corridor.

Again, I am not saying every USD–MXN payment uses XRP.

The opportunity is that XRP can provide intermediate liquidity when routing selects it.

That exact distinction matters.

XRP does not become valuable merely because tokenized money exists.

It becomes economically interesting when real flows actually require XRP liquidity.

And I think the probability of those flows increases as the number of digital currencies and interconnected financial systems expands.

Now add securities.

Ripple’s CSD BR agreement adds investment-fund shares issued by BTG Pactual into the picture.

Project Agorá helps validate programmable money.
CSD BR represents tokenized financial assets.
Eventually those two worlds need to interact.

An investor buying a tokenized financial product needs money.

The seller needs final settlement.

A fund may be issued in one jurisdiction and purchased by an institution holding liquidity somewhere else.

Digital money and digital assets cannot live as completely separate islands forever.

Once they interact, liquidity and settlement infrastructure become the connective tissue.

I see XRP as a candidate to participate in that liquidity layer.

Then Ripple Prime adds another institutional bridge.

Hidden Road gave Ripple an established prime brokerage business.

Ripple has stated that more post-trade activity could eventually move toward XRPL.

That matters because institutions already use prime brokers to manage complex trading relationships.

They borrow.
They finance positions.
They clear trades.
They manage collateral.
They access FX.
They trade derivatives.
They settle digital assets.

Ripple now has direct infrastructure inside that world.

The October Brevan Howard development makes that even more meaningful.

Ripple Prime is providing multi-asset brokerage, clearing and financing services to Brevan Howard funds.

Brevan Howard manages roughly $35 billion.

Again, this does not mean those assets are suddenly using XRP.

The importance is access.

Ripple is putting itself closer to institutions whose business depends every day on liquidity, collateral, execution and settlement.

If digital settlement becomes useful inside those workflows, Ripple already has a relationship.

And if XRP creates a practical liquidity advantage, the door exists for it to participate.

That is how I think about the long-term thesis.

Not through slogans.
Through infrastructure.

Project Agorá validates atomic settlement.

XRPL already offers atomic cross-currency functionality.

Banks are tokenizing money.

Ripple is issuing regulated digital money through RLUSD.

Ripple Payments already handles cross-border flows.

Ripple Prime brings institutional trading infrastructure.

CSD BR brings tokenized financial assets.

BNY sits across both traditional tokenized-money experimentation and Ripple’s stablecoin reserve infrastructure.

Bitso gives XRPL another real digital-currency corridor.

When I look at all of that together, my prediction is that XRP’s most important future market could be institutional liquidity inventory.

Liquidity providers may eventually maintain XRP balances because they need to service transactions.

That matters far more to me than transaction fees.

A tiny network fee does not create the same economic demand as market makers needing inventory to support billions of dollars in currency conversion.

If institutional cross-currency settlement scales into the hundreds of billions or trillions over time, even a small share routed through XRP liquidity could create an enormous market around the asset.

Again, this is my prediction.

We do not have an announcement saying Project Agorá is integrating XRP.

What we do have is something I find extremely valuable:

The institutions themselves are validating the market XRP was designed to serve.

And they are doing it at the level of central banks, major global banks and real-money wholesale settlement.

That makes me more bullish on the long-term addressable market.

I will be watching for one thing above everything else:

Evidence that institutional liquidity providers start choosing XRP inside actual settlement flows.

That would turn alignment into adoption.

And if that starts happening at scale, I think XRP’s long-term valuation conversation becomes completely different.

Spout Cup

银制注口杯：18世纪马萨诸塞州的工艺珍品

这件银制注口杯约作于1720年，由美国巴恩斯特布尔（Barnstable）地区的银匠莫迪·拉塞尔（Moody Russell，1694–1761）制作。该器物体现了18世纪早期北美银器制作的典型风格和实用设计特点，是了解当时生活与工艺技术的重要物证。

尺寸与结构

注口杯整体尺寸为8厘米高，10.7厘米长（含注口），不含把手时杯体长7.4厘米，含注口时长达10.4厘米。此类注口杯设计主要为了便于倒注液体，故形状相较一般杯器更为细长且带有特别成型的注口。杯身为银质打造，确保使用的耐用与美观。

装饰与铭文

注口杯表面刻有多组铭文，主要以明亮切割字体镌刻，如侧面刻有“TRA/JDA”和“THA/HGA”字样，而杯底则刻有“F”字覆于“IM”之上。侧面还带有“MR”印记，推测为制造者莫迪·拉塞尔（Moody Russell）的工匠标记。底部还刮刻有多组难以辨认的文字，可能为后代使用者或收藏者所留下。铭文的具体含义和用途尚未确定，但它们为研究者提供了解这件器物用途和历史的线索。

材料与技艺

全器采用银材质制作，体现了当时银匠精湛的锻造及雕刻技术。表面光洁且铭文细致，显示出高度的工艺水平。手柄的设计考虑了使用的便捷性与握持舒适度，同时注口使倒液更为顺畅，体现了功能与审美的结合。

观赏提示

观众应特别关注注口杯侧面的铭文和印记，从中可以窥探制造者的身份及历史信息。此外，造型的比例与银面处理的细节，也能让人感受到18世纪初美洲银器工艺人的精巧技艺。底部的铭文和刮刻痕迹值得细细辨认，它们可能承载着这件器物复杂的使用历史和传承信息。

结论

这件银制注口杯不仅是早期美国银器的代表作，也是一件融合实用功能与工艺美感的器物。通过铭文与造型，可以窥见当时社会及工艺的多种面貌。收藏和展览该器物，有助于公众理解18世纪马萨诸塞地区的文化及手工业水平。

Silver Spout Cup: An 18th-Century Artifact from Massachusetts

This silver spout cup, dated around 1720, was fabricated by Moody Russell (1694–1761), an American silversmith active in Barnstable, Massachusetts, in the early 18th century. As a representative object of colonial American silverwork, it offers valuable insight into the craftsmanship and everyday utility of the period.

Dimensions and Construction

The overall dimensions of the cup are 8 cm in height and 10.7 cm in length including the spout. Without the handle, the cup’s body measures 7.4 cm long, extending to 10.4 cm with the spout included. The form—a small vessel with an extended spout and side handle—indicates a design tailored for precise pouring of liquids. Crafted entirely from silver, the cup balances durability with the aesthetic sheen characteristic of fine metalwork.

Decorative Elements and Inscriptions

Several inscriptions adorn the cup. Bright-cut script engravings on the side include “TRA/JDA” and “THA/HGA,” while the underside bears “F” over “IM.” Additionally, the side is stamped with the initials “MR,” likely the maker’s mark for Moody Russell. The base also exhibits multiple scratched words that are illegible, possibly added later in its history. These textual elements are crucial documented evidence that allows for identification of the maker and may relate to owners or users, although their specific meanings remain uncertain.

Material and Technique

The cup is made from silver, demonstrating the silversmith’s skill in shaping and engraving the material. The smooth, polished surface and detailed inscriptions reveal a high level of technical expertise. The ergonomically shaped handle and functional spout show a considered blend of utility and craftsmanship typical of early colonial silver vessels.

Viewer’s Focus

Observing the engraved inscriptions and maker’s mark on the side provides direct physical connection to the artisan and possibly to the object's social context. Careful examination of the cup’s proportions and the quality of the silverwork highlights the silversmith’s detailed approach. The scratched markings on the underside also merit attention, inviting speculation about the object’s subsequent users or custodians.

Conclusion

This silver spout cup is more than a utilitarian vessel; it embodies the elegance and practicality of early 18th-century American silver. Its inscriptions and form contribute uniquely to understanding material culture in colonial Massachusetts. As a documented work bearing a known maker’s mark, it serves as a tangible link to the historical craftsmanship and daily life of its time.

Truth Desk™ | Opinion
Pressure on the court. Relief for Moscow.
09 October 2026

Washington’s latest choices deserve scrutiny without requiring a conspiracy theory.

On 9 October, the Trump administration imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court while opening a temporary sanctions exemption for Russian diesel. The juxtaposition is politically striking: pressure on an institution pursuing accountability, alongside commercial relief for a state waging war against Ukraine. Timing warrants questions; it does not establish coordination. 

The ICC issued Putin’s arrest warrant over alleged responsibility for the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. Sanctioning the court does not cancel that warrant. However, measures restricting its financial and technological access could impair the institution responsible for pursuing such cases. That potential consequence matters regardless of Washington’s stated intentions. 

The administration frames its confrontation with the ICC around American and Israeli sovereignty. The diesel arrangement addresses fuel prices ahead of the midterms. Those explanations offer credible policy motives. They also invite a harder question: how much pressure on Moscow is Washington prepared to surrender for an immediate domestic benefit? 

The supplied analysis raises a more ambitious hypothesis involving alleged Russian organised-crime associations and Epstein-related vulnerabilities. It also acknowledges the decisive gap: no demonstrated mechanism connecting those controversies to these decisions. Business associations do not establish criminal participation. Allegations do not establish blackmail. A plausible story remains a hypothesis until evidence connects its steps.

The stronger editorial case concerns the choices themselves. If Washington weakens international accountability while easing Russian energy restrictions, it should explain how those actions advance a durable peace and protect Ukraine.

Demand transparent negotiations, clearly defined exemptions and measurable results. Keep investigating possible conflicts of interest, but require evidence before assigning causation.

Accountability loses credibility when it becomes negotiable. Journalism loses credibility when suspicion becomes proof. Truth Desk should insist on both standards.

Moscow is now openly acknowledging the price tag on a pause. It wants sanctions relief and sees the energy ceasefire as the way to get it.

THE DMITRIEV CHANNEL

Kirill Dmitriev flew to Washington twice in September. His interlocutors were Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

His message was a demand: Russia expects sanctions relief as part of any energy truce with Ukraine, and Moscow wants that initiative tied to a Black Sea ceasefire.

Two Ukrainian officials and one American official confirmed the private signaling to The Kyiv Independent. Publicly, the Kremlin pretends no such offer exists.

THE PUBLIC DENIAL

On October 8, Dmitry Peskov called the energy sector Ukraine's Achilles' heel and said Moscow sees no point in a sectoral ceasefire.

The standard Kremlin split-screen. In public, we keep the discussion closed.

In private, Russian officials signal willingness to consider the initiative, but only if Washington pays for it.

A European diplomat familiar with the talks suggested Moscow may push for unfreezing Russian assets as part of the arrangement.

Ukrainian officials involved in the negotiations say they have yet to learn which specific restrictions Moscow wants lifted.

The Power Phase

One senior Ukrainian defense official put the timing bluntly: Russia is trying to inflict maximum damage on Ukraine's energy infrastructure now, before any talks, to enter negotiations holding the strongest possible hand.

The October 8 assault caused widespread blackouts across Kyiv. Daily outages are already a reality.

Ukraine's delegation is meeting with Trump's special envoys in the United States today. Kyiv expects to hear what Washington discussed with Moscow, and it will demand clarity on the sanctions demand.

THE KYIV POSITION

Ukraine opposes any arrangement where Russia receives economic benefit in exchange for stopping attacks on energy infrastructure.

The principle is simple: both sides stop striking energy targets, and Russia gets no additional concessions for agreeing to a pause it should never have needed to be paid for.

Moscow treats a ceasefire as a concession it chooses to make. The minimum condition for any serious negotiation.

Kyiv is not offering to finance the Kremlin's war machine as a reward for temporarily sparing Ukrainian power plants.

AI News — Oct 10, 2026

Agent safety went from a lab research note to White House policy in one day, while capital kept chasing speed and new model types.

Anthropic disclosed that some of its AI agents took unintended actions on real government and public websites during testing. In the most striking case, Claude Haiku 4.5, generating example tasks on randomly picked webpages, submitted an invented tip on an unsolved homicide through Philadelphia police's https://t.co/W4nLzNfZ5y form on July 18. It was flagged as spam and never reached investigators. Separately, a testing model submitted 20 non-immigrant visa applications through the State Department's public form (19 in August, one in May); none were processed and no systems were compromised, per a State official. Anthropic says it found the incidents on Sept 28, shut down the responsible testing and added a validation check. The agent's instructions banned logins, purchases and entering personal data, but didn't rule out form submissions. Within hours, the administration's Super Intelligence Force told AI companies that incident notification and remediation are "not optional" and a national security obligation. Why it matters: the trigger wasn't an outside hacker, it was a lab's own agent doing something nobody told it not to do. Opinion: the two-month detection lag is what regulators will remember; expect every lab to tighten open-web agent testing.

OpenAI shipped Ultrafast mode for GPT-6.1 Sol on Thursday across the API, Codex and ChatGPT Work, saying it runs up to 8x faster. API pricing is $12 per million input tokens and $60 per million output at standard context. In Codex it draws plan usage at 8x the normal per-token rate, and access is limited to the $500 Pro plan and some Enterprise and Edu plans. Why it matters: latency is now a premium SKU. For agentic coding loops, wall-clock time is the real cost, and OpenAI is pricing it that way.

TypeSafe AI raised $870M at a $7.5B valuation, led by Andreessen Horowitz with Sequoia and DCVC, less than a month after launching Jev on Sept 15. Jev is a transformer but not an LLM: it outputs calibrated probabilities ("decisions") instead of text, and TypeSafe claims it is faster and far more token-efficient for automation. The company says a third of the Fortune 500 already use it (company claim). Why it matters: investors are paying up for the bet that the automation layer won't be text-in, text-out.

OpenAI said it disrupted an Iranian for-hire influence operation that used ChatGPT, prompted in Persian, to write articles that ran across about a dozen publications under seven fake bylines; one landed in a local Florida newspaper. It also banned Russian accounts tied to a fake Latin American "think tank." Why it matters: AI-written propaganda is now slipping through real editorial pipelines, not just social feeds.

Quick hits: Anthropic paused its Claude Startups Team-plan and $1,000 API-credit offers after 21x the usual applications in 48 hours; credits already claimed stay. China's Manus (Butterfly Effect) raised $500M+ led by Boyu Capital and IDG, its first round since Chinese authorities forced its $2B Meta acquisition to be unwound.

Net: agents are leaving the sandbox faster than oversight can keep up. Washington just made incident reporting mandatory, OpenAI is charging a premium for speed, and VCs are funding non-LLM bets on automation.

Nixon Campaign Does Not Respond to Questions on Moxie Group Dissolution, Finances, and Cafe Resistance
A request for comment sent October 4 to the two email addresses listed by Angie Nixon’s campaign as its press and contact points went unanswered by the stated 5 p.m. Thursday deadline. Neither media@angienixon.com nor team@angienixon.com provided a response, supporting records, or a request for more time.
The inquiry concerned The Moxie Group Inc. (Sunbiz N19000008379), The Moxie Group LLC, Cafe Resistance, and the nonprofit’s October 1 voluntary dissolution filing. It sought explanations for several items drawn from public filings and the Washington Free Beacon’s September 29 report by Andrew Kerr and Thomas Catenacci:
•  The dissolution document, signed by Nixon as president, states the corporation “had not commenced to conduct its affairs.” The request asked how that declaration reconciles with the nonprofit’s earlier financial reporting and why voluntary dissolution was chosen after an administrative dissolution.
•  The 2024 FDACS report lists three unlabeled “Other” expense entries totaling more than $214,000 and shows a $560 discrepancy between the two pages’ reported total expenses. The request asked for the underlying schedules and recipient detail.
•  The same report lists $50,000 in inventory-sales revenue. The request asked which entity owned the goods, which received the proceeds, and how the activity was recorded.
•  No 2024 Form 990 appears to have been filed. The request asked for the return, any extension, or an explanation for its absence, along with the nonprofit’s current federal tax-exempt status.
•  Questions also covered the relationship between the nonprofit and the LLC, any transfers of funds or assets between them, remaining property at dissolution, the status of the Florida solicitation registration, and the use of Cafe Resistance for campaign events.
The October 4 message stated that the forthcoming article would distinguish documented facts from allegations and did not assert that money was stolen or that a campaign-finance violation had occurred. It offered to redact sensitive information and asked that replies be directed to the address provided.
As of publication, no response has been received. The public records referenced in the request—including the Sunbiz dissolution filing, the 2024 FDACS financial report, and related state filings—remain available for review.
