text:
originally made it for people who are unknowingly putting themselves in harms way on @reddit 

Adding Fuel to a Fire You Think Cannot Reach You

I am posting this under the discussion flair, but I will try to explain my position as completely as I can. I am interested in questions about the heart of this thread.

There are superpowers and other major powers in this world: the USA, the UK, China, Russia, France, Germany, and a few other honourable mentions. If you, as an individual, go against the interests of such powers, the consequences depend a great deal on where you are.

If you are on the front lines, as in Ukraine, it does not matter which side you are on: the death toll is enormous. If you are untrained, wearing a uniform, and do not even understand why you are there, you are putting yourself in a situation that can get you killed.

If you do not understand this, I get it. People are usually knowledgeable about their own work—hopefully—and much less knowledgeable outside it. But confidence does not always follow that distinction.

People watch this as though it were a football match. It is not. You might point to what is happening in France, but you get the broader idea: watching a confrontation and living inside it are different things.

There are limits to how much I want to explain publicly. I have no interest in placing myself or my family on the front lines of a conflict we do not want to be part of. My purpose here is to explain where you may end up without understanding what you are getting involved in.

I see Reddit as a largely left-leaning platform. It can feel like a position behind the lines, where direct physical confrontation is distant. But distance is not the same as complete protection. A state with intelligence capabilities may obtain information it considers valuable, including through infiltration or purchasing access to data.

Now, about Iran.

Iran is a nation with a distinct culture and social structure. Jewish history in the region reaches back before Islam, and the Book of Esther offers one ancient perspective on danger and power at a Persian court. It can be read as a story about existential fear, power, and violent reversals of fortune. I am referring to those themes, not suggesting that Jewish people collectively follow some ancient recipe.

Our own Shahnameh—the Book of Kings—contains an equally bitter warning. An Iranian army marched to avenge Siyavash, yet ended up killing his own son, Forud. Think about that: on the road to avenging the father, they killed another of his sons. A righteous cause does not stop pride, suspicion, and revenge from destroying the very people it supposedly serves.

My reading of the anger in Iran is that many people are not simply willing to seek revenge; they are becoming eager for it. They are like a spring compressed to its limit. Like a wounded, cornered tiger whose cubs are in someone else’s hands.

For some, the suffering feels beyond comparison—even with historical atrocities such as the Holocaust. You may want to argue about that comparison. I am describing the intensity of their perception, not establishing a historical ranking of suffering.

Consider the Mongol invasion and the devastation it brought to Iran. Yet there are Iranians who describe the Islamic Republic as the worst thing ever to happen to their country. That tells you something about how they experience the present.

I see a generation of young people ready for confrontation. In my view, a soft war has been going on for years, gradually shaping attitudes and bringing us to this point. What has happened cannot simply be undone.

You may discuss morality from wherever you feel comfortable. Inside a war, those moral boundaries can be violated every day. That does not make those violations right. It means that your expectations alone will not prevent them.

The people inside the government are not all the same, either. Some may believe in peaceful transitions or democratic change. Their motives need not be purely moral: they may also want themselves and their families to survive and have a future.

To me, the situation did not feel this bad three years ago. There are families, communities, and tribes for whom this has become a matter of defending their dignity. Many young people have come to associate the government primarily with repression and bloodshed.

Now I see a struggle to take hold of a giant and redirect it. The Islamic Republic was positioned against forces associated with the political right, including the adversary it is confronting. It has served interests and carried out actions over many years. But allegiances and ideologies can change when power is at stake.

The most important thing to understand about my argument is this: I fear there will be bloodshed in Iran again and again until the underlying conflict is resolved.

Where are the people supposed to go? Is an entire country—roughly 90 million people—supposed to migrate to Europe? They must be able to live in their own country. In my assessment, coexistence between this system and those who reject it has become impossible in its present form.

Now imagine being a Jewish person directly threatened by the Islamic Republic. If you have never lived under that particular threat, you cannot assume that you know what it feels like or how you would react. The same applies to Iranians living under threats that distant observers discuss as abstractions. We are all human beings, but we do not all experience the same dangers.

I turned down joining the Iranian government because I did not believe in aspects of what it stood for and did not believe it would succeed. Looking back, I can imagine the other path: participating in that system and securing a comfortable life for my family, even if it eventually ended badly for me.

I personally have moral values, and what I write on Reddit is bounded by them. But I can understand why some people might find power, privilege, and comfort for their families very appealing—even when those benefits come through serving a brutal system.

When I look at the privilege surrounding someone like Khamenei, I see the disturbing attraction of a system in which leaders can remain insulated from so much of the suffering associated with their decisions. Understanding that appeal does not mean approving of what they do. My point is that benefiting from repression and suffering under it are very different experiences.

I think about these things a great deal. Often, I feel that many people commenting on them have not thought through the consequences.

Does this situation favour Israel? In my assessment, very much so. But if you object to that, understand my argument: I do not see it as the product of one day’s work or a simple accident. There are long histories, strategic interests, and accumulated decisions behind the present situation. That does not mean every event was planned or controlled.

Ideologies change. Power is contested. This is a struggle for power, not a football match.

My fear is that this war is only beginning. If you have the choice to remain outside the violence, think carefully before giving that up. Many Iranians do not feel they have that choice. When I say they feel they must “finish the job,” I mean they believe they must bring the conflict with the system ruling them to a decisive resolution. I am not saying that everyone associated with that system is a legitimate target.

You may disagree with my assessment that their options have narrowed this far. But arguing that people should not feel trapped does not make their anger disappear.

If you get involved without understanding the stakes, you may discover that the destination is a ditch on the cold Pontic steppe. There may come a time in our own lives when we no longer have a choice, either. I have tried to avoid that situation. I am Iranian, and protecting my family matters to me.

There is a saying I associate with Abu Sa’id Abul-Khayr, which I would paraphrase this way: wisdom includes not allowing yourself to be drawn into a conflict you never intended to join.

This warning is aimed at people who speak casually from safety, adding fuel to the fire and making already angry people angrier while assuming they will remain untouched by the consequences.

Once people begin seeing everything through revenge, anyone who disagrees is in enemy colours. Anyone who hesitates is in enemy colours. Anyone who happens to stand on the wrong side of a line is in enemy colours.

In that mindset, people stop asking whether someone is uninformed, confused, or simply uninvolved. They see a threat. That is the danger I am trying to explain: individuals disappear behind labels, and even someone like Forud becomes a target.

I am not declaring people my enemies. I have no wish to join a camp in this conflict. My personal priorities are already clear: my family, our safety, and our life.

And to well-informed leftists: you already know you should do everything you can to protect your life and the lives of those you love. Apply that same seriousness to the people whose lives you discuss online. Before encouraging confrontation, understand who will actually bear its consequences—and whether you would still consider it worthwhile if that person were you.

If you can remain outside the violence, understand the value of that position. Do not mistake your distance from the fire for proof that adding fuel is harmless.

text:
Kautilya explained much of this over 2,000 years ago in the Arthashastra, particularly through his Mandala Theory, which views international relations as a continuous struggle among competing powers.

At the centre of this system is the Vijigishu, the ruler seeking to expand his power. Every neighbouring kingdom, ally, enemy and neutral state is assessed in terms of its relative strength and strategic usefulness. Alliances are not permanent, and neither are rivalries. What matters is the balance of power.

Kautilya also identifies three conditions of a state:

Vriddhi: Growth and increasing power.
Sthana: Stability and maintaining one’s position.
Kshaya: Decline and loss of power.

His argument is that a ruler must continually seek to move from decline to stability and from stability to growth. But growth is relative. Even if you maintain your existing territory and influence, a rival growing faster than you can eventually undermine your position.

Whenever one power weakens or retreats, another has an incentive to fill the space.

He also understood that military dominance alone cannot sustain an empire. Control over productive land, mines, forests, commercial routes, taxation, economic activity and a prosperous population provides the material foundation of power.

However, Kautilya makes an important distinction between expanding an empire and strengthening an empire.

He identifies six instruments of foreign policy: peace, war, neutrality, military mobilisation, seeking protection or alliance, and pursuing peace with one power while confronting another.

The objective is not endless territorial conquest but continuously improving one’s strategic position. He even argues that when peace and war offer comparable advantages, peace is preferable because warfare consumes wealth and strength.

This is where the contradiction of imperial expansion emerges.

An empire requires sufficient economic and military strength to maintain its dominance. Expansion can increase that strength, but every additional conquest also introduces administrative costs, military commitments and potential resistance.

Eventually, the cost of maintaining dominance may exceed the economic advantages derived from it. The very expansion that once strengthened the empire can become the source of its decline.

And that decline creates opportunities for competing powers, restarting the struggle for influence and control.

So I think Kautilya would largely recognise the cycle you’re describing, although the modern mechanism of exporting inflation through monetary dominance is separate from his framework.

His central insight is that power must continually be cultivated, but expansion without the economic capacity to sustain it ultimately weakens the empire.

An empire does not necessarily decline because it stops expanding. It can decline because it has expanded beyond what it can afford to govern, defend and maintain.

text:
Weekend Agriculture
Publishing Date: October 10, 2026

As mid October arrives across the nation's midsection, the 2026 row crop harvest is charging toward its peak. The USDA's latest Crop Progress report confirmed that national corn harvest leaped to 30% complete, holding steady ahead of the five year average of 27%, while soybean harvest surged to 43% complete nationwide, outpacing the 37% historical norm. Uninterrupted autumn breezes and warm temperatures across the Western Plains and Corn Belt allowed combines to make rapid progress, while fields across the Eastern Corn Belt dried down to support heavy fieldwork.

Grain and livestock boards closed Friday's session with active position squaring ahead of next week's October WASDE and Crop Production reports. Active CME contracts across corn and soybeans saw two way trade as harvest pressure countered solid foreign export interest. In livestock country, live cattle and feeder futures held firm, backed by tight fed cattle inventories and steady cash feedlot bids, while lean hog values traded near unchanged levels into the weekend.

USDA AND POLICY DIGEST

The grain trade spent the week processing USDA Crop Progress metrics alongside early harvest yield reports, as combine activity accelerates across primary production belts:

National corn maturity reached 87% complete, tracking ahead of the five year average of 83%. Condition ratings held steady at 58% good to excellent (45% good, 13% excellent), with 30% harvested nationally across reporting states.

Soybean maturity advanced rapidly, with 89% of the national crop dropping leaves (ahead of the 85% five year average). Crop condition ratings held firm at 58% good to excellent (46% good, 12% excellent). National soybean harvest reached 43% complete, driven by rapid cutting across Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, and the Delta.

Winter wheat seeding for the 2027 crop advanced to 51% complete nationally, matching historical averages, while emergence reached 25%. Producers across the Southern Plains welcomed recent topsoil moisture, though subsoil moisture deficits persist across dry western seedbeds.

On the policy and trade front, market participants actively monitored Mississippi River water levels and gulf export terminal logistics ahead of peak October shipping windows. Private export reporting channels remained active, confirming continuous sales of new crop soybeans to China and unknown destinations alongside steady corn movement to Latin America.

WEATHER, SOIL AND FIELD REALITY

Field conditions over the past week provided exceptional harvesting windows across primary growing regions:

In the Western Corn Belt and Plains, warm, dry weather allowed operators across Nebraska, Kansas, and South Dakota to push dryland harvest toward advanced stages. Rapid crop dry down allowed farmers to minimize on farm drying costs, though dry topsoils continue to complicate fall tillage passes.

In the Central Corn Belt, clear skies allowed field work across Iowa, Illinois, Minnesota, and Indiana to run at full capacity. Iowa soybean harvest made major gains, passing the halfway mark as field trafficability remained excellent on heavy soils.

In the Delta and Southeast, dry harvesting conditions allowed growers to finalize soybean, cotton, and rice harvesting while turning attention to fall field prep.

Across regional production zones:

In the Western Plains, field managers focused on managing grain drying setups and coordinating elevator delivery logistics as harvest volume peaks.

In the Central Corn Belt, producers prioritized harvesting fields with lodging concerns or weakened stalk strength caused by earlier wind events.

In the Northern Plains, custom harvest crews made rapid progress through dryland soybean and sunflower fields.

In the Southern Plains, winter wheat drilling gained momentum as operators evaluated soil moisture availability across fall seedbeds.

MARKET AND BOARD REVIEW

CME Group futures closed Friday's session with steady positioning across grain, oilseed, and livestock markets as traders prepared for upcoming USDA reports.

Friday CME closing settlements settled around these core baselines:

December CME Corn Futures (/ZCZ26): Settled Friday at $4.98 1/2 per bushel, holding firm near the $4.95 to $5.00 mark as harvest pressure was offset by export interest.

November CME Soybean Futures (/SX26): Settled Friday at $12.95 per bushel, finding steady support near the $12.90 to $13.00 level on continuous export flash sales and strong domestic crush demand.

December CME Wheat Futures (/ZWZ26): Settled Friday near $5.68 per bushel, balancing active U.S. winter wheat seeding progress against global export trade headlines.

December CME Live Cattle Futures (/LCZ26): Settled Friday at $222.85 per hundredweight, underpinned by tight fed cattle supplies and steady cash feedlot trade.
November CME Feeder Cattle Futures (/FCX26): Settled Friday near $332.80 per hundredweight, while October Lean Hogs settled near 78.40 cents per pound.

Cash grain prices across the Corn Belt reflected firm processor bids against heavy harvest throughput:

Corn Belt Cash Corn Bids: Country elevator bids posted between $4.68 and $4.88 per bushel, with interior country basis averaging 15 cents to 30 cents under the December contract. Ethanol processing facilities offered competitive local bids ranging from $4.92 to $5.08 per bushel.

Corn Belt Cash Soybean Bids: Country elevator bids ranged from $12.28 to $12.68 per bushel, while major crushing plants held firm bids near $12.82 to $13.12 per bushel to secure harvest deliveries.

Corn Belt Cash Wheat Bids: Country bids across winter wheat zones held firm between $5.38 and $6.02 per bushel, with basis holding steady on milling quality.

In livestock markets, cash fed steer prices traded with firm footing near $234.00 to $236.00 per hundredweight live in Northern feedlots, supported by light market ready numbers, while Choice boxed beef cutouts held near $356.80 per hundredweight.

TECHNICAL SPOTLIGHT, HISTORY AND HOMESTEAD

In agricultural technology, broader deployment of automated yield map normalization and cloud based combine telemetry gave farm managers real time insights into field level yield variances. By automatically cross referencing spatial yield data with soil moisture maps, operators are quantifying the exact yield impact of late summer moisture deficits versus well drained bottomland soils.

Looking back at historical milestones, mid October marks the mid 20th century widespread transition to high capacity self propelled combine harvesters and grain carts across the Corn Belt. By eliminating manual ear corn handling and hand shoveling, early mechanical harvest systems reduced farm labor requirements by over 70%, setting the stage for modern high speed grain logistics.

On the homestead and in the field:
Fall Pasture Strategy: Livestock managers monitored cool season grass regrowth following recent rain, managing stocking rates to prevent overgrazing before dormant winter periods.

Fix It Corner: Active harvest machinery maintenance remains critical, check combine concaves and rotor clearance settings, inspect auger flighting for razor edges, monitor grain cart tire pressures, and ensure bin aeration fans run during cool night hours.

Producer Voice: "The weather held up great this week and the beans are rolling in fast, yields are holding up well on the good ground."

Country Saying: "A dry August eats the profit that a wet July built."

Heard About the Super Godzilla Monster El Niño? Here’s How It Could Actually Affect You.

By Judson Jones
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/v4obMfGLWe
Judson Jones is a meteorologist and reporter for The Times.
09SEP2026
Leer en español
Yes, El Niño is unusually powerful this time. But that’s not always a bad thing.

It was raining. That was what first startled Alyssa Atwood when she stepped off the plane on Christmas Island in August.

Torrential downpours had already turned the dirt roads into impassable waterways, leaving her research team questioning whether their trucks could even reach their lodge.

When she finally waded into the Pacific Ocean, it wasn’t quite as she remembered it.

“You almost don’t want to wear a wet suit, it’s so hot,” said Dr. Atwood, a paleoclimate scientist at Florida State University who recently returned from the island, a remote coral atoll that sits in the Central Pacific at the geographical bull’s-eye of El Niño.

The typical winter peak of El Niño is months away. Yet on Christmas Island, also known as Kiritimati, the ocean was already at least two degrees warmer than average, hovering between 30 and 30.5 degrees Celsius, and the reef was actively bleaching. It was an ominous sign of what forecast models suggest could become a record-breaking El Niño, and stark proof that the ocean had already entered uncharted territory amid what some have called a “super El Niño” or even a “Godzilla El Niño.”

It has already helped make this the hottest summer on record in the United States and boosted Pacific hurricane activity with rare, damaging storms near Hawaii. At the same time, it has kept hurricanes away from the Atlantic, making parts of the Caribbean drier than usual. And as winter approaches, experts are closely monitoring what El Niño’s most intense phase will mean for the day-to-day weather.

The dire warnings may leave everyday people around the world with a central question: How concerned should they be?

Who gets more rain? Who gets less?
First, a brief explanation: El Niño is a natural weather pattern that comes around every few years. It typically develops in the spring or summer, gets stronger through the fall, and peaks in the winter. It doesn’t, by itself, mean a wetter winter in California or a warmer Christmas in New York, but more often than not, when El Niño arrives, that’s what tends to happen. A stronger El Niño like this one can make it more likely.

Emily Becker, a climate scientist at the University of Miami, explained that seasonal forecasts, like the ones making headlines as the off-the-charts scale of this year’s pattern became clear, represent shifting probabilities rather than precise predictions. A winter forecast can offer a strong signal that December, January and February will likely be above or below average, she said, but not when a single storm will hit and how bad it will be.

Think of the El Niño pattern as a dance between the ocean and the atmosphere. As winds in the tropical Pacific weaken, a pool of warm water that otherwise would have stayed in the western Pacific near Indonesia instead sloshes east, dragging the ocean’s primary zone of thunderstorm activity with it. This shift acts like a boulder dropped into a stream, rippling upward through the atmosphere to alter the jet stream and disrupt weather patterns worldwide.
“I see El Niño as an artist that is providing some broad-brush preliminary sketches on what to expect for upcoming seasons,” said Michelle L’Heureux, an El Niño expert at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “But the details of the final portrait will be determined by events we cannot predict months in advance.”

California, being on the Pacific, is often the first land mass affected by this new pattern. The state gets most of its annual precipitation in the winter, so an El Niño year leads to the kind of storms that live on in popular memory for decades. That’s what happened in 1997, when relentless storms left more than a dozen people dead and caused a half-billion dollars in damage.

But while a strong El Niño loads the dice, it does not offer a guarantee.

In 2015, another “Godzilla El Niño” year, forecasters expected winter storms to help break a multiyear megadrought. But the storms were forced around California by more regional weather patterns.

“Our return interval in California is two-thirds,” Dr. Becker said. In other words, California sees above-average rainfall in only two out of every three El Niño seasons. So there’s a one-in-three chance that the winter stays dry.

This time around, weather experts believe California is more likely to end up with more rain, said Jon Gottschalck, who works at NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center. But that forecast is based on the similar statistics used in 2015, and even Mr. Gottschalck cautions that California is often more difficult to predict with certainty than other parts of the country during El Niño.

Parts of the South, too, are likely to end up with more rain this winter, Mr. Gottschalck said. The jet stream routinely pins itself across the southern United States during El Niño, delivering a steady conveyor belt of Pacific moisture across Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas.

That could be a good thing, said Weston Anderson, a crop scientist.

“This El Niño may actually bring some needed relief to the area, with increased precipitation in the Southern U.S.,” Dr. Anderson said, noting that winter wheat crops in Kansas and Oklahoma stand to benefit significantly after years of La Niña-driven drought.

Unlike in California, the signal El Niño provides for above-average winter rainfall across the Gulf Coast, the Southeast and up the Eastern Seaboard of the United States is among the most reliable seasonal forecasters can read.

“The probability there’s pretty high,” said Ben Kirtman, a climate scientist at the University of Miami.

What if you’re in the Northeast? It’s complicated.
While it’s extremely likely that there will be more storms, and that they will move up the East Coast as they do every winter, those systems don’t always translate into snowfall as they move into the Northeast, as they might in a year without El Niño.

Why? Because the northern half of the United States leans toward significantly warmer temperatures during El Niño. That means potential snowstorms often shift into rain or ice in the major Northeast cities, because it’s not always cold enough for snow to fall or accumulate.

“There’s a reasonably strong relationship between El Niño and a warmer winter throughout the northern tier,” Dr. Becker said.

But don’t put your winter coat back in the attic quite yet. A generally warm northern winter does not rule out sudden, severe blasts of Arctic cold.

Amy Butler, a research scientist at NOAA’s Chemical Sciences Laboratory, explained that El Niño frequently triggers what weather people call “sudden stratospheric warmings” high above the North Pole. These warmings can push the cold Arctic air farther south.

If you’re in New York, for example, it wouldn’t be impossible to be enjoying a warmer than usual Christmas Eve, only to need that heavy parka by the time the New Year rolls around.

This El Niño may enter uncharted territory.
As global temperatures continue to break records, scientists are grappling with how climate change, caused primarily by the burning of fossil fuels, is altering El Niño itself.
https://t.co/HVSMfQjDKB

“El Niños have been acting like a stair step,” said Dr. Kim Cobb, a climate scientist at Brown. Global temperatures tend to spike during an El Niño, and when the cycle winds down, temperatures drop — only never back to the previous baseline. “That’s what frightens me about El Niño,” she said.

Dr. Cobb works with Dr. Atwood on Christmas Island, where they are watching corals bleaching before El Niño has even reached its winter stride. Super El Niños are recurring on tighter timelines, and fragile ecosystems no longer have sufficient time to recover between shocks.

That acceleration concerns her. “People should be planning for worst-case scenarios,” she said.

Dr. Michael McPhaden, the director of a NOAA buoy network that has monitored El Niño conditions since the 1990s, offers a different framing.

“Ignorance is the foundation of fear,” he said. “El Niño should not be feared. It should be understood for what it does, what it can do, and what you can do to prepare for it.”

That preparation is being tested like never before. Historical statistical models are fed data on past El Niño patterns to predict how the next one will behave. They have struggled to keep up with the extreme heat of the ocean this year.

There’s another type of projection, called a dynamic physical model, which calculates atmospheric physics based on current data rather than relying on past examples. Those models are forecasting a much stronger, more disruptive El Niño period.

“We are very much in uncharted territory,” Dr. Kirtman said. “What I feel completely confident in is that things are going to happen that are entirely unanticipated — things we didn’t even think of.

A winter forecast can offer a strong signal that December, January and February will likely be above or below average, she said, but not when a single storm will hit and how bad it will be.

Think of the El Niño pattern as a dance between the ocean and the atmosphere. As winds in the tropical Pacific weaken, a pool of warm water that otherwise would have stayed in the western Pacific near Indonesia instead sloshes east, dragging the ocean’s primary zone of thunderstorm activity with it. This shift acts like a boulder dropped into a stream, rippling upward through the atmosphere to alter the jet stream and disrupt weather patterns worldwide.
“I see El Niño as an artist that is providing some broad-brush preliminary sketches on what to expect for upcoming seasons,” said Michelle L’Heureux, an El Niño expert at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “But the details of the final portrait will be determined by events we cannot predict months in advance.”

California, being on the Pacific, is often the first land mass affected by this new pattern. The state gets most of its annual precipitation in the winter, so an El Niño year leads to the kind of storms that live on in popular memory for decades. That’s what happened in 1997, when relentless storms left more than a dozen people dead and caused a half-billion dollars in damage.

But while a strong El Niño loads the dice, it does not offer a guarantee.

In 2015, another “Godzilla El Niño” year, forecasters expected winter storms to help break a multiyear megadrought. But the storms were forced around California by more regional weather patterns.

“Our return interval in California is two-thirds,” Dr. Becker said. In other words, California sees above-average rainfall in only two out of every three El Niño seasons. So there’s a one-in-three chance that the winter stays dry.

This time around, weather experts believe California is more likely to end up with more rain, said Jon Gottschalck, who works at NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center. But that forecast is based on the similar statistics used in 2015, and even Mr. Gottschalck cautions that California is often more difficult to predict with certainty than other parts of the country during El Niño.

Parts of the South, too, are likely to end up with more rain this winter, Mr. Gottschalck said. The jet stream routinely pins itself across the southern United States during El Niño, delivering a steady conveyor belt of Pacific moisture across Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas.

That could be a good thing, said Weston Anderson, a crop scientist.

“This El Niño may actually bring some needed relief to the area, with increased precipitation in the Southern U.S.,” Dr. Anderson said, noting that winter wheat crops in Kansas and Oklahoma stand to benefit significantly after years of La Niña-driven drought.

Unlike in California, the signal El Niño provides for above-average winter rainfall across the Gulf Coast, the Southeast and up the Eastern Seaboard of the United States is among the most reliable seasonal forecasters can read.

“The probability there’s pretty high,” said Ben Kirtman, a climate scientist at the University of Miami.

What if you’re in the Northeast? It’s complicated.
While it’s extremely likely that there will be more storms, and that they will move up the East Coast as they do every winter, those systems don’t always translate into snowfall as they move into the Northeast, as they might in a year without El Niño.

Why? Because the northern half of the United States leans toward significantly warmer temperatures during El Niño. That means potential snowstorms often shift into rain or ice in the major Northeast cities, because it’s not always cold enough for snow to fall or accumulate.

“There’s a reasonably strong relationship between El Niño and a warmer winter throughout the northern tier,” Dr. Becker said.

But don’t put your winter coat back in the attic quite yet. A generally warm northern winter does not rule out sudden, severe blasts of Arctic cold.

Amy Butler, a research scientist at NOAA’s Chemical Sciences Laboratory, explained that El Niño frequently triggers what weather people call “sudden stratospheric warmings” high above the North Pole. These warmings can push the cold Arctic air farther south.

If you’re in New York, for example, it wouldn’t be impossible to be enjoying a warmer than usual Christmas Eve, only to need that heavy parka by the time the New Year rolls around.

This El Niño may enter uncharted territory.
As global temperatures continue to break records, scientists are grappling with how climate change, caused primarily by the burning of fossil fuels, is altering El Niño itself.
https://t.co/HVSMfQjDKB

“El Niños have been acting like a stair step,” said Dr. Kim Cobb, a climate scientist at Brown. Global temperatures tend to spike during an El Niño, and when the cycle winds down, temperatures drop — only never back to the previous baseline. “That’s what frightens me about El Niño,” she said.

Dr. Cobb works with Dr. Atwood on Christmas Island, where they are watching corals bleaching before El Niño has even reached its winter stride. Super El Niños are recurring on tighter timelines, and fragile ecosystems no longer have sufficient time to recover between shocks.

That acceleration concerns her. “People should be planning for worst-case scenarios,” she said.

Dr. Michael McPhaden, the director of a NOAA buoy network that has monitored El Niño conditions since the 1990s, offers a different framing.

“Ignorance is the foundation of fear,” he said. “El Niño should not be feared. It should be understood for what it does, what it can do, and what you can do to prepare for it.”

That preparation is being tested like never before. Historical statistical models are fed data on past El Niño patterns to predict how the next one will behave. They have struggled to keep up with the extreme heat of the ocean this year.

There’s another type of projection, called a dynamic physical model, which calculates atmospheric physics based on current data rather than relying on past examples. Those models are forecasting a much stronger, more disruptive El Niño period.

“We are very much in uncharted territory,” Dr. Kirtman said. “What I feel completely confident in is that things are going to happen that are entirely unanticipated — things we didn’t even think of.

text:
NFL Week 5 Preview

Here’s what I’m looking at on this slate

- Bears icon Mike Ditka passed away on Friday, adding yet another layer to this week’s already intriguing installment of Bears at Packers.

- The pressure is on Green Bay in this spot. They are reeling, they are down their two best defensive players, they have the worst offensive line they’ve had in recent memory, but they also have their starting quarterback in Jordan Love and despite their struggles, they are still a manageable 2-2.

- From Green Bay’s end, I would expect them to have a game plan more tailored to their current reality coming off a long week. Speedster duo Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are the team’s biggest matchup problem for opponents, but the Packers have been very pass heavy and it’s nearly impossible to effectively throw downfield without reliable pass protection. Even more so when you have no run game and opposing pass rushers can pin their ears back. So, I’m expecting Green Bay to try to get their running game going more here, while leaning into more manufactured touches and quicker route combinations in the passing game. If they have success in this sense, then I’d expect a few downfield shots to their speedsters.

- On the Bears end, I’d make Green Bay show they can consistently stop the run given Chicago’s current situation. Kyle Monangai is out with turf toe, so there should be a lot on D’Andre Swift’s plate with Roschon Johnson supplementing.

- I would not put this game in Tyson Bagent’s hands unless I absolutely have to, he was a few plays and a couple penalties away from having a nightmare game against the Jets last week.

- Speaking of, a second wrinkle in this game is Caleb Williams had a limited practice Friday and was listed as questionable as of Friday night. I would guess that was a test run for Week 6, perhaps Week 7, but interesting, nevertheless, especially given the opponent and the important of Ditka to the city of Chicago. I’d get it if Caleb was pushing to play, but I hope he isn’t rushed back.

- Seahawks vs. 49ers is the best matchup on Sunday.

- San Francisco has one of the better coaches in Kyle Shanahan and Brock Purdy has been better than most realize for several years. That said, I think public perception is flying a little high on the Niners, and a trip to Seattle is a tremendous test for Purdy and this offense, who were shut down until the 4thquarter against Denver last week.

- Seattle gave up 26 points to the 49ers over three games last season, including just 9 across their Week 18 tilt and Division Round matchup, both Seahawks victories.

- I mentioned this once recently; Bill Belichick would treat Jaxon Smith-Njigba like a punt gunner on gotta have it passing situations. He would not like JSN beat him in those spots and quite frankly, I’m not sure why no one is trying this. Fear of being different and wrong, I’d expect.

- From what I have seen, Sam Darnold is still a solid quarterback but Seattle’s offense is a step less without Klint Kubiak, and perhaps Kenneth Walker. If the 49ers win this game, I’d expect their defense to drive that outcome, like they did against Denver last week.

- The Jaguars vs. Eagles game in London has seen an enormous line movement from -2.5 to -7.5. I do not recall a line movement that large that wasn’t related to a quarterback injury. Given that, it would be Jaguars or pass for me, as the Eagles have so many injuries, a greatly reduced offensive line, and I have no hope that their offensive coaching staff will create any margin against what has been a very good Jaguars defense with a top 10 front.

- In truth, this looks like a potential implosion spot for Philadelphia’s offense, against a Jaguars team that is looking like a contender.

- If the Eagles have a shot in this game, their defense needs to play up and carry them. In particular, their underachieving front four needs to play their best game of the year against a middling Jaguars offensive line. Edge Jonathan Greenard, who has been banged up, could really give the Eagles’ a boost if he’s near full strength.

- The problem with that is Trevor Lawrence has become who everyone has thought he was going to be under Liam Coen.

- I sincerely hope Jayden Daniels is completely fine and not risking his future playing in this game. Given that, really high chance Washington goes out of their way to protect Daniels, which looks like run centric game plan, quick hitter passing game, Daniels only runs if he has a clear lane.

- One interesting aspect the Giants have going forward against Washington is New York has a very rangy linebacker group that should help them manage mobile quarterbacks like Daniels.

- If I’m Washington, I run at very talented, but 252 lbs edge Abdul Carter to both try and neutralize him on pass sets and because he can be moved in the run game.

- From what I’ve seen, the Giants should give Tyrone Tracy some significant run starting this week. Najee Harris is a professional running back, but he has limited juice and he fumbled last week. Cam Skattebo, as physical and as hard of a runner as there is, looks like his burst is already down. Mixing Tracy with Skattebo would give opposing defenses much different looks.

- Jameis Winston is a wild card. He’s a backup that is capable of throwing for 300 yards without it being an accident, but he’s also capable of losing a game entirely on his own. He had good games against the Lions and Packers last year, but he has not been very good in Jaxson Dart’s absence this season, though he did at least have some positive moments last week against Arizona.

- I am not a Tyler Shough guy, but I was open to being wrong after how well he played in Baltimore in Week 2. Despite that moment of doubt, I don’t think I’m wrong. Shough facing Brian Flores’ defense, while being without his left tackle, is a very messy situation. I’m very curious to see what Kellen Moore tries to do against Flores. Given that Moore was a college QB and he’s coming off a real rocky game in Atlanta, I’m expecting an uptick in screens and quick hitters.

- Minnesota is down the left side of their offensive line. While the Saints don’t have a high-end front to really take advantage of that, it’s still a huge limitation for Kyler Murray, who was fine against bottom of the barrel Miami but he’s been mediocre as a Viking so far.

- Starting today I’m going to begin openly wondering aloud if Brian Daboll is among the worst active play callers in the NFL. I thought he was bad in New York, he’s shown me nothing in Tennessee.

- The Texans pass rush has an advantage in this game, and they are coming off one of, if not their worst showing in years against Dallas last week, in an absolute must win game at 0-4.

- I have no confidence in Daboll and I’d be pretty surprised if Houston’s defense doesn’t bounce back in a significant way, but the Titans path to an upset is their own front taking over this game. CJ Stroud has played pretty well this season, but the Texans have a sub part offensive line and the one true strength of the Titans football program is their front, headlined by interior disruptor Jeffery Simmons.

- Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are currently both still questionable, but truth be told I think Joe Burrow’s Bengals can still win this game even if both play makers miss. First, I don’t think Burrow needs his elite play makers to have an efficient game on offense, against this bottom tier pass rush/ secondary combo.

- Cincinnati’s front four is also going to be a problem for Miami’s offensive line.

- I think the Jets beat the Browns in a game between two teams that are pretty similar roster wise. If anything, the Jets offensive line is ahead of Cleveland’s, where I’d say New York is a better landing spot for a new future at quarterback.

- The X factor here is Deshaun Watson, who is still not Houston level Watson, but he’s currently enjoying his best run since joining Cleveland. Todd Monken and the Brown’s young, talented skill group deserve a good amount of the credit for that, but I first noted that Watson played promisingly in Week 2 and that has been a thing for three games in a row.

- KC Concepcion could be a problem if Cleveland can get him in space against the Jets.

- Geno Smith is the poster child for the idea that sacks are a quarterback stat, because he takes some of the worst sacks you’ll ever seen. Mason Graham being out is one of the reasons I lean Jets, because New York can provide help on Jared Verse without much reservation.

- I’d put Klint Kubiak in the Dave Canales and Liam Coen cluster for coaches, which is a compliment. That also makes Kubiak vs. Mike Vrabel a really interesting coaching matchup.

- Kirk Cousins has played very well so far and Kubiak has elevated this offense. Specifically, I absolutely love how he’s leaning into Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer as the core of the passing offense (along with Ashton Jeanty). Good coaches use what they have instead of trying to fit square pegs into round holes. I’m really looking forward to seeing how Vrabel tries to handle Bowers.

- I’d cluster the Raiders pass rush with Buffalo’s, more of a mid-range pass rush (Buffalo’s is better but has a worse headliner), so I expect Drake Maye to be fine in this matchup.

- The Steelers are coming off a long week and a loss, to face a Colts team coming off a London game. Given Pittsburgh’s second half schedule, this is close to a must win.

- I imagine that Shane Steichen isn’t going to come out slinging it with Daniel Jones against this defense, especially not after last week where Jones was atrocious on foreign soil. I would think muddy, run centric game plan, try to keep this game close and ugly for as long as possible is the Colts best path. If the Colts’ defense fails them against a flawed Steelers offense, Indianapolis could be in trouble here.

- Monster tight end Darnell Washington saw some interesting usage against Cleveland last week. To Mike McCarthy’s credit, which is a phrase that was not easy for me to say, it seems like he and his staff have recognized that Washington is a pretty unique player in the league and maybe they should do more with him. Kudos to them, I hope to see it continue.

- The Chargers offensive line was already bad in the interior, now they are down both of their offensive tackles, who are two of the four best players on the whole team. This Chargers offensive line this week is among the worst I’ve ever seen assembled, and they are facing a quality Broncos front.

- If there is one positive for the Chargers offense, it’s that both of Denver’s perimeter corners are out.

- Sean Payton is taking over play calling duties, so I’d expect this game to go through the run game behind this offensive line, with Jaylen Waddle seeing a spike in usage, including some manufactured touches.

- On a personal level, I’ve always thought Sean Payton was a very good play caller that sets things up and leans into what his team has personnel wise. I saw nothing over the last four weeks that made me think Davis Webb should be running the offense instead of Payton.

- The Cardinals are down their left tackle and Jacoby Brissett was bad in New York last week, and I mean bad. If that version Brissett is close to what we see on Sunday, behind what is now a significantly less reliable offensive line with Paris Johnson out against a top 10ish Lions pass rush, I could see Detroit winning this game with some distance.

- If Brissett plays well, which we’ve seen at times in Arizona over the last 12 months, this game will shoot out as expected.

- If Marvin Harrison Jr. still doesn’t do much against this Lions’ injury depleted secondary, it’s at least time for a change of scenery.

- The truth of the Atlanta Falcons is somewhere in the middle of their first two, brutal games without Michael Penix, and their last two blowout victories with Penix. They get lucky in drawing the Ravens with Lamar Jackson sidelined, which has become a pretty frequent occurrence for Baltimore.

- Tyler Huntley isn’t a bad backup quarterback. I envision the Ravens trying to ride Derrick Henry with Zay Flowers seeing pretty concentrated volume.

- No Trey Hendrickson is a pretty big blow to Baltimore, as they’ll likely need to bring heat to pressure Penix.

- I could envision the Ravens containing Bijan Robinson, same with Drake London, as Jessie Minter was able to keep both players in relative check with a worse defensive roster the last time he faced Atlanta (although Kirk Cousins was the Falcons QB in that matchup).

- It would not shock me if Baltimore forced a few turnover Sunday night.

- Rams vs. Bills is among the best possible matchups the NFL has to offer in 2026. LA has a better roster than Buffalo, even with Myles Garrett sidelined. They also have the better coach, making this a bit of a Josh Allen vs. the world kind of matchup.

- Both teams are top 10 in both trenches.

- Puka Nacua and Davante Adams against the Bills secondary looks like a pretty significant advantage for the Rams. I’d imagine Puka in particular is a very unique cover for cornerbacks that haven’t faced him. Not just because of his physicality, but because of when Matthew Stafford will give him targets (as soon as he breaks, when he’s covered, throws to spots). It’s a pretty unique dynamic to deal with.

- The last time Nacua faced Buffalo he went 12-162-1.

I have watched every NFL game for roughly a decade. I have done this for the purpose of sports speculation.

I run a reality-based program here.

Engagement is how I reach new users. So as long as engagement remains strong (comments/ shares) I’ll continue pumping this and similarly detailed insights out every week.

text:
Grok Build alpha 1.0.51.

A big one: /share is removed and memory settings simplify to on or off, there's a new /density command for tool call detail, new /workflow commands to list, stop and resume background workflow runs, "always allow"/"never allow" domain options on web fetch approval cards, headless grok -p now waits for background goals, and 118 bug fixes land across hooks, worktrees, permissions, the dashboard and headless mode.

1.0.51 — 10/09/2026

Breaking Changes
• Cancel and edit-resend on long sessions no longer unexpectedly revert workspace files.
• Memory settings simplified: rollout and file_writes_enabled options removed; memory is on or off.
• Removed the `/share` command and related session sharing features from the CLI and SDK.

Features
• Inline viewports can now be restored at a previously saved screen area without extra cursor queries.
• Headless `grok -p` now waits for background goals to finish and reports their outcome.
• `/imagine` and similar commands now run the matching bundled skill when the required tools are unavailable.
• New `/density` command and Tool call density setting let you choose how much detail tool calls show in the transcript.
• Web fetch approval cards now include "always allow" and "never allow" domain options that persist for the folder.
• Slash command completion now updates live when skills are added or changed during a session.
• Request form now securely collects and fills sensitive details like passwords or card numbers without sending values to the model.
• Chrome profiles can now be persisted across restarts using durable state directories.
• Workspace server sessions now share one Chrome instance for cookies and storage.
• `/feedback` Drafts tab now supports `G` / `Home` and `End` to jump to the first or last draft.
• Pinned sessions on the dashboard now stay in the order you pinned or reordered them.
• Shift+Enter, Ctrl+., Ctrl+/ and Ctrl+[ / ] now work inside tmux when extended-keys are enabled.
• grok -p --output-format json now reports the exact worktree folder used (useful after -w name collisions).
• Bare hook commands such as `my-guard` now run from PATH when not found next to the hook file.
• Headless JSON error output now includes the worktree folder when a session was started.
• grok sessions list and /resume now show worktree sessions started from the same subfolder.
• /exit (and aliases) in a dashboard details view now closes only that session instead of quitting Grok.
• Editors offering file access now receive a one-time transcript notice that the agent reads and writes disk files.
• --background-wait-timeout now also stops an active headless goal after the timeout and exits with an error.
• Interactive sessions now include the Grok Build user guide location so the agent can answer usage questions.
• New `/workflow` commands let you list, stop, and resume background workflow runs without sending them to the model.
• Background workflow runs now appear in the tasks pane with a stop button.
• Hooks that ask about web searches or file deletes now show the hook name on the approval card.
• config.toml now accepts an [update] section without breaking other commands.
• Hook load errors listed in /hooks can now be expanded to see the full message.
• `grok worktree` commands now work correctly inside Jujutsu repositories.
• Images pasted with skill commands like /pr-workflow are now sent to the model.
• Pressing Ctrl+C on a goal now pauses the goal instead of letting it continue.
• grok -p now runs auth_provider_command when no login is stored.
• Reopening a chat with an active goal now continues the goal automatically.
• Browser tabs can now be restored on demand instead of all at once when a session resumes.
• `grok agent stdio` now supports listing sessions via ACP and returns consistent reply envelopes.
• Answering an approval with a message now tells the model it is a follow-up.
• --allowed-tools is now accepted as an alias for --allow in headless mode.

Bug Fixes
• Slash command suggestions no longer make the text after the cursor disappear while typing.
• Running workflows in the dock now show the same pulsing indicator as in the main scrollback.
• Mode switch tool calls now appear in the transcript with the target mode name.
• Always-approve mode now automatically approves web requests without extra prompts.
• The follow indicator no longer appears when only blank padding sits below the viewport.
• Search failures now keep the original pattern instead of showing an empty Search "".
• Sessions that open without a model list now use the public Auto id and succeed on every account.
• Background wake turns that request plan changes or mode switches are now handled correctly.
• Model-call retries now show progress status instead of a generic waiting message.
• Foreground subagent activity now appears correctly after resume.
• Very large pasted prompts are now offloaded to a file instead of being sent inline.
• Sign-in failures now show a clear plain-English message with the next step instead of raw errors.
• Logging out now stops any running turns on local sessions instead of leaving them active.
• The send-now shortcut no longer accidentally enables always-approve mode while a permission card is open.
• `/find` now keeps match counts and navigation accurate while replies or command output stream in.
• Images from tools are now validated so bad files no longer break the current turn or future replays.
• Screenshots and other image artifacts saved by the browser tool are now stored as real image files.
• Rate-limit errors now show the expected message; very small images are rejected early.
• Send-now (Ctrl+Enter) no longer accidentally answers an open question card.
• Opening the queue with Up now scrolls so the selected follow-up is visible.
• Command output that contains clear-screen codes is no longer discarded.
• Dashboard cursor and overlay counter now correctly track the active grouping view.
• Headless JSON output now reports the correct stop reason when the turn limit is reached and removes duplicate error prefixes.
• Session picker footer no longer lists the same shortcut twice.
• Dragging images from a file manager onto terminals like GNOME Terminal or xfce4-terminal now attaches them correctly.
• Plan comments added while a revision runs are now preserved and sent when the plan is approved.
• Permission prompts that fail now show a clearer message without blaming the interface.
• --disallowed-tools now accepts the exact names shown to the model (run_terminal_command, spawn_subagent, etc.).
• Long pastes without bracketed-paste markers are now read completely instead of stalling after ~1 KB.
• A feedback send now shows "Sending feedback…" immediately; failed sends no longer repeat the lead phrase.
• Typing, arrows or Enter while an approval card appears no longer accidentally approve the action or enable always-approve mode.
• Error hints for legacy session import now appear in full instead of being cut off by the pager.
• Skills in the folder where grok started now correctly show as (local).
• Worktree creation no longer hangs when the repo contains named pipes or sockets.
• --no-subagents flag now works correctly in headless / -p sessions.
• Resumed sessions now correctly show aborted subagent tasks as cancelled instead of failed.
• Large parallel shell batches no longer drop calls with "hook state lost" errors.
• Write approval cards now show the existing file contents that will be replaced.
• Slash command completion now shows the correct name for files under commands/ instead of always showing /commands.
• PreToolUse hooks now validate rewrites against the tool schema and deny invalid ones before running the tool.
• Ctrl+C during a turn now cancels the turn even when a modal such as /mcps or the block viewer is open.
• grok -w now opens the session at the worktree root (with a note) when the original launch folder does not exist in the new worktree.
• `/cd` and the location picker now accept quoted or escaped folder paths.
• Web search hooks now fire under the correct `web_search` name and carry `query`.
• Large file writes or many screenshots no longer end the session.
• Glob tool hooks now match under `list_dir` and carry the correct directory.
• `/find` now scrolls to the exact wrapped row containing the current match.
• Downloads via FetchMcpResource are now refused in plan mode and resolve paths consistently.
• Pinned dashboard sessions now survive restarts and layout changes instead of disappearing from the saved list.
• Slash commands like /imagine now work regardless of capitalization and correctly substitute skills when tools are missing.
• Turning off bypass mode without naming a session now correctly restores prompts in all open sessions.
• /delete with extra text now shows an error instead of deleting the current session.
• Failed /feedback status messages now wrap inside the dialog instead of clipping at the border.
• Number-key picks in the dashboard peek no longer leak to the wrong agent after Up/Down navigation.
• Worktrees created with -w are now correctly tracked and resumable even when GROK_HOME is reached through a symlink.
• `grok worktree rm` and `gc` now clean up names after manually deleting a worktree folder so `-w NAME` works again.
• Hook scripts that read stdin with `read` now receive a complete line.
• A policy that disables non-managed hooks now applies to the next session instead of only after restart.
• `/resume` and `grok sessions list` no longer show worktree sessions from a sibling submodule or separate-git-dir repo.
• A hook listed under two different matchers now runs only once per tool call.
• Typing a hidden command such as `/cd` in a session and pressing Enter now runs it instead of accepting a near-match skill.
• @-file completion no longer accepts a match from an earlier query when you type quickly.
• Tool hooks now run one at a time per session and stop promptly on cancel or exit.
• PostToolUse hooks now receive a correct whole-millisecond duration.
• PreToolUse hooks for shell commands now see the model's block_until_ms value.
• MCP tool calls now show hook permission prompts and cards name the hook that asked.
• Typing while a permission or ask card is visible no longer selects or answers the card.
• grok worktree list now shows unfinished copies left by an interrupted create.
• Auto mode now asks before deleting files that the classifier has not already allowed.
• Fixed intermittent List/Read/Open failures during concurrent v2 hardening migrations.
• grok -p -s with a reused session id now shows the plain refusal message instead of JSON-RPC noise.
• Settings saves no longer re-insert the built-in default fork model into config.toml.
• Fixed several pager rows that showed wrong paths, truncated names, or hid failure/cancel states.
• --system-prompt now correctly appends rules from --append-system-prompt instead of dropping them.
• /new now inherits always-approve mode from the tab it was run from instead of another tab.
• Multi-select questions now let you toggle several answers with number keys before submitting.
• Slash-command notices typed while a reply streams no longer hide the streaming reply.
• @ file search no longer accepts keys or moves the highlight while results are still updating.
• Worktree db rebuild now restores names so `rm` and `show` by name work again.
• A prompt blocked by a hook no longer titles the session.
• Background subagents now respect saved approvals and --always-approve after the parent turn finishes.
• Per-session system prompt overrides now correctly use only the session's own rules.
• Connection stalled errors now show a clearer message with network advice.
• Invalid model provider tables now produce a clear startup error instead of silent fallback.
• Narrow feedback dialog now shows full draft titles and readable confirm prompts.
• /workflow stop|resume <name> now correctly targets the live run instead of an ended first run.
• Dialogs like /feedback no longer disappear on very short terminal windows.
• Delete operations now respect the same permission rules as shell rm commands.
• Hooks can no longer rewrite a web-search call to restrict domains.
• Workspace server now starts with per-session private Chrome by default.
• Notification hooks for permission prompts and task completion now run reliably before a headless session exits.
• Headless goal runs no longer print a spurious "Goal paused" message after completion.
• Legacy UI density settings now combine correctly across config tiers and produce expected folding.
• Approval answers sent after a turn ends no longer affect the turn.
• Background shell commands now fail immediately when the working directory does not exist.
• `grok worktree rm` without `-f` now safely keeps worktrees when the unsaved-work check fails or times out.
• The dashboard slash menu now shows skills from the home session even when opened early.
• `grok worktree rm` and `gc` now correctly remove worktrees whose only untracked content is empty folders.
• Editing a queued prompt now prevents accidental removal with a stale client view.
• The model is now told when memory is turned off or on for the session.
• Hook results in the UI now correctly distinguish between notes and tool outcomes.
• Permission cards for MCP tools can no longer be tricked into showing fake option rows.
• The agent stdio mode now returns clearer errors for malformed client requests and consistent recap replies.
• Scroll logging and acceleration calculations no longer produce backwards timestamps under load.
• Hooks and tool commands started from the TUI can no longer read or write the interactive terminal.
• Delete operations now correctly match `Bash(rm …)` ask/deny rules even when the path contains `..` or the cwd is a symlink.
• Web search and image approval cards now only offer always-approve mode to clients that support it.
• Closing a session in the dashboard no longer leaves it listed under Inactive.
• Running /compact on an empty session no longer resets the reported context window.
• With goals disabled, a headless `/goal` line is now treated as a normal prompt instead of failing.
• Background shell commands no longer flip back to running when late output arrives.
• Only slash commands at the start of a message trigger skills.
• Browser tabs restore and close more reliably with fewer races.
• Fast model names in the footer no longer show double parentheses.
• SubagentStart and Notification hook activity is no longer reported to the UI.
• Voice error messages now display with correct punctuation.
• disable_zdr_incompatible_tools changes now apply to new turns without restarting the worker.
• Project skills are now labeled correctly for nested projects.

Performance
• Opening the resume picker is now much faster on machines with many worktrees.
• grok worktree commands start faster by skipping unnecessary model catalog work at boot.

#News James Talarico claimed he was in a Dallas urgent care the same night he was holding a fundraiser in New York, now Republicans in Texas are calling him a liar.  

Talarico was supposed to be in Edinburg on September 30 for an in-person forum at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley. He joined by video instead. 
#newyork 
On the video, he said  

“Last night, it got so bad that I went to urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu.”  

He said he had a fever and was in the “most contagious” stage and that he could not live with himself if he got someone’s grandmother or someone’s baby sick, and that the best thing was to put safety and health first.  

He also said, “I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail.” 

However, it appears as though his schedule doesn't match his excuse.  

🔵Monday, September 28, 7 p.m., downtown Manhattan fundraiser: 

➡️Tickets ran from $500 to $27,000. Talarico attended. 

🔵Tuesday, September 29, Greenwich Village, a second fundraiser, on his campaign’s invitation.  

➡️Tickets ran from $1,000 to $13,500. He held the reception.  

🔵A Tuesday night reception in Greenwich Village, New York and a Tuesday night urgent-care visit in Dallas is not the same thing.  

The campaign hasn't given an explanation, proof of a flight, a timestamp, or even a clinic name.  

While Talarico was in New York collecting out of state  money - his events in Texas were being cancelled.  

➡️The Edinburg forum on September 30 went virtual. 

➡️The Central Texas African American Civic Engagement Symposium was canceled.  

➡️An Austin fundraiser set for Tuesday was scrapped. 

#Austin 
Ken Paxton’s spokeswoman Madison Cercy said Talarico had time for a New York fundraiser but “can’t find time for Texans,” and that Paxton is working while Talarico “hides behind recycled rally footage and canceled events.”  

🔵On October 7 the campaign launched a “Where’s Jimmy?” count:  

“It’s been 11 days since James Talarico was last seen campaigning in Texas.”  

At President Trump’s San Antonio rally, Paxton led a “Where is Talarico?” chant. 

Republicans say if he was in Dallas with the flu, the Greenwich Village fundraiser needs an explanation. If he was in Greenwich Village taking checks, the urgent-care story needs one. The campaign has offered neither. 

Do you believe a man can be at a New York donor reception and a Dallas urgent care on the same night? Or are Republicans right in saying that Talarico is lying?

text:
OpenAI and Anthropic poach Trump officials as industry fights for Washington’s trust | Kai Nicol-Schwarz, CNBC

Anthropic and OpenAI are poaching officials from the Trump administration for senior roles as the AI sector scrambles to strengthen ties to Washington, with frontier tech increasingly viewed as a national security issue.

This year, Anthropic has appointed at least two former Trump officials, one to its board and another as the head of its frontier compute strategy. OpenAI has hired at least three from the president’s administrations to work across strategy and special projects.

Companies developing frontier AI have been racing to build relationships with the U.S. President Donald Trump’s White House, amid growing calls for regulation and in the wake of a number of cybersecurity incidents caused by rogue AI systems.

"Frontier AI companies are aware that the Trump administration has a lot of levers over their business, from federal procurement and supply-chain designations to export controls and everything in between, and that it's willing to use them," said Michelle Nie Duncan, visiting fellow with the technology and national security program at the Center for a New American Security.

"They have learned from the Anthropic episode that it pays to be on the good side of the White House," she told CNBC. A U.S. appeals court upheld a Pentagon designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk in September, after a public spat between the two parties at the start of the year.

OpenAI directed CNBC to previously released statements about two of its former Trump official appointments when approached for comment. Anthropic and the White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Ties to Trump

While Trump has called AI safety concerns a "hoax" and advocated for self-regulation from AI companies, he has also said the Department of Justice and other law enforcement bodies could "rein" in AI.

Anthropic, in particular, has had a particularly antagonistic relationship with the Trump administration this year, but CEO Dario Amodei has looked to smooth his relationship with the U.S. president in recent times. He joined a lunch between Trump and AI bosses as well as dining with Trump in September.

Sihao Huang joined Amodei's AI lab in September as head of frontier compute strategy. He was previously a senior policy advisor for AI and emerging technology at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP). Huang's website states that he was responsible for leading the "AI team at OSTP & coordinating national security, science policy, and semiconductor issues."

He'll be working on Anthropic's infrastructure expansion and "planning for rapid AI progress," Huang said in a post on X in September.

The company appointed Chris Liddell, who served as the deputy White House chief of staff during Trump's first term, to its board of directors in February.

Anthropic has been racing to ink AI data center deals big and small as it looks to secure the infrastructure it needs to train and serve its models. Anthropic had struck a roughly $45 billion cloud deal with neocloud Nscale, CNBC reported in August.

Leverage

Both Anthropic and OpenAI are also currently hiring for multiple political engagements roles.

"With companies like OpenAI and Anthropic gearing up for some of the largest IPOs of all time, many also see this as a chance to be part of something historic," said Nie Duncan, adding that the companies are often able to offer attractive compensation packages beyond what would be possible in the public sector.

"The AI labs are becoming some of the most consequential institutions in the world, and for officials who are serious about shaping the future of AI governance, inside the labs is where a lot of leverage currently lies."

OpenAI confirmed last week that Thomas Lind, who had led AI policy at the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), has joined the company to lead on cyber and strategic risk on its national security policy team. The ONCD is the principal advisor to the president on cybersecurity policy and strategy.

"[Lind's] expertise is even more important as AI becomes central to the national security agenda, with the Office of the National Cyber Director playing a growing role in shaping AI policy," said Sasha Baker, who leads OpenAI's national security policy team and served as deputy under secretary of defense for policy in the Biden Administration.

Dean Ball, who served as a senior policy advisor at OSTP in 2025 and was involved in drafting the Trump administration's flagship America's AI Action Plan, joined OpenAI in July as head of strategic futures.

Ball will "help us pressure-test our assumptions and think through issues ranging from frontier safety and the economic impacts of increasingly capable systems to the evolving relationship between governments, companies, and society," said OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon.

OpenAI also hired Peter Bowman-Davis to work on model training and hardware engineering in March, according to his LinkedIn page. He previously served as Chief AI officer at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

News edit

A Ukrainian drone strike caused Russian internet giant Yandex to suspend operations at one of its key data centers on Thursday.

AI agent startup Manus has raised more than $500 million in its first funding round since Meta was forced to abandon its acquisition of the company.

Apollo and several banks are in talks to finance SpaceX's $40 billion Nvidia GPU purchase, a source told CNBC.

Google has been ordered to halt work on two data centers it's developing in Finland, a month after the tech giant committed to investing $15 billion in artificial intelligence infrastructure in the country.

Mistral on Tuesday unveiled a new AI model it said ranked among the best open models in the world, as Western companies race to close the capability gap with Chinese developers in the market.

One more thing

Microsoft is one of the most valuable tech companies in the world with a market cap approaching $4 trillion.

Under CEO Satya Nadella, the tech giant has continued its ascent as a software and cloud powerhouse.

But, as my colleague Jordan Novet writes, almost four years into the AI boom, Microsoft has yet to find a breakout hit at the model or application layer.

text: The provided statement is historically inaccurate, as Palestine was not a conflict buffer zone for a Jordanian majority, nor was Israel established to settle local tribal fighting. Prior to British control, the region was populated predominantly by Palestinian Arabs (Muslim and Christian) who had resided there for generations [Sykes-Picot Agreement], alongside a small Jewish minority, while Transjordan was administratively separated by Britain in 1921. The creation of Israel was the culmination of decades of diplomatic efforts by the Zionist movement and British colonial policy [History of the Question of Palestine - UN], aimed at establishing a Jewish national home in the wake of severe European antisemitism, rather than an intervention in localized fighting. Furthermore, Palestinians were not offered sovereignty through joining Israel; the United Nations actually proposed two separate, independent states to ensure mutual self-determination [UN Resolution 181 - United Nations], and the subsequent 1948 war resulted in the displacement of over 700,000 Palestinians, leaving the remaining population without a sovereign state.

text:
The sequence therefore runs from a direct behavioral delay, to an optical signature inside the tubes, to a broader claim that the tubes matter for consciousness, to supporting conditions that could keep delicate effects alive, and finally to pharmacological confirmation that the tubes influence the on/off switch of https://t.co/bMx4Nx6Mzi is the same set of new claims and biomarkers, put into plain language and arranged as a clear sequence.When rats are given a drug that stiffens and stabilizes the tiny protein tubes (microtubules) inside their brain cells, it takes them noticeably longer to fall unconscious under ordinary anesthetic gas. On average the delay is about a minute longer. The same kind of effect shows up in mice when similar drugs are used. In everyday terms, protecting those protein tubes makes it harder for the anesthetic to switch consciousness off.
The same protein tubes contain dense networks of a particular amino acid called tryptophan. When these networks are intact they glow more strongly under ultraviolet light than the amino acids do by themselves. The glow gets stronger as more tubes join together. Researchers see this as a sign that the tubes can act collectively, like a group of light emitters firing in unison rather than one by one.
A 2025 review paper gathers the rat anesthesia result, the stronger ultraviolet glow, and a few other laboratory observations. The author argues that, taken together, they make it reasonable to treat the protein tubes as a real physical base for consciousness rather than just scaffolding. The paper also claims this picture helps explain how many separate signals can bind into one unified experience and how that experience can have causal effects.
Other recent measurements show that water trapped in very narrow biological spaces can keep certain quantum-like motions at ordinary body temperature, and that certain ring-shaped molecular structures can maintain electrical currents under the same conditions. These findings are offered as extra support that the interior of a living cell need not destroy delicate quantum effects as quickly as once thought.
Different drugs that either stabilize or disrupt the protein tubes change how quickly animals go under anesthetic and how quickly they wake up, sometimes in opposite directions. This adds a practical check: altering the tubes really does move the threshold at which consciousness disappears and returns.
