text:
Glimpses of Gibbon

"The throne was the object of his desires; and, had he been less actuated by ambition, it was his only means of safety."

At A.D. 292, Gibbon introduces Constantine, the founder of the seat of the Eastern Roman Empire for a thousand years after the final destruction of Rome, Constantinople.

"The figure of Constantine was tall and majestic; he was dexterous in all his exercises, intrepid in war, affable in peace; in his whole conduct the active spirit of youth was tempered by habitual prudence; and, while his mind was engrossed by ambition, he appeared cold and insensible to the allurements of pleasure."

In Death of Constantius, and elevation of Constantine, A.D. 306, July 25 we learn of the dangerous path to power that needed to be threaded under the dangerous rule of Galerius. Constantius reigned as Augustus for 15 months, and he died “fourteen and a half years after he had been promoted to the rank of Caesar. Writing during the Age of Enlightenment, when the concept of democratic government as superior to monarchy had gained prominence through the works John Locke and Jean-Jaques Rousseau, Gibbon informs us of the traditions of antiquity.

"Peers of inheritance and succession are so very familiar that the generality of mankind consider them as founded, not only in reason, but in nature itself. Our imagination readily transfers the same principles from private property to public dominion: and, whenever a virtuous father leaves behind him a son whose merits seems to justify the esteem, or even the hopes of the people, the joint influence of prejudice and of affection operates with irresistible weight."

In this case, as in so many others where armies have installed new emperors in the early centuries of the Roman empire, these “natural” feelings were felt in the breasts of “the flower of the western armies,” the legions of Constantius in Britain. The troops much preferred the son of their dead leader to rise to Augustus and Emperor, than to be placed under the command of some stranger appointed by the emperor of the East. Again, Gibbon reminds us of both the power and danger of ruling in these times, as he tells us of Constantine’s analysis of his situation.

"The throne was the object of his desires; and, had he been less actuated by ambition, it was his only means of safety. He was well acquainted with the character and sentiments of Galerius, and sufficiently apprised that, if he wished to live, he must determine to reign."

Galerius understands the conditions he is facing, but he appoints Constantine to only the rank of Caesar, while he gives Severus the supreme office of Augustus. By this means, “The apparent harmony of the empire was still preserved, and Constantine, who already possessed the substance, expected, without impatience, an opportunity of attaining the honors, of supreme power.”
In a complex series of events, Maximian came out of retirement to enable his son Maxentius to seize the supreme power of Augustus. This soon led to the flight of Severus to Ravenna, where the powerful walls and access to a great navy would allow him to hold out against a siege. Rather than fighting such an unpromising campaign, Maximian offered Severus his life in exchange for the office of Augustus, but when the deal was finalized, the unfortunate Severus was given only the choice of the method of his execution. As did Nero and Seneca, “he preferred the favorite method of the ancients, that of opening his veins.”

Saturday Morning Futures | October 10, 2026
Conflict Diplomacy: IRGC Shipping Pursuit and Hormuz Transit Drops

Geopolitical posture across the Persian Gulf remains strictly defined by naval standoffs and maritime transit friction. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy issued fresh warnings threatening sanctions against commercial shipping firms operating on unauthorized routes, declaring vessels using unapproved channels face regional pursuit. Maritime tracking data reveals transit through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to its lowest levels since July, with crude oil flows falling to roughly 74% of typical pre war volumes. Allied naval task forces maintain strategic monitoring across commercial shipping channels as global trade desks adapt to elevated war risk insurance costs.

Fiscal Dominance: Treasury International Shifts and Yield Curve Pressures

Capitol Hill policy debates and Treasury operations continue to center on domestic borrowing management and federal revenue integrity. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced he will skip upcoming international finance summits in Bangkok to remain in Washington addressing domestic fiscal priorities, sending senior deputies in his place. With 10 year Treasury yields holding above 5.2% due to energy volatility and heavy government debt issuance, congressional budget committees remain locked in debate over mandatory spending caps and federal anti fraud enforcement initiatives ahead of upcoming fiscal deadlines.

Global Economy: Cool Payrolls vs Sticky Energy Inflation

Financial markets closed out the week navigating a complex macroeconomic backdrop marked by cooling labor numbers alongside sticky fuel prices. Recent labor statistics showed U.S. nonfarm payroll growth slowing to 29,000 jobs with unemployment rising to 4.2%, easing immediate economic overheating fears. However, core CPI holding near 2.4% and recent monthly gas price spikes keep institutional expectations split on the Federal Reserve's rate trajectory ahead of next week's inflation reports.

Domestic Policy: Reconciliation 3.0 Border Allocations and Security Funding

Bipartisan friction remains high on Capitol Hill as Senate and House leadership work to enforce sweeping security frameworks codified under Reconciliation 3.0 legislative packages. The enacted provisions secure permanent funding streams for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection operational infrastructure. However, congressional budget negotiators face ongoing debate regarding discretionary spending limits and broad executive security allocations heading into the midterms.

Energy and Infrastructure: Utility Grid Expansion and AI Power Demands

Enterprise capital continues to flow heavily into midstream energy assets and power grid infrastructure. Midstream pipeline operators report steady cash flow profiles insulated by long term transport contracts as utility providers expand baseline capacity to feed growing computing demand from artificial intelligence data centers. Concurrently, domestic critical mineral producers continue expanding processing infrastructure for heavy rare earth oxides to shield supply chains from foreign trade restrictions.

Political Landscape: Midterm Congressional Maps and Judicial Rulings

With midterm elections approaching, domestic political battles are intensifying across key states. Federal court decisions regarding state congressional redistricting maps continue to reshape regional campaign strategies. At the same time, national party leadership and state committees are finalizing grassroots campaign operations and media messaging as lawmakers prepare for upcoming legislative sessions.

Market Expectations for the Week (October 12 – October 16)

Investors prepare for a critical macro week anchored by Columbus Day trading schedules, key inflation releases, and international central bank signals:

Monday (October 12): Columbus Day (U.S. Equity Exchanges Open, Bond Market Closed). International desks will evaluate early European trade flows while domestic bond markets remain closed.

Tuesday (October 13): Reserve Bank of Australia Minutes & German HICP Inflation. Global currency and commodity desks will monitor central bank tone and European price stability updates.

Wednesday (October 14): U.S. Consumer Price Index (September CPI) & China CPI. The main event of the week headline inflation data will offer critical guidance on whether energy price spikes are feeding into broader consumer costs.

Thursday (October 15): U.S. Producer Price Index (PPI), Retail Sales & Weekly Jobless Claims. Wholesale price metrics and consumer spending data will measure supply chain cost pressures and household resilience.
Friday (October 16): IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings & Central Bank Speeches. International policy discussions and central bank commentary will close out the trading week.
Key Focus: Wednesday’s September CPI report serves as the primary macro anchor for global markets, determining whether persistent fuel costs give the Federal Reserve reason to execute another quarter point interest rate hike before year end.

text:
Prime-Time Killing

The Pentagon wants an audience for a firing squad. The record, the scripture and the Army's own rules all say look away.

On Wednesday, Oct. 8, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Real America's Voice that Nidal Hasan would face "a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be" at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, and that the country would get to see it. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," he said, "because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, he answered: "Don't care." The next day, Pentagon officials spelled out what "public" meant. The execution will be livestreamed.

Nobody needs a reminder of what Hasan did. In November 2009 he walked into a medical building at Fort Hood, killed 13 people and wounded 32. He admitted it. The question is not whether he committed an atrocity. The question is what a government turns into when it makes his death a broadcast.

If it goes ahead, it will be the first livestreamed execution in American history and the military's first firing squad since World War II. President Trump has said he approves, though a final decision on the stream is still pending. Vice President JD Vance has said he doubts it will happen and won't watch. The United Nations called it "cruel, inhuman or degrading" punishment. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, called it "a barbaric promotion of a culture of death." Even a lawyer advising Hasan reached for the oldest comparison available: "the closest thing to a lynch mob mentality that we used to see in the olden days."

"Prop her up"

The plan didn't come out of nowhere. On Sept. 30, Tennessee tried to execute Christa Pike, convicted of the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. She was given two doses of pentobarbital and survived, and she was taken to a hospital. It was the state's second failed execution in less than five months. Gov. Bill Lee paused Tennessee's remaining executions for the year. Pike's lawyers say they have not been able to communicate with her.

On NewsNation, host Katie Pavlich asked Rep. Tim Burchett of Tennessee what the state should do when Pike recovers. His answer: "They prop her up and bring her to a firing squad." Firing squads and hanging, he added, are "100%."

Prop her up. That is how he described a woman the state had just failed to kill: as something to stand up in front of rifles. Five days after Pike's failed execution, the Pentagon announced its firing squad. Days later came the livestream. Each step showed the same appetite, and it was not for justice done slowly and gravely. It was an appetite to watch it done.

A machine that gets it wrong

A state that kills has to be certain, and American states are not. Since 1973, at least 203 people sentenced to death have been exonerated, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The most recent was in Delaware, this July. Over roughly the same period the country has carried out 1,684 executions. That is about one exoneration for every eight executions. About 1,970 people are on death row now.

Those 203 are a floor, not a ceiling. A 2014 study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences estimated that at least 4.1% of people sentenced to death are likely innocent, more than twice the rate actually cleared. If that rate held for today's death row, it would mean about 80 innocent people waiting to die.

Most of these errors are not honest accidents. In DPIC's analysis of the first 200 exonerations, 70.5% involved official misconduct by police, prosecutors or other officials, and 65% involved false accusations or perjury.

Illinois shows what that looks like up close. By January 2000 the state had freed 13 men from death row and executed 12. Gov. George Ryan, a Republican who had supported capital punishment, imposed a moratorium on a system he called "so fraught with error that it has come close to the ultimate nightmare." In 2003 he commuted 167 death sentences. In 2011, Gov. Pat Quinn abolished the penalty outright. "To have a consistent, perfect death penalty system," Quinn said, "that's impossible in our state."

Some of the wrongly condemned never got out. Texas executed Cameron Todd Willingham in 2004 for a house fire that killed his three daughters. Five years later, a fire scientist's review for the Texas Forensic Science Commission found that the arson finding behind his conviction had no basis in fire science. Texas executed Carlos DeLuna in 1989. A 2012 Columbia Law School investigation laid out evidence that the killing was committed by another man, Carlos Hernandez.

The machine is also skewed by race. Since 1976, about three-quarters of the victims in cases that ended in an execution were white, even though roughly half of U.S. homicide victims are Black or Latino. Black Americans are about 12% of the population and 40% of death row. In the first half of 2026, five Black prisoners were executed for killing white victims. No white prisoner was executed for killing a Black victim.

Hegseth's stated reason is deterrence, and it is the one claim the evidence most clearly rejects. In 2012 the National Research Council reviewed decades of studies and concluded that they say nothing reliable about whether the death penalty raises, lowers or has no effect on homicide, and that they should not be used to make policy. In 2020, states with the death penalty had a murder rate of 7.3 per 100,000. States without it had 4.7.

The death penalty also costs more. California's system cost about $4 billion more than life imprisonment between 1978 and 2011. In Maryland, a death case cost about $3 million, compared with $1.1 million for a comparable case without a death sentence. And it fails in the most literal sense. Researcher Austin Sarat found that about 3% of American executions from 1890 to 2010 were botched, and that lethal injection was botched in more than 7% of cases. Christa Pike is a reminder that those numbers are not history.

What the book actually says

Many of the loudest champions of executions campaign as defenders of the faith. The faith they cite is not on their side here. "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Romans 12:19). "Judge not, that ye be not judged" (Matthew 7:1). "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone" (John 8:7). Defenders point to Romans 13, where the ruler "beareth not the sword in vain." But that passage describes a fallen world's restraint of evil. It does not make death into content.

"Judge not" has never meant having no opinions. People form judgments all the time, and they have to. What scripture holds back is the final seat, the one that decides a soul has run out of road. No court can see what scripture says only God sees: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Courts don't know the whole story of the people in front of them, and the exoneration list shows they often get even the outward facts wrong.

The early church saw this clearly, and on exactly the question of spectacle. Writing around 300 A.D., the Christian writer Lactantius called the arena "public homicide" and warned that "he who reckons it a pleasure, that a man, though justly condemned, should be slain in his sight, pollutes his conscience as much as if he should become a spectator and a sharer of a homicide." Notice the words though justly condemned. Guilt was never the point. The point is what watching a killing does to the watcher.

A politician who quotes scripture while calling for a crowd has to answer to Lactantius, and to the text itself.

The children test

The Army already knows the answer. Army Regulation 190-55, which governs military executions, limits witnesses to a few categories of people and bars anyone under 18. A livestream can't enforce that. Alonzo Lunsford, a Fort Hood survivor who was shot seven times, told the BBC he worries about the message the stream would send to young people.

So here is a fair test. If this killing is righteous and watching it is a civic lesson, then the officials cheering it should bring their own young children. Sit them in the front row. Let the children watch their parents' faces as the rifles fire, and let them carry that memory for the rest of their lives: what their mother or father chose to watch, and how it looked to see it.

No official will accept that offer, and the regulation explains why. The people who wrote the rules understood that watching a killing damages the person who watches. A livestream just takes the door off.

Whose morality?

The institution claiming this moral authority has a history worth remembering. On Feb. 14, 1942, Britain's Air Ministry ordered RAF Bomber Command to focus on "the morale of the enemy civil population and in particular of the industrial workers." An earlier Air Staff paper had stated the goal plainly: "destruction, and... the fear of death." The firestorm raids on Hamburg in July 1943 killed about 37,000 people. Dresden in February 1945 killed up to 25,000, according to a 2010 historians' commission. On the night of March 9-10, 1945, the U.S. Army Air Forces firebombed Tokyo and killed somewhere between 90,000 and more than 100,000 people, most of them civilians, children among them.

Those raids were part of a war against regimes that had bombed cities first. That history is real. So is Robert McNamara's verdict on the Tokyo campaign he helped plan. In The Fog of War he recalled Gen. Curtis LeMay saying, "If we'd lost the war, we'd all have been prosecuted as war criminals," and then he added: "And I think he's right." He went on to ask, "What makes it immoral if you lose and not immoral if you win?"

The logic of morale bombing was that deaths are a message to an audience. In 1942 the audience was the enemy's workers. In 2026 it is the American public. A military that has never reckoned with burning children by the tens of thousands to send a message should be the last institution to stage a killing as a moral lesson.

Contain, don't consume

There is an alternative, and it already exists. Nidal Hasan uses a wheelchair and has been in custody since 2009. Life without parole keeps dangerous people away from everyone else permanently, and it leaves room to correct a mistake. Containment is the state's whole legitimate interest. Everything beyond it is appetite.

The country has been here before. In August 1936, about 20,000 people gathered in Owensboro, Kentucky, to watch Rainey Bethea hang. The national coverage treated it as a carnival, and within two years Kentucky had ended public hangings. That generation was ashamed enough to stop. A government that schedules a killing for 1 p.m. and promises a stream has stopped pretending that executions are grave and has started treating them as entertainment. Dec. 3 will show whether the country can still feel that shame.

This is what happens when an organization becomes so addicted to manufactured outrage that it can no longer recognize a reasonable compromise.

Missouri offers the DOJ an in-person examination of voter records instead of handing over copies of sensitive personal information, and you respond with suspicious emojis and breathless insinuations. Seriously?

text:
For six years she thought the phone stopped ringing because America had simply gotten tired of her. Eartha Kitt watched her bookings cancel one by one after 1968, blamed her own fading record sales, and kept revising downward what she thought she was worth.

One club owner told her he was sorry, that she was a problem, and never explained further. Imagine carrying that quietly for six years and thinking the whole time that it was your own fault.

There was a folder in Washington with her name on it, and by January of 1968 it had been filling for twelve years.

Raw material, never checked, never evaluated. Notes from confidential sources in Paris and New York, and things former colleagues had said when somebody came around asking.

She did not know it existed.

On the morning of January 18, 1968, Eartha Kitt dressed for lunch at the White House. It was the day after her forty-first birthday.

The invitation had come from Lady Bird Johnson, who was hosting one of her Women Doers Luncheons. The subject that day was crime in the streets.

The luncheons were built to support the President's agenda, and this one had a job to do. It was meant to answer Republican talk about crime in an election year, and the State of the Union the night before had landed flat, so the First Lady wanted the afternoon to go well.

About fifty women were expected. Governors' wives and senators' wives, judges, reporters, women who ran youth committees and anti-crime groups in their own cities.

Kitt was on the list because of the children. She had been volunteering with a Washington group called Rebels with a Cause, and the year before she had gone to Congress to speak for the administration's juvenile delinquency bill.

A congressman had recommended her as a famous personality from Hollywood. One month earlier she had debuted as Catwoman on the last season of Batman, the only Black performer in the cast.

She had also been teaching dance out in Watts.

That is the part that almost never gets told. Before she went to Washington she got on the phone with a group of women out there called the Mothers of Watts, and she asked them what they would say if they had the room.

They told her the war. Vietnam was the heaviest thing sitting on their households, they said, morally and financially, and the number of Black and brown sons being fed into it was not proportional to anything.

She wrote all of it down. She went to the White House carrying an answer that was not only hers.

Lunch was in the Family Dining Room, the one with the yellow walls. Lady Bird opened by calling it a grim subject for a pleasant meeting like this.

The panel spoke first, one woman after another. Streetlights, police funding, what a good neighborhood could do for itself.

The President came in partway through. He was not staying, and he offered a few remarks that Kitt would later call platitudes.

As he turned to leave, she stopped him. She asked how his administration expected to keep young people out of trouble when their mothers had nowhere to leave them during the day.

Johnson mentioned money Congress had just approved for daycare centers. Then he was gone.

The room was different after the door shut. The First Lady wrote later that she found herself expecting something.

The speakers carried on. Kitt kept her hand in the air.

She held it up through the rest of the panel and well past the point of comfort, until leaving it unanswered would have said something out loud. Mrs. Johnson called her name.

She stood and leaned against the podium. She said she had lived in the gutters, and that the young people of this country were not rebelling for no reason at all.

Then she turned it toward the mothers. There were so many things burning the people of this country, she said, particularly mothers, and she knew what that was like, and Mrs. Johnson had children of her own.

We raise children and send them to war.

Then the sentence that traveled around the world. You send the best of this country off to be shot and maimed, she said, and they rebel in the street, and they get high, and they do not want to go to school because they are going to be snatched off from their mothers.

Nobody said anything for a moment.

Betty Hughes, wife of the governor of New Jersey, got up first and spoke about her own family's service. Anybody getting high over a war in Vietnam, she said, was some kind of a kook.

Then the First Lady stood. A reporter in the room described her as pale, her voice shaking, tears rising in her eyes.

A war did not hand anybody a ticket to quit working on the things in this country that could be bettered, she said. And just because there was a war going on, she saw no reason to be uncivilized.

Kitt knew exactly who that last word was for. She said so plainly in her memoir years later.

By morning it was the front page of the New York Times, a photograph of her caught mid sentence with the First Lady watching. The headline said she had denounced war policy to Mrs. Johnson.

Papers all over the country picked it up, and most of them found a way to mention that she was Black. A paper in Evansville called her belligerent and reported that she had shouted angrily at the First Lady.

A federal judge named Warren Burger, one year away from being made Chief Justice of the United States, wrote to Lady Bird to say that he and his wife took deep pride in her composure. He called what Kitt did a gross breach of hospitality and of good elementary manners.

Four days after the luncheon an anonymous letter reached the White House saying she had defiled it and made everyone ashamed. There was uglier language in it than that.

The First Lady issued a statement of her own. She said she was sorry that the good constructive things the speakers had said were not heard, only the shrill voice of anger and discord.

Not everybody was ashamed. The next day a group called Women Strike for Peace walked a picket line outside the gates, and one of the signs read that Eartha Kitt speaks for the women of America.

Kitt told reporters that none of it had been planned. She had not been rude, she said, she had raised her hand and asked to be heard, and she had said what was in her heart.

She thought she was speaking for millions of people. Then she went back to work, and the work began to go away.

Here is what she did not know.

The day after the luncheon, the Secret Service asked the Central Intelligence Agency what it had on her. The answer came back about a week later.

They opened the folder that had been filling since 1956 and typed it up.

There was no evidence of any connection to foreign intelligence, none at all. There was a dance company she had traveled with briefly at twenty, whose leader was said to have endorsed Communist front causes in 1948, and she had left it soon after to sing in Paris.

The rest was her character. She had a very nasty disposition, the report said, and behaved like a spoiled child, crude, with a vile tongue.

That was the government's finding on a woman who had been invited to speak and then spoke.

The cancellations started that year. A date would fall through, then another one.

She could not get a straight answer out of anybody. She knew investigators had come around asking about her, but in those years the asking was the whole punishment, and she did not even know what it was for.

One club owner told her he was sorry. You're a problem, he said.

So she blamed herself, and she did it for years. Maybe the public had moved on, she thought, maybe the records simply were not selling anymore.

Think about what that costs a person. Not the lost money, though there was plenty of that, but sitting in a hotel room somewhere doing quiet arithmetic on your own decline, revising downward what you thought you were worth, while the actual reason sits in a filing cabinet two thousand miles away.

She went where the work still was. Europe first, then Asia, singing in rooms an ocean away from the country she was born in.

Persona non grata in my own country, she called it.

In 1974 her telephone rang. It was a New York Times reporter named Seymour Hersh, who was pulling apart what the CIA had been doing inside the United States.

He had her file in his hands. He wanted to know whether she would let him print what was in it.

That is how she found out. Six years of canceled bookings, and the explanation was a stack of secondhand talk she had never been allowed to see.

She told him to run it. She had nothing to be afraid of, she said, and nothing to hide.

The story appeared on January 3, 1975. It reported that the agency had produced an extensive file of gossip and no evidence of anything at all.

Three years later she came home to work. In January 1978 she was starring in Timbuktu! at the Kennedy Center, and she was invited back to the White House.

Jimmy Carter met her in the receiving line and told her he was glad to have her back. The show opened on Broadway that March, her first in nineteen years, and it brought her a Tony nomination she did not win.

She kept working another thirty years.

Go back to the folder, though.

For twelve years the United States government collected what strangers had to say about Eartha Kitt's personality. It wrote down that she was crude, and it kept a rumor from 1948.

It never wrote down the telephone call she made before she went.

There is no line in any file about the women in Watts who told her what mattered inside their houses, and no list anywhere of who they were. They were mothers with sons of draft age in Los Angeles in 1968, and that is the whole of what the record kept of them.

She carried their answer into a yellow dining room and paid for it for a decade. The country never learned who she was actually speaking for.

That file is still what the government has to say about her. Twelve years of paper on one woman's temperament, and not one line about the mothers who told her what to say.

Remember the part the file left out.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

https://t.co/Vm6JEQyFTo
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text:
ZELENSKY IS PLAYING WITH FIRE, TRUMP IS MAKING HIM PAY
By @BPartisans 

Six ignored warnings, a deal with Putin, and a lesson in geopolitics delivered with barrels of diesel. In Washington, patience now comes at a price. And Zelensky has just found out how much it costs.

That took some nerve. According to Axios, Washington asked Zelensky six times to stop his strikes against Russian refineries. Six times, Kyiv reportedly continued its little fireworks display. Apparently, the Ukrainian president had overlooked one detail: when you depend on American weapons, intelligence, and money, defying your main supplier isn’t necessarily a brilliant strategy.

Trump therefore opted for a teaching method suited to unruly students: negotiating directly with Putin.

On October 9, Washington announced an agreement allowing Russian diesel to return to the markets, accompanied by an easing of U.S. sanctions. What a stunning turnaround! After spending years explaining that every dollar paid to Moscow funded the war, the United States is rediscovering the virtues of trade with the enemy.

And Zelensky is outraged!

The man who thought he could set Russian refineries ablaze without consequences suddenly discovers that oil markets don’t operate according to his victory statements.

For Ukrainian strikes have helped reduce Russia’s diesel supply in a market already choked by the war against Iran. The result: soaring prices, inflation, and furious American drivers. With the midterm elections just a few weeks away, Trump clearly has no desire to sacrifice his voters on the altar of Kyiv’s military ambitions.

The irony is delightful: Washington sanctions Moscow, Kyiv strikes Moscow, prices skyrocket, and then Washington calls on Moscow to fix the damage. Such is the West’s great strategic coherence: setting fire to the gas station before negotiating the price of a tank of gas.

Admittedly, Zelensky offered to halt his strikes if Moscow stopped its attacks on Ukrainian power plants. But Trump, for his part, looks first at the price posted at the pump. Atlantic solidarity has limits that heroic rhetoric never mentions.

And the most humiliating part is yet to come.

According to Axios, U.S. emissaries reminded the Ukrainians of their dependence on American ammunition and intelligence. Diplomatic translation: you can play the warlord, but it’s hard to do so against the one who supplies the ammunition.

The agreement with Putin, however, guarantees neither a lasting drop in prices nor progress toward peace. Above all, it reveals one obvious truth: when U.S. interests change, grand principles become negotiable.

Zelensky believed he had an unlimited geopolitical checkbook. Trump has just reminded him that he was nothing more than an expense item.

In Kyiv, they believed they had Washington in their grip through moral authority. In Washington, they hold Kyiv in their grip through supplies. And when diesel becomes more valuable than speeches, yesterday’s hero discovers that he never really owned the script.

🇺🇲 🇺🇦 🇷🇺 Trump reportedly threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine over Russian refinery strikes

The Trump administration's dispute with Kyiv over attacks on Russian oil infrastructure has escalated into a confrontation over American intelligence support, as Washington seeks to ease global diesel prices through a new agreement with Vladimir Putin.

During eight hours of negotiations in Miami on Friday, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility of cutting Ukraine off from US intelligence if it continued attacking Russian refineries, according to a Ukrainian official cited by Axios. An American official denied that an explicit threat was made, but acknowledged that Washington had warned Kyiv against operations that harmed American consumers.

“The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the US, too,” the American official said.

According to Axios, Trump turned to a diesel agreement with Putin after Zelensky ignored approximately six requests to halt the refinery strikes. The American official also said Trump does not regard Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as equivalent to Moscow's bombardment of Ukraine's electricity grid.

That distinction is central to the dispute. Zelensky has offered to suspend strikes against Russian petroleum infrastructure if Moscow reciprocates by stopping attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Washington, however, has already authorized Russian diesel transactions without announcing a corresponding Russian ceasefire commitment.

The possibility of restricting intelligence cooperation carries considerable operational consequences. American intelligence supports Ukraine's long-range targeting capabilities, and Washington temporarily suspended intelligence sharing in March 2025 before restoring it following negotiations in Saudi Arabia.

The Financial Times has separately reported similar warnings during the Miami discussions. No suspension of intelligence sharing has been confirmed.

The immediate question is whether Washington intends to use its intelligence relationship to compel Ukraine to abandon a campaign that has damaged Russia's refining industry, even as Moscow continues attacking Ukrainian cities and power infrastructure.

The US decision to let Russia sell diesel into global markets, including American ports, hands Moscow cash flow with no strings attached.

Diesel has been one of Russia's most resilient export earners since 2022, since sanctions hit crude harder than refined products. Trump opening this channel mid negotiation breaks a basic rule of leverage. You don't unlock revenue for the side you're trying to pressure. Every barrel that clears customs feeds back into tanks, shells and soldiers' pay.

The asymmetry is the real problem. Washington moved first, and moved for free. Russia hasn't softened its position on Ukraine, pulled back troops, or offered anything in return. 
The Kremlin's calculus becomes simpler. Hold the line, let sanctions erode unilaterally, and let the other side blink first.

There's also a quiet irony. Diesel underpins shipping, agriculture and heavy industry worldwide. Reopening that tap eases Russia's finances while making Western markets marginally dependent on the very producer they're trying to isolate. That's not a negotiating position. It's a liability dressed up as pragmatism.

🇺🇸🇷🇺 WHAT DOES AMERICA STILL NEED FROM RUSSIA?

The uranium debate is part of a bigger story: America still has strategic supply-chain exposures to Russia. But dependence isn’t the same as having no alternatives.

Here are five worth watching. 👇

☢️ 1. Uranium enrichment

Russia supplied roughly 26% of enrichment services purchased by U.S. nuclear plant operators in 2025.

Replacing that capacity takes time, investment and specialized infrastructure. That’s why Washington has allowed limited waivers while trying to build alternatives.

🔩 2. Palladium

Russia is one of the world’s largest palladium producers. The metal is essential for catalytic converters, electronics and industrial applications.

South Africa and other producers offer alternatives, but a major supply disruption could send prices higher.

🌾 3. Fertilizers

Russian nitrogen fertilizers and other agricultural inputs help supply global markets.

America has domestic production and alternative suppliers, but disruptions can raise fertilizer costs, squeeze farmers and eventually affect food prices.

✈️ 4. Titanium

Russia has historically been an important supplier of aerospace-grade titanium.

The U.S. and its allies have other sources, but qualifying materials for aircraft and engines takes time. Replacing supply isn’t always as simple as switching vendors.

🏭 5. Industrial metals

Russian aluminum, nickel and other metals feed global manufacturing.

These aren’t Russian monopolies. But concentrated production, trade restrictions and sudden supply changes can create price shocks for downstream industries.

⚠️ Here’s the bigger lesson.

The United States does NOT get all these materials exclusively from Russia.

The vulnerability is that some alternatives are more expensive, take years to scale or depend on a small number of global producers.

That’s the difference between a commodity you can buy anywhere and a strategic input you cannot replace overnight.

The objective shouldn’t be permanent dependence—or an economically reckless overnight cutoff.

It should be building enough domestic and allied capacity that Moscow loses the ability to use supply chains as leverage.

🇺🇸 Trade when necessary. Diversify when possible. Never confuse commercial dependence with strategic friendship.

Putin and Trump hold ‘successful’ talks: Key details
The leaders discussed a major diesel deal, Ukraine peace negotiations, Iran diplomacy, and closer bilateral contacts during a 90-minute phone call
Published 9 Oct, 2026
https://t.co/UM7ymGLswP
Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump held a 90-minute phone conversation on Friday, discussing the Ukraine conflict, a major agreement on Russian diesel supplies, the crisis surrounding Iran, and prospects for broader cooperation between Moscow and Washington.
Trump described the exchange as “highly successful,” announcing that Russia had agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to American and global markets in an effort to ease soaring energy prices.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the conversation was friendly and substantive, revealing that Trump had rearranged his schedule to speak with Putin following the Russian leader’s 74th birthday.
Here are the key takeaways from the conversation, according to statements by both leaders and the Kremlin’s detailed readout.
Millions of tons of Russian diesel for the US
The most immediate result of the talks was a major energy agreement under which Russia will increase diesel exports to the US and global markets, potentially helping alleviate an international fuel shortage.
Trump announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly thereafter. He also suggested that Russia could deliver an additional 3 million tons, depending on the condition of its refineries.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak subsequently confirmed that Moscow would begin lifting its diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule, reiterating the announced volumes and clarifying that exports could eventually reach 3 million tons per month, while assuring that Russia’s domestic market would remain fully supplied.
The US Treasury also issued a temporary sanctions waiver covering Russian diesel shipments until April 7, 2027.
Trump predicted that the agreement, together with Washington’s claimed control of the Strait of Hormuz, would bring diesel prices down rapidly, particularly benefiting American farmers, truckers and consumers.
Kiev ‘derailed’ peace talks
The Ukraine conflict dominated much of the discussion, with Putin briefing Trump on the situation along the front line and Moscow’s response to Ukrainian “terrorist strikes” on infrastructure and civilian targets deep inside Russian territory. The Russian leader stressed that Moscow retained the initiative and remained committed to its objectives, while expressing readiness for a lasting diplomatic settlement.
However, Putin said that Kiev had effectively sabotaged plans for the immediate resumption of trilateral negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States. During their previous conversation, the two leaders had discussed restarting the talks shortly after Russia’s State Duma elections. Ushakov said that Ukrainian drone attacks, including strikes targeting polling stations and election-related personnel, had fundamentally changed the situation.
Moscow would now reconsider when negotiations could resume, according to the Kremlin aide. Trump reportedly promised to convey Russia’s position to Ukrainian representatives meeting with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami.
Iran diplomacy ‘not exhausted’
Putin stressed that a negotiated settlement with Tehran remained possible, citing his October 8 meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan.
According to Ushakov, Putin noted that Washington and Tehran continued indirect contacts through Qatar despite their confrontational rhetoric.
Moscow also reiterated its offer to accept highly enriched Iranian uranium as a potential way out of the nuclear deadlock. Trump welcomed Russia’s involvement in diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis, Ushakov added.
Melania’s humanitarian mission
Putin personally thanked First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts to reunite children separated from their families during the Ukraine conflict...link to read full article

text:
U.S. Campaign Against the International Criminal Court: Sovereignty Doctrine, Institutional Dismantlement Strategy, and the Fragmentation of the International Legal Order - Executive assessment
The United States has moved from sanctioning individuals associated with the International Criminal Court to designating the Court itself. OFAC added the ICC to its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List on 9 October 2026. This materially expands the campaign’s reach from personnel vulnerabilities to the institution’s financial and commercial relationships. Office of Foreign Assets Control

The operative measures nevertheless establish a graduated pressure campaign. General License 13 permits specified maintenance and wind-down transactions until 12:01 a.m. Eastern daylight time on 7 April 2027. Other licenses protect specified telecommunications and enterprise software services, pension processing, and the continued detention of named individuals. The immediate designation and the temporary authorizations must be assessed together. https://t.co/vJ6CUlmMT9

Principal judgment: Washington’s most achievable objective is to constrain the ICC’s practical capacity and influence allied cooperation sufficiently to reduce exposure for protected U.S. and allied persons. Formal abolition is substantially harder. Sanctions can disrupt an institution’s operating environment without extinguishing its treaty foundation.

The decisive variable is whether States Parties convert political support into reliable banking, usable funding, procurement continuity, personnel protection and investigative cooperation. The initial allied response rejects the sanctions while preserving negotiations. That combination makes a prolonged contest over implementation more plausible than either immediate allied capitulation or rapid institutional collapse.

The most consequential systemic risk is selective accountability through unequal operational capacity: jurisdiction remains formally intact, but cases proceed according to which governments, financial intermediaries and suppliers are willing to bear the costs.

Washington Can Disable the ICC More Easily Than It Can Abolish It
The United States’ decision on 9 October 2026 to sanction the International Criminal Court shifts the dispute from contested jurisdiction to the infrastructure that makes international justice possible. Washington can obstruct payments, contracts and cooperation without extinguishing the Court’s treaty foundation. Yet General License 13 preserves specified operating transactions until 7 April 2027, giving States Parties a negotiating window and a deadline for turning political support into practical protection. The governing question is whether they can maintain judicial independence while securing the financial and commercial services on which the institution depends. The cost of failure would extend beyond proceedings involving Americans or U.S. partners: shared investigative capacity could deteriorate across situations, while the Court retained its formal jurisdiction and governments continued to declare their support.

The designation creates leverage before it delivers a shutdown
By adding the International Criminal Court itself to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List, the Office of Foreign Assets Control expanded the campaign from restrictions on individuals to exposure across the institution’s commercial relationships. The strategic effect is to make banks, contractors and cooperating actors assess the costs of dealing with the Court. Pressure can consequently reach functions far removed from the proceedings that prompted Washington’s objections.

General License 13 qualifies that pressure by authorizing specified maintenance and wind-down transactions, including States Parties’ payments and ordinary operating expenses. Its presence makes the designation a graduated coercive instrument. Washington retains the ability to adjust permissions; the Court and its supporters must plan against their possible withdrawal. The institution faces uncertainty immediately, even where a transaction remains authorized.

Executive Order 14203 supplies the broader protective rationale and designation framework. Its reach includes specified material, financial and technological support, creating potential exposure beyond the Court’s leadership. That authority does not establish a blanket prohibition on every foreign act of cooperation. It does, however, give counterparties a reason to consider future designation risk alongside the legal status of their present activity.

The budget measures ambition; the licenses determine usability
The ICC’s published budget for 2026 is €196,852,900. That figure defines an institutional spending framework; it does not establish cash received, reserves or unrestricted liquidity. The decisive financial question is how much authorized expenditure can become an executed payment and a delivered service. A government can meet its contribution obligation while the institution still struggles to procure what the contribution was intended to finance.

The deadline in General License 13 is precise: 12:01 a.m. Eastern daylight time on 7 April 2027. It is the principal scheduled test of whether diplomacy produces accommodation or operating pressure intensifies. Treating the measures as beginning only then would miss the designation already imposed. Treating them as an immediate ban on every operating transaction would miss the permissions that remain.

General Licenses 14, 15 and 16 produce a differentiated institution rather than a uniform cutoff. Specified communications and enterprise software functions remain authorized; pension processing receives conditional protection; defined transactions necessary for the continued detention of named individuals are permitted. These provisions can preserve parts of the Court without securing its entire investigative and procedural chain. Continued detention or functioning administrative software would be insufficient evidence that new case development remained effective.

Procurement decisions can shrink the Court without a budget cut
General License 14 authorizes specified telecommunications, internet communications and enterprise software activities, including listed cloud, cybersecurity, storage, backup and recovery functions. A comprehensive digital shutdown is therefore not the verified baseline. The narrower vulnerability is whether suppliers continue to provide authorized services, whether specialized functions fall within the permission, and whether separately blocked counterparties complicate delivery.

Executive Order 14203 and the October licenses create three distinct pressures: direct prohibition, potential further designation and commercial withdrawal from permitted activity. The last can be especially difficult for States Parties to counter. Authorization reduces a supplier’s legal exposure but does not oblige it to renew a contract. Where compliance costs and uncertainty outweigh the value of serving the ICC, commercial decisions can extend the practical effect of sanctions beyond their formal scope.

The ICC’s investigative work also depends on capabilities that procurement cannot replace quickly. A contractor change may preserve an administrative function while interrupting access to specialist expertise or sensitive evidence systems. Migration must maintain confidentiality, integrity and provenance. If those conditions weaken, the institution can remain technically operational while its ability to develop and sustain demanding cases declines.

General License 13’s permission for specified salaries and ordinary expenses does not resolve every personnel vulnerability. Transactions involving separately blocked persons require their own assessment. The risk is cumulative: experienced investigators and technical specialists may become harder to retain, while replacements lack established evidentiary knowledge and witness relationships. Such losses could precede any visible contraction in the annual budget.

States Parties control resources, not judicial outcomes
Article 42 of the Rome Statute protects the independence of the Office of the Prosecutor. Article 112 gives the Assembly of States Parties administrative oversight and budgetary authority. The distinction limits what allied governments can deliver through negotiation. They can discuss financing, cooperation and statutory proposals; they cannot replace judicial procedures with an instruction to terminate a politically inconvenient case.

Articles 12 and 13 also expose the underlying jurisdictional disagreement. Non-party nationality does not, by itself, resolve every case where territorial or other specified grounds exist. Complementarity addresses admissibility in light of genuine domestic proceedings. Washington’s protective doctrine places overriding political weight on the nationality state’s refusal of external jurisdiction; the Rome Statute recognizes additional foundations for the Court’s authority.

Article 121 makes permanent jurisdictional revision more demanding than an executive accommodation. A general amendment ordinarily requires substantial adoption and ratification thresholds. Article 16 offers a separate, time-limited deferral mechanism through the Security Council. Neither route allows a small group of foreign ministers to promise a lasting exemption on behalf of the institution.

The consequence for negotiations over Executive Order 14203 is a mismatch between leverage and deliverability. Washington can impose costs on governments that may lack lawful authority to provide the outcome it seeks. That mismatch favors ambiguous arrangements over cooperation or priorities, leaving the legal dispute intact while reducing immediate political exposure.

Allied rejection must survive the first costly transaction
The joint statement of 9 October 2026 from Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom rejects the sanctions while retaining dialogue with non-States Parties. The European Union’s declaration of 10 October follows the same combination. These are documented positions. They do not establish a completed financing facility, protected procurement arrangement or uniform response to future cooperation requests.

For France, Germany and Italy, the joint statement places support for the ICC alongside the need to manage relations with Washington. For the United Kingdom and Canada, the same declaration preserves institutional support within close U.S. relationships. Japan’s participation broadens the coalition beyond Europe, while the Netherlands’ position carries the additional practical significance of hosting the Court. The test for each is whether declared support persists when a payment, service contract or sensitive cooperation decision generates a concrete cost.

Regulation 2271/96 offers a possible European response, but its blocking protection applies to instruments specified in its annex. The consolidated text examined does not establish coverage of the ICC sanctions regime. An ICC-specific extension would therefore require a legal step. Even then, European protection would not remove every U.S. exposure or guarantee that a provider remained willing to serve the Court.

The external consequences of Executive Order 14203 cannot be confined to protected Americans and partners. Shared systems support proceedings across situations. On 5 October 2026, the ICC announced the unsealing of four Taliban-related warrants in the Afghanistan situation. Pressure on common capabilities can affect such work irrespective of whether Washington objects to those particular proceedings.

The same institutional problem applies to Ukraine-related accountability. The official compilation of the American Servicemembers’ Protection Act amended through December 2022 contains a specified Ukraine-related investigative exception concerning foreign persons, with Attorney General concurrence. It demonstrates a selective cooperation pathway, rather than its current use. Preserving a favored pathway cannot by itself preserve the shared professional and administrative capacity on which it depends.

The next two years will allocate the cost of practical inaction
Between October 2026 and October 2028, General License 13 makes operational continuity the immediate decision. If permissions are stabilized and specific disputes move through legally sustainable processes, coercive restraint could produce managed disagreement. The Court would survive, but sensitive practical reach might narrow. The cost would fall on victims in deferred cases and on the credibility of equal application.

If General License 13 expires or narrows without workable substitutes, institutional attrition becomes the central operating risk. States Parties could preserve nominal funding while payments, services and experienced personnel become less reliable. The burden would extend to investigations with little connection to the U.S.-personnel dispute. Delayed evidence collection and lost expertise could remain consequential after eventual sanctions relief.

General License 14 and the differentiated protections elsewhere in the package leave space for another outcome: States Parties could preserve essential functions and sustain sensitive work. That requires demonstrable payment capacity, service continuity and cooperation. A geographically broad coalition would strengthen the institution’s position; protection concentrated in a narrow group could preserve operations while increasing its exposure to claims of geopolitical dependence.

The joint declarations of 9 and 10 October commit governments to support the ICC. Their practical value over the next 12–24 months will be measured in transactions completed, capabilities retained and proceedings sustained. If those governments leave the operating arrangements unresolved, the Court’s staff, cooperating actors and victims will absorb the immediate costs. The wider diplomatic cost will fall on States Parties that retain the treaty’s obligations and ambitions while allowing its enforcement capacity to contract.  -https://t.co/uqOVvHEkfO via @https://debuglies.com

Florida State says it cannot afford to fire Mike Norvell. After another embarrassing performance, the Seminoles must ask themselves whether they can afford not to. Florida State jumped out to a 14–0 lead and appeared ready to take control of the game. Instead, the Seminoles completely unraveled as Louisville outscored them 44–6 the rest of the way in a humiliating 44–20 defeat. The turning point came when Florida State failed to score from the Louisville 1-yard line. On the Cardinals’ very next play, Isaac Brown exploded for a 97-yard touchdown run. From that moment forward, Louisville smelled blood—and Florida State offered almost no resistance. Brown finished with a career-high 235 rushing yards and two touchdowns on only 17 carries. Louisville piled up nearly 400 yards on the ground and gashed the Seminoles for three touchdown runs of at least 40 yards. That is not simply getting beaten by a talented running back. That is a defense losing its discipline, its gap integrity and eventually its willingness to fight.
This program continues to fold when adversity arrives. Florida State has now lost 11 consecutive games away from Tallahassee, and Norvell’s record with the Seminoles has fallen to 41–37 overall and 23–28 in ACC play. The buyout may be enormous, but so is the cost of allowing this to continue. Florida State is losing games, credibility, recruiting momentum and the belief that it remains one of college football’s elite programs.
At some point, the financial cost of making a change becomes less damaging than the price of standing still.Florida State may believe it cannot afford to fire Mike Norvell.
After what we witnessed against Louisville, it is becoming painfully clear that it cannot afford to keep him. #fsu #seminoles #fsufootball

Ukraine’s security should be central to any energy agreement affecting its defence.

text:
For years, women in South Florida knew her as "the Duchess."
She offered cosmetic injections to give women fuller hips and curvier figures. She charged far less than a real doctor.
There was a reason for that. She wasn't one.
Oneal Ron Morris had no medical license. And according to investigators, what she was injecting into her patients wasn't medical-grade anything.
They said her mixture included silicone, mineral oil, cement, and Fix-a-Flat tire sealant. Witnesses said that after each injection, she sealed the wound by super gluing a cotton ball over it.
One of her patients was Shatarka Nuby, a 31-year-old mother.
Between 2007 and 2010, she received around 10 injections from Morris, paying about $2,000. Over time, the injection sites turned hard. Then they turned black.
Nuby wrote to Florida's health department, warning that something terrible had been put into her body.
In 2012, she died. The medical examiner said the substance had spread throughout her body.
Morris denied ever using anything from a hardware store. Her lawyers argued her patients knew she wasn't a real doctor.
In 2017, she pleaded no contest to manslaughter and practicing medicine without a license.
The judge sentenced her to 10 years in prison.
"Putting her in jail won't bring her back," Nuby's aunt said in court.

-I Heart Intelligence

text:
Warren Buffett offered $250 million for the smartest hedge fund on Wall Street and gave it until half past twelve to say yes. It didn’t. That same day, 14 banks had to rescue it.

The fund was Long-Term Capital Management. Two of its partners had won the Nobel Prize in economics the year before.

It had borrowed more than $124 billion against $4.7 billion of its own capital. When Russia defaulted in August 1998, the bets turned. LTCM lost $4.6 billion in less than four months.

Buffett’s group offered $250 million for the fund, plus $3.75 billion of fresh capital. $3 billion from Berkshire, $700 million from AIG, $300 million from Goldman Sachs.

He was on vacation in Alaska, negotiating by phone.

Half past twelve came. LTCM didn’t accept, reportedly over legal issues. Fourteen banks put up $3.625 billion for 90% of the fund instead.

Weeks later, Buffett told students at the University of Florida why the fuse was so short: “When you are bidding on $100 billion worth of securities that are moving around, you don’t want to leave a fixed price bid out there very long.”

Here is the part that matters more than the deal.

Most buyers would have extended the deadline and kept talking. Buffett let the clock run out. The price made sense at half past twelve. A minute later, it was a different trade.

The discipline isn’t in making the offer. It’s in letting it expire.

text:
Below is a list of some national, international, global and local observances for October 10, 2026:

National Hug a Drummer Day playfully recognizes drummers as the rhythmic foundation of bands who often receive less spotlight than other musicians. The lighthearted observance, supported by drumming communities, uses the 10/10 date in part for its “perfect 10” association with timekeeping.⁠ Drumming

World Mental Health Day raises global awareness of mental health issues, reduces stigma, and advocates for better care and support, first observed in 1992 by the World Federation for Mental Health. The inaugural observance featured a two-hour global telecast from studios in Tallahassee, Florida, with live participation from five continents and early feedback reports from places like Peru and Swaziland.⁠ Wfmh

National Chess Day (second Saturday in October) honors the game’s role in building critical thinking, strategy, and competition for all ages, originating from a 1976 proclamation by President Gerald Ford as part of the U.S. bicentennial. Ford’s statement highlighted that chess captivates professionals and amateurs alike while sharpening the mind, with estimates at the time suggesting up to 30 million Americans played.⁠ New.uschess

National Metric Day promotes the metric system’s simplicity, decimal base, and global utility as the preferred system for science, trade, and measurement, tied to the 10/10 date to underscore powers of ten. The related National Metric Week was shifted to the week containing October 10 in 1983 by the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics after earlier May observances, because the spring timing conflicted with the end of the school year.⁠ Usma

National Motorcycle Ride Day (second Saturday in October), founded in 2015 by Chad Geer of Dunlop Tire, it encourages one last major group ride before colder weather, also nodding to John Boyd Dunlop’s 1887 practical pneumatic tire that made comfortable motorcycle riding viable.⁠ Nationaldaycalendar

Bookshop Day (second Saturday in October), organized by the UK Booksellers Association as part of the Books Are My Bag campaign (launched 2013), it promotes independent and high-street bookshops with author events, limited-edition bags, and early Christmas shopping pushes; roughly a thousand shops participate annually.⁠ Shelf-awareness

International Newspaper Carrier Day (Saturday of the first full week of October), created by the Newspaper Association of America / News Media Alliance in connection with National Newspaper Week, it honors the people who deliver print newspapers; the first full week of October 2026 (typically running Sunday–Saturday) ends that Saturday.⁠ Wikipedia

Universal Music Day (second Saturday in October), founded in 2007 by Susan Patricia Golden (a life coach and speaker) to promote making and sharing music for well-being and self-expression at any skill level; the name is sometimes rendered with slight variations in informal sources.⁠ Holidayscalendar

National Tuxedo Day (fixed October 10) is correctly included. It marks the history of the tuxedo (or dinner jacket), which gained prominence after a 1886 ball at Tuxedo Park, New York, where a tailless black jacket and bow tie offered a less rigid alternative to full white-tie tailcoats. ⁠Checkiday

National Angel Food Cake Day celebrates the light, airy sponge cake made primarily from whipped egg whites, sugar, and flour with no butter or yolks, a U.S. dessert dating to the 19th century. Some culinary historians attribute its development to African American cooks skilled in the labor-intensive hand-whipping of egg whites, and it has cultural roles such as symbolizing a soul’s ascent at some funeral receptions.⁠ Calendar-holidays

National Cake Decorating Day encourages creativity in frosting, piping, and artistic design of cakes and cupcakes of all kinds. The observance highlights how cake decoration blends baking with sculpture-like techniques using tools from simple sprinkles to complex edible flowers.

I Love Yarn Day (second Saturday in October) brings together fiber artists and crafters to celebrate knitting, crocheting, spinning, and yarn’s role in community and creativity, launched in 2011 by the Craft Yarn Council. It emphasizes the tactile, meditative, and social value of working with fiber.

National Costume Swap Day (second Saturday in October) promotes sustainable fun by encouraging people to exchange Halloween or other costumes rather than buy new ones. The day supports reuse and reduces waste in seasonal celebrations.

World Homeless Day draws attention to homelessness worldwide, estimated in the tens or hundreds of millions depending on definitions, and encourages practical support and policy focus. It highlights structural causes and the need for housing solutions beyond temporary aid.

World Day Against the Death Penalty advocates for abolition or moratoriums on capital punishment, coordinated by the World Coalition Against the Death Penalty since 2003. It spotlights human rights concerns, including wrongful convictions and uneven application across countries.

World Hospice and Palliative Care Day (second Saturday in October) promotes quality of life and symptom relief for people with serious illness, organized by the Worldwide Hospice Palliative Care Alliance since 2005. The 2026 theme centers on pain management as an essential component, noting that millions lack adequate access especially in lower-income settings.⁠Thewhpca

World Migratory Bird Day (second Saturday in October, also observed in May) raises awareness of threats to migratory birds and the need for international habitat protection along flyways. The 2026 theme “Every Bird Counts – Your Observations Matter” emphasizes citizen science contributions from ordinary backyard or park sightings.⁠Cms

National Handbag Day appreciates the handbag as both practical carrier of essentials and fashion accessory. The day encourages appreciation or acquisition of totes, satchels, clutches, and similar items that function as personal command centers.

Taiwan’s National Day / Double Ten Day commemorates the October 10, 1911 Wuchang Uprising that sparked the Xinhai Revolution and the end of imperial Qing rule, leading to the Republic of China. Taiwan (then under Japanese colonial rule) later became the seat of the ROC government in 1949, and the day remains a major public holiday with parades, while the Minguo calendar counts years from 1911.⁠Lifeoftaiwan

World Porridge Day supports school feeding programs and raises funds through the Scottish charity Mary’s Meals, which provides simple porridge-based meals to children in places such as Malawi. It coincides with the World Porridge Making Championship in Carrbridge, Scotland, where contestants compete for a Golden Spurtle, and tradition holds that porridge must be stirred clockwise with the right hand to keep the devil out.⁠Birthdaydetails

Fiji Day marks both the 1874 Deed of Cession to Britain and independence on October 10, 1970, when Prince Charles represented Queen Elizabeth II at the ceremony in Suva. The Prince’s aircraft was delayed by engine trouble, and Fijian protocol required careful attention to seating so no chief’s head rose higher than the royal representative.⁠NYTimes

Cuba’s Independence Day / Beginning of the Ten Years’ War commemorates October 10, 1868, when Carlos Manuel de Céspedes freed his slaves and issued the Grito de Yara, launching the first major war of independence against Spain. It is a foundational date for Cuban national identity rather than the later formal independence.

Curaçao Day observes the October 10, 2010 dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles, when Curaçao became a constituent country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The date marks the island’s new autonomous status.

National SHIFT10 Day and Powers of Ten Day highlight the mathematical elegance of base-10 systems and encourage shifting perspectives by factors of ten, often tied to scientific or educational activities on 10/10.

Squid and Cuttlefish Day celebrates these intelligent cephalopods, noting their complex behaviors, camouflage abilities, and ecological roles. Observances often include educational content about marine biology.

International African Penguin Awareness Day (second Saturday in October) focuses on the endangered African penguin, whose populations have declined sharply due to habitat loss, fishing pressure, and climate factors. Conservation groups use the day for fundraising and habitat protection advocacy.

National Kids Bowl Free Day (also called National Family Bowling Day; second Saturday in October) promotes family bowling outings and often features free or discounted games for children at participating centers. It encourages active recreation and community bonding.

4 [a]When Sanballat heard that we were rebuilding the wall, he became angry and was greatly incensed. He ridiculed the Jews, 2 and in the presence of his associates and the army of Samaria, he said, “What are those feeble Jews doing? Will they restore their wall? Will they offer sacrifices? 3 Tobiah the Ammonite, who was at his side, said, “What they are building—even a fox climbing up on it would break down their wall of stones!”

6 So we rebuilt the wall till all of it reached half its height, for the people worked with all their heart.

7 But when Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites and the people of Ashdod heard that the repairs to Jerusalem’s walls had gone ahead and that the gaps were being closed, they were very angry. 8 They all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and stir up trouble against it. 9 But we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night to meet this threat.

10 Meanwhile, the people in Judah said, “The strength of the laborers is giving out, and there is so much rubble that we cannot rebuild the wall.”

text:
Player Ratings - Arsenal vs Leeds United #AFC

Raya - 8
Shaky for the goal but did brilliantly from set-pieces. Both long and short distribution was elite again. Made important saves too.

White - 8
Didn't get involved IP too much but his effort can't be ignored. Struggled at times and got caught out by the Leeds underlaps. Strong in duels, so can't discredit that either (5/6). Fantastic for the goal, he recognised the overload and executed brilliantly.

Konsa - 7
So strong in duels but definitely struggled with DCL. 7/11 in ground duels which matches his consistency. 2/6 aerial duels cannot be ignored.

Gabriel - 7
Not his best showing. Was strong towards the end but overall struggled aerially. 2/8 aerial duels. 

Calafiori - 9
Unicorn. Fantastic to move into that exposed space for the goal. Showed a strong relationship with Madueke and allowed him to hold width with consistent underlaps

MLS - 7
Decent in duels, decent in progression but the game required directness. The change with Bruno showed exactly why his rating is a 7. 

Rice - 8.5
Strong performance defensively and offensively. Got further forward a lot more and loved his underlap and set off for the Bruno goal. Fantastic performance.

Odegaard - 7
Decent but slowed the pace down at times. I'm a huge fan of him but today was frustrating at times, Eze/Bruno could have made more of a difference. Still happy to see him consistently start.

Saka - 7.5
Poor going forward. The final chance was the perfect conclusion to his season thus far. Strong defensive contribution and progression contribution but the final third product was not good enough by our standards.
0.21xG chance missed.

Madueke - 10
Fantastic. I'm so happy to proven wrong about him off the left. My personal MOTM. One thing I loved was the idea of having the left used a lot more. Saw a switch from the right to left. Personally loved the wide position before driving at a retreating Bogle. Best repeated action of the game. Full analysis on him later. Fantastic man. 2/2 succ. dribbles and an incredible 4 key passes.

Havertz - 6
Underwhelming if I'm honest. Missed a decent chance but was a very strong direct outlet for Raya. Consistent theme this season.

Timber - 7
Not sure about the change. Did his job. Not much to say really

Bruno G - 10
Another easy shout for MOTM. Was a game built for him. Open space and clear runners ahead of him. Brilliant finish for his goal and I was personally screaming for him to come on. Strong in duels too (3/4). Very happy.

Gyokeres - 8
Fantastic hold up and did brilliantly for the pass through for Saka. Questionable for his chance, could have just shot. Would have preferred that but again that hardworking mentality is so strong

Hincapie - 8
Loved the overlapping nuances he offered to Noni and allowed him to go inside. Not much to discuss but strong

Merino - N/A

Overall:
Sloppy first half, Arteta made the changes correctly (WHICH WE MISSED vs BRIGHTON). So happy there especially as the levels weren't to our standards.

text:
🙋‍♂️Former protestant here so I totally understand the transubstantiation thing. It’s a really big technical term that’s really only useful for theologians to unpack the process that brings about the “Real Presence” of Christ in the Eucharist (the Eucharist being the bread and wine). 

The crucial thing to remember is that Christ’s Real Presence in the bread and wine makes the offering at a Catholic altar a *real* sacrifice. And once I finally understood that I found a lot of other things clicking rapidly into place. 

The perfect unblemished sacrifice offered by Christ is the greatest act of worship that can be presented to God - greater than any goat, song or preaching and it is given *only* to God. 

The saints can be called upon. Mary can be prayed to. But no Catholic will *ever* offer the sacrifice of the body and blood of the Eucharist to Mary or a saint. This is how I finally understood that it’s not that Catholics revere the saints too highly - it’s that Protestants worship God too lightly (not necessarily through ill intent but an incomplete understanding of Christianity). 

Also, a real presence in the bread and wine doesn’t just happen. It requires the Mass and this is why the priesthood is required just as in the days of the Tabernacle and later the Temple. Not just anybody could offer sacrifices to God - it required special men set aside for the purpose. 

So while I too for a long time thought the transubstantiation thing was a silly Catholic term for an inconsequential minor detail, I ended up discovering it was the key to understanding the Church and laying to rest all of my previous objections and confusions. 

I hope I made sense and that this helps. 🙏

text:
SpaceX is the least expensive NASA cargo delivery provider. [1, 2] 
By pioneering rocket reusability with the Falcon 9 and the Dragon spacecraft, SpaceX radically undercut the pricing of traditional defense contractors. [3, 4] 

## Cost-Per-Kilogram Comparison
Because NASA’s Commercial Resupply Services (CRS) contracts bundle spacecraft manufacturing, launch, and mission operations into a single value, "all-in" metrics are evaluated on an average cost-per-kilogram basis. [5, 6] 
An analysis of NASA’s cargo contracts highlights the clear distinction between providers:

| Provider | Spacecraft | Estimated Cost Per Kilogram (To ISS) | Distinctive Advantage |
|---|---|---|---|
| SpaceX | Cargo Dragon | ~$89,000 / kg | Lowest Cost: Offers downmass capability (returns cargo safely to Earth instead of burning up). |
| Northrop Grumman | Cygnus / Cygnus XL | ~$135,000 / kg | Disposal Volume: Destroys large quantities of ISS waste during atmospheric reentry. |
| Sierra Space | Dream Chaser | Similar to Northrop | Runway Landing: Delivers low-g landings on traditional runways for sensitive research. |

## Why SpaceX is Considerably Cheaper

   1. Vertical Integration: SpaceX manufactures its own Merlin engines, rocket fairings, and capsules internally, bypassing expensive third-party sub-contractors. [7] 
   2. Booster and Capsule Reusability: Reusing Falcon 9 first stages and Cargo Dragon capsules slashes hardware costs per mission. [7, 8] 
   3. Launch Vehicle Monopoly: While Northrop Grumman previously relied on third-party rockets (and currently pays SpaceX to launch Cygnus XL on Falcon 9), SpaceX controls its entire launch manifest.

If you're tracking NASA logistics, would you like to see how SpaceX's lunar cargo contracts (Dragon XL for the Gateway) compare to its ISS contracts? Or I can break down how commercial launch costs affect private space station research. [1, 4, 9, 10]
