Watching people die by violence, even if those people have it coming, damages the spectator irreversibly. I don’t mean physical or emotional damage, though many who see unnatural deaths up close do vomit and suffer from uneasy dreams afterward. Rather, I mean something more like the loss of their humanity and dignity, through partaking in the process of treating a person—in many ways so similar to themselves—like a machine to be turned off or ripped apart, a malfunctioning printer or an old car. To see this process is to be diminished, and the decision to make the execution visible to all is an invitation to self-harm, sent out to everyone with an internet connection. It is hard to appreciate how awful this viewing experience will be, until you have it. And then of course it will be too late. I have seen videotaped executions and have been diminished by every single one.

In August 2014, Hasan wrote a letter from prison to Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, then the leader of the Islamic State, and asked to be granted citizenship as a “soldier of Allah.” No response was recorded. Ironically, it seems likely that Hasan would sympathize with Hegseth’s penchant for public execution, because the Islamic State interpreted the Quran to require that execution be carried out in public. Fornicators, according to Quran 24:2, should be flogged, and their punishment should be “witnessed” by a “group of believers.” By extension, the Islamic State determined, such a group should witness the punishment of all scripturally ordained crimes. Certain crimes, such as brigandage, are to be punished with crucifixion, an inherently public method of killing that the Islamic State carried out on video. Regrettably, I have seen footage of such a death.

From the July 2025 issue: Inside America’s death chambers
https://t.co/LY6qPPL37N

In the years before Hasan’s 2013 court-martial, he stopped shaving, in Islamic defiance of Army regulations that prohibit soldiers from growing beards. Mike Simpson, an Army officer and emergency-room doctor near the facility where Hasan was incarcerated, told me a few years later that he put the word out to colleagues that if Hasan ever had a medical emergency (not unlikely, given that he suffered paralysis and other conditions after being gunned down in the course of his terror attack), Simpson would like to be called to shave Hasan personally. The shaving would arise out of medical necessity—the patient might need a mask, with a reliable seal around the face—but Simpson, for his own pleasure, wanted to shear the bastard himself.
But the pleasure that might come from shaving Hasan would be quite different from what one might experience by shooting him in the heart. The Army won’t struggle to find a dozen willing soldiers to act as an execution party for Hasan. Hasan has said he wants death. Hegseth said he “doesn’t care” what Hasan’s final wishes might be. But I suspect that the volunteers’ enjoyment of their duty will be dampened if they notice signs of ecstasy from Hasan, as he is tied to a post 15 paces away from them and prays his way to the end. Hamlet could not bring himself to kill Claudius in prayer, because killing him in the midst of a holy act—“to take him in the purging of his soul, when he is fit and season’d for his passage”—would be too merciful.

In this world, denying Hasan the pleasure of death on his own terms, and letting him instead spend a few more earthly decades in tedious incarceration, would seem a much more onerous punishment. Therefore I would propose an alternative to public execution: public incarceration. Hasan should be placed in a small space, with a Pentagon-funded livestream of his remaining years. If the purpose of the spectacle of his death is to demonstrate to others the “serious consequences” of murdering 13 people, I doubt any execution would be more frightening than the slow, public aging of this repulsive murderer, as biology and time carry out his sentence. I would tune in to the livestream myself now and then, until I grew bored and found better things to do, and better ways to spend my own remaining time. This would take Hasan’s life and make from it a small gift to the rest of us, rather than taking something irrecoverable from us as we give martyrdom to him.

Major General Mohamedin Ismail Ahmed Defects from Tasis Alliance and Joins Sudanese Army, Accuses Dagalo Family of War Crimes and Attempting to Seize Control of Sudan with Foreign Backing

Successive defections shake the UAE-backed militia and its allies as senior commanders denounce the Dagalo family's atrocities, apologize to the Sudanese people, and join the national army amid mounting battlefield defeats. 

Major General Mohamedin Ismail Ahmed, Deputy Chief of Staff for Administration of the Sudan Liberation Forces Gathering, an armed movement allied with the UAE-backed Rapid Support Militia (Janjaweed) under the Tasis Alliance, has declared his defection and joined the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), alongside a group of officers, non-commissioned officers, and soldiers. In a recorded statement addressed to the Sudanese people, Ahmed accused the militia's leadership, particularly the Dagalo family, of committing war crimes, ethnic cleansing, rape, and widespread looting. He said these atrocities, along with his realization that the militia's political promises were deceptive, prompted his decision to abandon the alliance and join the national army.

His defection comes just two days after Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq Al-Fanjari, commander of the Rapid Support Militia's Special Missions Group, defected alongside approximately 300 officers and soldiers and 30 military vehicles. The two departures reflect an accelerating pattern of defections from the militia and its allied armed groups, coinciding with a series of military defeats in North Kordofan.

Sudan's state news agency, SUNA, reported on October 3 that a force led by Mohamedin Ismail, also known as Abu Dharra, had joined the Sudanese Armed Forces in the Al-Tina sector of North Darfur. According to the report, the force consisted of 106 fighters, including 18 officers, accompanied by several military vehicles. His recorded statement provides further details about the reasons behind his departure, his assessment of the militia's leadership, and his position on the ongoing war.

Ahmed said his decision to join the army followed the general amnesty offered by General Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan, Chairman of Sudan's Sovereignty Council and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces. He outlined three principal reasons for his defection, beginning with his rejection of the atrocities committed against Sudanese civilians.

Ahmed accused the Dagalo family of taking complete control of the Rapid Support Militia and attempting to seize control of Sudan with the encouragement and support of foreign powers. He said the militia's leaders had committed war crimes, ethnic cleansing, rape, and looting, and credited the Sudanese army and the Sudanese people with thwarting their plans. He explained that he and his comrades had initially believed they were fighting for a legitimate cause, only to discover that the militia had no genuine cause worth fighting for and that its promises of political change and justice had been used to deceive and recruit fighters.

Reflecting on how their association with the militia had affected their standing in society, Ahmed said that he and his fellow commanders had once been respected community leaders who welcomed guests and protected those seeking refuge. Their involvement with the militia, however, had placed them alongside people he described as traitors and thieves. He said the crimes committed during the war were fundamentally incompatible with their values, customs, and traditions, leaving them ashamed of their association with the group. Instead of the promised reform and justice, he said, they had witnessed nothing but death, destruction, and devastation, beginning in their home region of Darfur and spreading across Sudan.

Speaking on behalf of himself and his comrades, Ahmed issued a direct apology to the Sudanese people for having supported the militia. "We ask the entire Sudanese people for forgiveness because we stood on the wrong side. But I swear, we had been deceived," he said. He maintained that neither he nor his fighters had participated in atrocities or violated the rights and dignity of civilians, insisting that they had consistently opposed such abuses and expressing confidence in their innocence. His remarks are particularly significant because they come from a senior commander of an armed movement allied with the Rapid Support Militia, who now publicly acknowledges that he and his comrades were misled by promises of change and justice.

Ahmed also addressed General Al-Burhan directly, declaring that he and his fighters were ready to mobilize as soon as they received military orders and participate in operations against the Rapid Support Militia. He said they were prepared to fight from Kordofan all the way to Um Dafog and would always be found on the front lines alongside the Sudanese Armed Forces. He also praised commanders and fighters who had defected before them, thanking them for encouraging and helping his group make the decision to return to the army.

Ahmed's departure is particularly significant because of his senior position within the Sudan Liberation Forces Gathering, led by Al-Tahir Hajar, which is allied with the Rapid Support Militia through the Tasis Alliance. His defection suggests that divisions are spreading beyond the militia's own military formations to armed movements that joined its political and military coalition.

Just two days earlier, Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq Al-Fanjari had publicly declared his defection from the militia in a recorded statement, apologizing to the Sudanese people for the suffering, displacement, and loss caused during the war. He repudiated abuses against civilians, including violations of their lives, property, and honour, and urged his former comrades to abandon the militia and stand behind the Sudanese Armed Forces, declaring that "this war has no just cause and no future." His remarks closely resemble Ahmed's statements about having been deceived, the absence of any legitimate cause for continuing the war, and the need to seek forgiveness from the Sudanese people.

The militia has experienced several other prominent defections throughout 2026, including Major General Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, known as Al-Nour Al-Gubba, and Brigadier General Ali Rizgallah, known as Al-Savna. Their departures followed reported disagreements with the militia's leadership, allegations of marginalization, and complaints about the Dagalo family's control over military decisions and resources. Other forces reportedly defected under Brigadier General Musa Khamsin, Abu Bakr Dahloub, and field commander Al-Tayeb Al-Ahideb. These developments followed the high-profile defection of Abu Agla Keikal, commander of the Sudan Shield Forces, in October 2024, which represented one of the most significant blows to the militia during the earlier stages of the war.

The repeated defections have exposed longstanding disputes within the militia over leadership, resource allocation, and unequal treatment of different tribal groups. Former commanders have complained about the Dagalo family's dominance over military decision-making and allegations of discrimination against fighters from communities outside its closest circle. Reports of marginalization and mistreatment have emerged among sections of the Misseriya and Mahamid communities, raising questions about the militia's professed commitment to equality, justice, and building a state that transcends tribal divisions. This contradiction has become increasingly apparent as commanders from allied armed movements, including Ahmed, publicly acknowledge that the promises of political change and justice that initially attracted them to the alliance resulted in destruction and atrocities.

The defections have also coincided with a series of battlefield defeats suffered by the militia in North Kordofan. Sudanese Armed Forces and allied units regained control of Sudri and Um Sharu in September, followed by Al-Mazrub on October 2, after military operations that reportedly inflicted substantial losses in personnel and equipment. These setbacks have increased pressure on the militia's leadership and fighters, particularly as internal disagreements intensify and confidence in its ability to sustain military operations weakens. Despite the extensive UAE support that has helped the militia continue fighting through weapons supplies, financing, and logistical networks, such assistance cannot necessarily resolve the growing divisions within its military formations and alliances.

Major General Mohamedin Ismail Ahmed's defection, coming just two days after Lieutenant Colonel Mohamed Azraq Al-Fanjari's departure, adds another dimension to these developments. The growing number of defections now extends beyond the militia's direct military command to armed movements allied with it under the Tasis Alliance. As military operations continue in Kordofan and commanders and fighters increasingly abandon the militia, questions are mounting over its leadership's ability to maintain the cohesion of its forces and political alliances, particularly as former commanders and allies publicly accuse it of deception and atrocities while urging remaining fighters to abandon the group and return to the Sudanese Armed Forces.

text:
Senator Patty Murray’s selective outrage is a textbook case of moral inversion.
When the Pentagon moved to livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan—the radical Islamist Army major who murdered 13 people and wounded more than 30 others at Fort Hood in a jihadist attack—Murray rushed to denounce it as a “grotesque public spectacle,” warned about kids seeing “bloodshed,” and demanded the decision be revoked. She framed the issue as a matter of national character and not “glorifying violence.”
Yet when American citizens are murdered by people who entered the country illegally—Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray, Rachel Morin, and others—she has offered no comparable public sympathy, no naming of the victims, and no condemnation that centers their deaths as a consequence of failed border enforcement. Searches of her statements, Senate website, and X account turn up nothing. The Laken Riley Act, named after one such victim, drew only her opposition on procedural, cost, and due-process grounds; she did not use the occasion to acknowledge the murder itself.
This is not a neutral application of principle. Murray has been willing to treat the punishment of a convicted mass-murdering jihadist as a moral crisis requiring immediate intervention, while remaining effectively silent on the preventable killings of young American women and girls by people who had no legal right to be here. She has, by contrast, repeatedly intervened on behalf of undocumented immigrants facing detention or deportation, even in cases with no serious criminal history, emphasizing due process, family unity, and the supposed excesses of enforcement.
The pattern reveals a hierarchy of concern that tracks political incentives rather than the gravity of the harm: criticism of state violence against a jihadist killer is urgent; the deaths of American citizens at the hands of illegal aliens are not. That is not consistent opposition to violence or consistent concern for human life. It is selective moral accounting in which some victims count and others do not, depending on whether highlighting them advances or complicates preferred policy outcomes. The gap between her reaction to Hasan’s execution and her silence on the “angel victims” is not subtle, and it does not require special insight to notice.

**Trump just green-lit Russian diesel exports with a Treasury waiver through April 2027, announced hours after a call with Putin while a Ukrainian delegation sat in Miami negotiating an energy truce.** The volumes are modest—roughly a day-and-a-half of U.S. demand in the first tranches—but the move reverses recent sanctions pressure and hands Moscow revenue precisely as Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries had tightened global supply.[[1]](https://t.co/4MKO5eWB0Y)

### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A shocking betrayal of Ukraine and the sanctions regime, with Trump handing Putin cash to prolong the war while Ukrainian negotiators were sidelined or used as cover.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Trump is treating sanctions as a negotiable lever to deliver lower diesel prices ahead of midterms, extracting supply from Russia in exchange for temporary relief while testing whether an “energy truce” can be forced on both sides.

### 2. Observations
- The timing is the tell: announcement on October 9 came during or immediately around Ukrainian-U.S. talks in Miami involving Witkoff and Kushner, with Zelensky later calling it a “smokescreen” and “weak decision by strong partners.”[[2]](https://t.co/Wm32f0uAEW)
- Volumes are small enough that analysts across outlets note they will not materially move U.S. pump prices; the political signal and precedent matter more than the barrels.[[3]](https://t.co/9IdWqYX9b6)
- Trump had just signed broader Russia sanctions legislation in September; the Treasury’s general license waiving diesel sanctions until April 2027 is a direct carve-out that undercuts the law’s intent on energy revenue.[[4]](https://t.co/RQKMtxq3x4)
- Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries helped drive the price spike Trump is now trying to ease; Moscow had banned its own diesel exports earlier. The deal effectively rewards the side whose infrastructure was under pressure.
- Zelensky’s public line—that this is an “investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”—aligns with Kyiv’s consistent position that sanctions relief without Russian concessions on strikes or territory simply funds the aggressor.[[5]](https://t.co/AnrVyF3FRJ)
- Putin’s side gets immediate revenue and a precedent for further waivers; Trump gets a domestic win on fuel costs and a talking point that he is “dealing” rather than escalating.

### 3. Snapshot
On October 9, 2026, President Trump announced on Truth Social that Russia would immediately supply over 300,000 metric tons of diesel (plus larger follow-on volumes) to U.S. and global markets after a “highly successful” call with Putin. The U.S. Treasury issued a temporary general license allowing Russian diesel sales through April 7, 2027. Ukrainian President Zelensky condemned the move while his delegation was in Florida for war-resolution talks. Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure continued in the broader context of stalled energy-truce discussions.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- September 18, 2026: Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions legislation targeting energy revenues and related networks (LT).
- October 9, 2026: Trump-Putin call; Trump posts deal details on Truth Social; Treasury issues general license for Russian diesel (LT).
- October 9–10, 2026: Ukrainian delegation in Miami meets U.S. envoys; Zelensky issues public criticism calling the move a “gift to Putin” and “smokescreen” (LT).
- Ongoing: Ukrainian drone campaign on Russian refineries; Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure; high U.S. diesel prices (~$6.28/gallon reported) (IT).

### 5. Sides
**Trump administration (Populist Realist / IT priority):** Best case is that domestic fuel costs and voter pressure on truckers/farmers outweigh abstract sanctions purity; leverage sanctions relief to extract supply now and test Russian willingness for broader de-escalation.  
**Critique:** LT on the waiver and volumes; IT on political timing before midterms. The reversal of recent sanctions law is explicit.

**Ukrainian government (Technocrat / security-first):** Sanctions and pressure on Russian energy are core leverage to force negotiations from strength; easing them without reciprocal Russian restraint on infrastructure attacks funds the war and signals weakness.  
**Critique:** LT on the revenue flow to Russia; IT on the optics of talks occurring simultaneously with the announcement.

**Russian side:** Gains hard currency and a precedent for sanctions erosion while its refineries remain under Ukrainian pressure; frames the move as cooperative on global energy stability.  
**Critique:** Standard revenue-maximizing behavior; no evidence yet of linked concessions on strikes.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
- **Known Knowns:** Specific volumes announced, Treasury license details and expiration, Zelensky’s public statements, recent sanctions law, and price context (LT).
- **Known Unknowns:** Whether additional Russian diesel will actually reach U.S. shores versus global markets; exact linkage (if any) between the waiver and Ukrainian refinery-strike pause; net price impact after logistics and quality factors.
- **Unknown Knowns:** Internal U.S. intelligence or negotiating records on what Putin privately offered beyond diesel supply; full scope of Miami talks.
- **Unknown Unknowns:** Secondary effects on European energy solidarity, Russian use of new revenue, or escalation if Ukrainian strikes continue despite the deal.

### 7. Incentives map
Trump gains midterm messaging on lower prices and “results” with Putin. Russia gains revenue and precedent. Media and opposition gain outrage content. Ukraine loses leverage narrative. The attention stack (fear/anger over energy costs and war prolongation) rewards the dramatic reversal framing more than the modest barrel count.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Track actual delivered volumes, any measurable price effect, and whether Russian behavior on Ukrainian infrastructure changes. Sanctions are a tool, not a sacrament—use them when they produce outcomes, drop or adjust them when they don’t. Domestic energy costs are a legitimate voter priority; pretending otherwise is theater.

**Evil AI Advice:** Announce the deal, pocket the political win on prices, let the Ukrainians scream, and quietly expand the waiver later. Revenue to Moscow is someone else’s problem; the midterms are now.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch Treasury license enforcement and actual export data for real volume versus announcement.
- Monitor Ukrainian refinery-strike tempo and any Russian response on energy infrastructure as the clearest test of linkage.
- Compare delivered diesel prices in coming weeks against pre-announcement levels and analyst forecasts.
- Note any follow-on sanctions actions or further carve-outs as signals of the administration’s broader Russia policy direction.
- Treat volume claims skeptically until tankers move and independent tracking confirms.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Large, verifiable additional Russian diesel volumes reaching U.S. markets with measurable downward pressure on prices.
- Documented Russian halt or sharp reduction in strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure tied directly to the waiver.
- Explicit U.S. demands or conditions on future waivers that produce measurable Russian concessions beyond diesel supply.
- Re-imposition or tightening of diesel sanctions without new supply deals.

text:
[Take 10/15 · D-5]
**Trump just handed Putin a six-month sanctions holiday on diesel exports the day after signing a law to squeeze Russia’s war machine, right as diesel hit $6.28 a gallon and midterms loom.**[[1]](https://t.co/4MKO5eWB0Y)[[2]](https://t.co/B1IedyRNdb) The volumes are modest relative to U.S. consumption, but the signal is not: price relief now trumps sustained pressure on Moscow’s energy revenues. Zelensky calls it a birthday gift to Putin and a smokescreen for talks; the White House frames it as consumer relief.[[3]](https://t.co/uHocgQDCS7)

### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A pragmatic Trump move to flood markets with Russian diesel and crush pump prices ahead of November midterms, clashing with Ukraine’s war effort and exposing fractures in the anti-Russia coalition.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Trump is prioritizing domestic fuel-price stability and midterm voter economics over long-term sanctions enforcement, using a temporary Treasury license to extract short-term supply while Ukrainian refinery strikes and the Iran conflict keep global diesel tight. The deal tests whether Kyiv will de-escalate strikes on Russian energy infrastructure in exchange for continued U.S. support.

### 2. Observations
- Trump signed a bipartisan sanctions-tightening law last month targeting Russian energy revenues, then delivered a six-month general license (until April 7, 2027) on diesel the moment prices spiked—classic election-cycle override of his own prior policy.[[4]](https://t.co/9rC1PZ6ozx)
- The announced volumes (300k tons immediately + 500k Nov + 1M + up to 3M later) equal roughly a few days of U.S. diesel use at most; analysts note it will not materially move prices, yet the political optics and Treasury action are real.[[5]](https://t.co/9IdWqYX9b6)
- Zelensky’s “smokescreen” charge lands because the diesel announcement landed while his envoys were in Miami with Trump’s team (Witkoff and Kushner) discussing peace proposals; Kyiv offered reciprocal refinery/power-plant de-escalation, which Washington reportedly rejected as non-equivalent.[[6]](https://t.co/sXYLssJcuK)
- Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have been effective at tightening Russian diesel supply and exports; Trump publicly criticized them and appears to have moved unilaterally after multiple ignored U.S. requests to stop.[[7]](https://t.co/iJD5X7h6BW)
- Russia’s own export ban on diesel (tied to domestic shortages from Ukrainian hits) is being lifted in tandem, creating a coordinated supply bump that benefits Moscow’s revenues without requiring battlefield concessions.
- The move reverses years of Western policy aimed at starving Russia’s war chest; it is the first extended diesel sanctions relief since 2022 and arrives amid U.S. involvement in the Iran conflict that is also pressuring fuel markets.

### 3. Snapshot
On October 9, 2026, President Trump announced via Truth Social a phone agreement with Putin for Russia to release up to 4.8 million tons of diesel into U.S. and global markets. The U.S. Treasury immediately issued General License 135 suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7, 2027. Zelensky condemned it as an unfair gift to Putin that funds the war. The move responds to diesel prices at $6.28/gallon and comes weeks before midterms, while parallel U.S.-Ukraine talks in Miami on ending the war were underway.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Last month (September 2026):** Trump signs bipartisan law tightening sanctions on Russian oil/gas importers. (LT)
- **Recent months:** Ukrainian drone strikes damage Russian refineries, prompting Russia’s diesel export ban and contributing to global tightness. (IT)
- **October 9, 2026:** Trump-Putin call; Trump posts deal details on Truth Social (300k tons immediate, 500k Nov, 1M thereafter, +3M conditional). Treasury issues 6-month general license. (LT)
- **October 9, 2026:** Zelensky statements call it a “gift to Putin,” “investment in war,” and “smokescreen” for negotiations; offers reciprocal de-escalation on strikes. (LT)
- **October 9–10, 2026:** Kremlin confirms willingness to supply; Russian officials lift domestic export ban. (LT)
- **Ongoing:** U.S. diesel at multi-year highs amid Iran conflict and refinery disruptions. (IT)

### 5. Sides
**Trump administration / U.S. consumer-priority faction (IT/LT mix):** Steelman — High diesel prices hurt farmers, truckers, and voters; temporary supply relief is a legitimate executive tool to stabilize markets without permanent policy reversal. Sanctions remain on other Russian assets. Critique: LT — The license is explicitly temporary and narrow. IT — It undercuts the just-passed sanctions law and rewards refinery attacks without reciprocal Ukrainian relief.

**Ukrainian government (IT):** Steelman — Any sanctions relief without battlefield or de-escalation concessions prolongs Russia’s ability to fund the war; using peace talks as cover for a unilateral deal betrays partnership. Critique: LT — Volumes are small and time-limited. IT — Continued refinery strikes were already straining U.S. patience and global prices; Kyiv’s refusal of unconditional pause contributed to the outcome.

**Russian side (IT):** Steelman — Revenue from diesel exports helps sustain the war economy while Ukrainian strikes damage domestic supply; the deal demonstrates that Western unity on sanctions can be broken by price pressure. Critique: LT — Russia still faces broader sanctions and export limits tied to its own shortages. IT — It gains hard currency and breathing room without major concessions.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
- **Known Knowns:** Trump announced specific volumes and a Treasury license on Oct 9; Zelensky condemned it the same day; diesel prices are elevated; Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have been ongoing and effective.
- **Known Unknowns:** Exact impact on pump prices; whether the Miami talks produced any side agreements or warnings to Kyiv; duration and scope of any future sanctions relief.
- **Unknown Knowns:** Internal U.S. assessments of how much Ukrainian refinery strikes contributed to price spikes versus the Iran conflict; precise Russian refinery repair timelines and export capacity.
- **Unknown Unknowns:** Secondary effects on European energy security or NATO cohesion; Russian use of new revenues; whether this accelerates or stalls broader peace negotiations.

### 7. Incentives map
Trump/Republicans gain short-term voter relief on a visible pocketbook issue before midterms; media attention favors the price-drop narrative over sanctions consistency. Zelensky/Ukraine lose leverage and face potential cuts in support if strikes continue. Russia gains revenue and a precedent for sanctions erosion. Media and opposition gain outrage content. Bureaucracy (Treasury) executes the license as directed. The dominant stack is Fear/Anger (prices, war funding) over sustained Truth (long-term sanctions efficacy).

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Price spikes from war and refinery attacks are real; temporary, narrow relief can blunt domestic pain without ending sanctions. But rewarding non-reciprocal behavior risks signaling that energy coercion works. Demand verifiable de-escalation steps from both sides or the relief becomes pure extraction.

**Evil AI Advice:** Sell the “price relief for Americans” line hard, pocket the political win, and let Ukraine and Europe absorb the strategic hit. The volumes are small enough to claim it changes nothing while the precedent and cash flow to Moscow do the real work. Rinse and repeat on the next commodity.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch actual delivered volumes and U.S. diesel prices over the next 30–60 days; rhetoric exceeds likely impact.
- Track whether Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries pause or intensify and any corresponding U.S. response on intelligence or aid.
- Monitor Treasury license extensions or expansions beyond April 2027.
- Note any linkage (or lack thereof) between this deal and the Miami peace talks or broader sanctions enforcement.
- Compare statements from Trump, Zelensky, and Putin on reciprocity versus one-sided relief.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Sustained, material drop in U.S. diesel prices directly attributable to the Russian volumes.
- Ukrainian agreement to unconditional halt on refinery strikes with no further U.S. sanctions relief.
- Extension of the license into 2027 or broadening to other Russian energy products without battlefield progress.
- Public evidence that the Miami talks produced a coordinated de-escalation framework tied to the diesel license.

text:
WHY I'M STILL BULLISH ON IREN $IREN — DESPITE THE RECENT SELL-OFF
IREN's share price has come under pressure, but I haven't changed my long-term view.
The recent OpenAI revenue headlines have raised fresh questions about the economics of the AI infrastructure boom.
But I'm more interested in what's happening inside IREN's business.
Can it turn growing AI cloud demand into sustainable cash flow and shareholder returns?
That's the question behind my bullish thesis.
🟢 1. THE AI CLOUD TRANSITION IS GAINING MOMENTUM
Look at FY2026:
🔹 AI cloud revenue: $128.8M, up from $16.4M
🔹 Q4 AI cloud revenue: $70.5M, more than double Q3
🔹 Contracted annualised revenue run rate: $4B for 2026 capacity
🔹 Operating annualised revenue run rate: $1B as of August 26
That's meaningful progress for a company transitioning from Bitcoin mining into AI infrastructure.
But there's an important distinction.
Contracted ARR isn't recognised revenue. And revenue isn't free cash flow.
IREN still has to deliver the infrastructure and earn attractive returns.
🟢 2. MICROSOFT PROVIDES IMPORTANT VALIDATION
IREN delivered its first 50MW Horizon deployment to Microsoft in August, and Microsoft accepted it.
That matters.
It's evidence that IREN can deliver infrastructure to one of the world's largest technology companies.
Three additional 50MW phases were targeted for Q4 2026, with contractual grace periods extending into 2027.
But one successful deployment doesn't eliminate execution risk.
The next test is delivering the remaining phases and converting them into revenue.
🟢 3. POWER AND INFRASTRUCTURE ARE STRATEGIC ASSETS
AI computing needs more than GPUs.
It needs electricity, land, cooling, networking and data-centre capacity.
IREN has spent years developing the physical infrastructure behind that demand.
Management's August targets included:
🔹 Approximately 300MW of cumulative IT capacity in 2026
🔹 Approximately 800MW in 2027
Its broader development pipeline also exceeds 5GW.
That's a significant opportunity.
But secured power, planned capacity and operational AI cloud capacity aren't the same thing.
Execution will determine how much of that potential becomes revenue.
🟢 4. IREN IS BUILDING MORE THAN GPU CAPACITY
This is another reason I remain interested in the business.
IREN isn't simply trying to own more GPUs.
It's building an AI cloud platform combining infrastructure, compute and software.
Its acquisition of Mirantis strengthens the software and managed-services side of that strategy.
IREN AI Cloud offers:
🔹 Dedicated bare-metal clusters for demanding AI training and high-performance inference
🔹 Virtualised environments for flexible, secure, multi-tenant workloads
Mirantis has also completed NVIDIA-Certified Hypervisor validation for its k0rdent AI virtualisation stack on NVIDIA GB200 systems.
Why does that matter?
Because AI customers don't all need the same infrastructure.
Some prioritise maximum performance. Others need flexibility and workload isolation.
IREN's opportunity is to serve both.
If that flexibility improves customer adoption and GPU utilisation, the economics could become more attractive.
But technical capability still needs to translate into commercial results.
🟢 5. CUSTOMER DEMAND IS BECOMING MORE DIVERSIFIED
Microsoft is important, but IREN's opportunity extends beyond one customer.
In its July $2.8B contract announcement, IREN named customers including NVIDIA, Perplexity, Figure AI, Together AI, Fluidstack, Fireworks AI, Fal AI and Hume AI.
That matters because different AI customers have different computing requirements.
A broader customer base could support growth across training, inference and other AI workloads.
But diversification doesn't eliminate customer concentration risk.
The real test is how much contracted demand becomes recurring, profitable revenue.
🟠 6. FINANCING IS THE BIGGEST TEST
This is where my bullish thesis becomes more cautious.
IREN reported approximately $14B in existing cash, committed GPU financing and customer prepayments in August.
That's a substantial funding foundation, but it isn't $14B of unrestricted cash.
And the scale of future investment remains enormous.
During its August 27 earnings call, management guided to approximately $25B–$30B in FY2027 capital expenditure.
That's an enormous investment programme relative to IREN's current revenue base.
Investors need to watch:
🔻 Additional debt and financing costs
🔻 Potential shareholder dilution
🔻 Construction and deployment delays
🔻 GPU depreciation and utilisation pressure
🔻 Whether cash generation keeps pace with investment
Financing can accelerate growth. It doesn't guarantee attractive returns.
🔴 7. THE RISKS ARE REAL
Competition from Nebius, CoreWeave and hyperscalers is intense.
GPU rental pricing could weaken as supply expands.
Customer demand could disappoint.
And there's another issue I wouldn't ignore.
On October 7, SemiAnalysis raised reliability concerns about IREN's older facilities in Prince George and Mackenzie, citing reported power, networking and storage problems.
Those allegations deserve scrutiny, although the underlying incidents haven't been independently established here.
The firm also reportedly assessed IREN's newer Texas developments more favourably.
As IREN scales, operational reliability will matter just as much as securing power and deploying GPUs.
And even if IREN delivers rapid revenue growth, shareholders could still see disappointing returns if financing costs and dilution become too high.
A successful AI infrastructure business isn't automatically a successful investment at every valuation.
🎯 MY TAKEAWAY
I'm still bullish on IREN because I believe it has an opportunity to become an important independent provider of AI computing infrastructure.
The transition from Bitcoin mining to AI cloud is gaining traction.
Microsoft's acceptance of Horizon 1, expanding customer relationships and a broader cloud platform are encouraging.
But the next phase matters more than the headlines.
The market has seen the contracts.
Now it needs to see whether IREN can convert:
CAPACITY → REVENUE → CASH FLOW → SHAREHOLDER RETURNS
My bullish thesis isn't that IREN will spend the most.
It's that IREN could build a valuable AI cloud business capable of earning attractive returns on the capital invested.
And that's where the real investment test begins.
Can IREN scale without allowing debt, dilution and capital expenditure to overwhelm the value created for shareholders?
Still bullish on $IREN — but watching execution, financing, utilisation and returns much more closely than the headlines.

15 DAYS. 3.3 MILLION VIEWS. A FAKE GUY WHO’S ALREADY MAKING HIS CREATOR MONEY.

one fictional character. millions of views. a real business opportunity.

here’s a tutorial for testing the format yourself ↓

—

meet Milton Bumford.

ginger bowl cut. round glasses. old-fashioned suit. completely confident in situations where he looks wildly out of place.

his profile already shows:

→ 17.9K followers
→ 324.8K likes
→ restaurant dance: 1.5M views
→ boxing clip: 3.3M views

the interesting part is how much mileage one recognisable character gives the creator.
—
1 → A FACE YOU REMEMBER
the hair, glasses, outfit and silhouette make Milton easy to recognise.

put him in a restaurant, a boxing ring or a car, and viewers still know who they’re watching.

each scene builds familiarity with the same character. that creates a reason to watch his next appearance.

—

2 → THE RESTAURANT CLIP FEELS ACCIDENTALLY CAPTURED

people walk across the frame. someone films him on their phone. chairs block the camera.

those details make it feel like somebody witnessed something ridiculous during dinner.

Milton dances with absolute confidence. his appearance and behaviour create the surprise; the ordinary surroundings make it convincing.

—

3 → THE COMMENTS ARE PART OF THE APPEAL

“he looks like a card from Guess Who.”

“Nigel Thornberry out here getting it.”

“is this not AI?”

people can joke about his face, compare him to familiar characters or question the footage.

a distinctive design gives viewers something specific to react to.

—

HERE’S HOW I’D TEST IT

→ build your character

choose a memorable face, hairstyle, outfit and silhouette.

create a reference sheet with close-ups, full-body images and several angles. preserve those details across videos.

→ pick one clear situation

an awkward dance at dinner. an overconfident boxing lesson. a dramatic entrance into an ordinary shop.

the idea should make sense immediately.

→ plan the shot

decide what the character does, where the camera sits and what happens around them.

aim for believable surroundings, natural movement and casual framing.

→ generate and inspect

Milton’s bio credits Higgsfield AI. the exact workflow behind this clip isn’t public.

use consistent references and check the face, clothing, movement and interactions with the background.

→ test several scenes

some videos on his profile sit around 2K–4K views.

the results vary. keep testing the situation and opening instead of assuming every appearance will reach millions.

—

HOW THE FORMAT CONNECTS TO MONEY

Milton’s profile includes an AI tool discount offer.

the videos demonstrate a result. curious viewers ask how it was made. the creator gives them a product to explore.

sponsored scenes, personalised videos and merch are other possible offers once people care about the character.

15 days is a compelling result, and you can too.

start with one character and three situations. see which one gives people a reason to stop, watch and comment.

text:
On the chronic decline of classical music in higher education, from @amwilson_opera ‘s new book, Culture Vultures: When Activism Meets the Arts? (and I’m not just citing this bit because she quotes me). More below

Where once classical music reigned supreme, the pendulum has swung completely in the opposite direction today. Popular music, almost entirely ignored in the musicological curriculum thirty years ago, now looms large at many British institutions. Classical music is being pushed so far to the fringes of the discipline that in some contexts its position on the curriculum is in total jeopardy. And we have an absurd situation where young people are being told to ‘deconstruct’ a canon of works that they have probably not yet even had a chance to get to know. But where one canon is struck off, another will inevitably rise up in its place. As Ian Pace writes, a university curriculum can never be free of canons: ‘Canons of some type are necessary to teach any body of work, historical period or intellectual tradition. Anyone who has had to do this within ten short lectures will know the brutal choices which need to be made; the idea that such teaching can eschew any sort of “exclusion” is a fantasy.’47 If popular music dominates the curriculum then that becomes the new canon. Will it be critiqued as such? Probably not. The rise of popular music, studied predominantly through approaches that are sociological and anthropological, has been driven in part by ideological impulses to ‘flip the canon’ and partly by pragmatic pressure from university managers who make assumptions about what will attract students. The fee-based payment model that is now in full force across the English-speaking world has created a situation where universities rush to give students what they want (or what they are perceived to want), rather than what they might need in order to gain an in-depth understanding of a subject. This is problematic: the point of an education, surely, ought to be to introduce you to things you do not yet know, rather than to wrap you up in a comfort blanket by reinforcing your existing tastes. Moreover, in terms of solving a recruitment crisis, this strategy patently hasn’t worked. University music departments are now in serious trouble. The reasons for this are many and varied, but jettisoning classical music in favour of pop has certainly not been the salvation for a discipline in jeopardy some managers evidently assumed. Long-established music departments with good reputations are now closing or seeing staff numbers cut, in Britain, the US and Australia.48 In many cases, the departments in question are ones that offered traditional music degrees, comprising elements of history, theory, composition and performance.49 Some courses are being rebranded as something else – typically the ‘creative industries’, which tends to mean bland, pseudo-vocational, business and tech-focused programmes that have little if anything to do with the conventional study of music. This might be seen as a desperate attempt on the part of universities to show to governments that the arts are just as important to the economy as STEM, but in fact there is typically nothing of the arts left in such courses. Many of them will not give students any rich subject knowledge and are, at the same time, only pseudo-vocational. This may be a short-lived experiment: the numbers opting for such courses are unlikely to be high. In 2023, for instance, Oxford Brookes University replaced its long-running MAs in Music and Film with an MA in the Creative Industries. By early 2026 that course had already been suspended and closed to recruitment.’ (1)

Thanks for asking. Do yourself a favor and go immerse yourself in the Gospels:

Matthew 5:9: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God.

Matthew 5:21: Jesus goes beyond prohibiting murder to confront the anger and contempt that contribute to violence.

Matthew 5:38: Rejects retaliation and teaches turning the other cheek.

Matthew 5:40: Calls for generosity rather than responding to mistreatment with coercion or revenge.

Matthew 5:43: Commands love for enemies and prayer for persecutors.

Luke 6:27: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and bless those who curse you.

Luke 6:29–30: Turn the other cheek and respond to mistreatment without retaliation.

Luke 6:32: Extend mercy and love even to enemies, reflecting God's own character.

Luke 6:37: Reject condemnation and cultivate forgiveness.

Luke 6:31: Treat others as you would want to be treated.

Matthew 7:12: The Golden Rule establishes reciprocal care as a fundamental ethical principle.

Matthew 26:51–52: When a disciple uses a sword during Jesus' arrest, Jesus commands him to put it away, warning that those who take the sword will perish by it.

Matthew 26:53–54: Jesus refuses the possibility of overwhelming heavenly force to defend himself.

Mark 14:47–49: Jesus challenges the armed crowd that comes to arrest him, contrasting their weapons with his public teaching.

Luke 22:49–51: Jesus stops his disciples' violent resistance and heals the wounded servant's ear.

John 18:10–11: Jesus commands Peter to put away his sword rather than resist arrest.

John 18:36: Jesus tells Pilate that his kingdom is not from this world, explaining that otherwise his servants would fight to prevent his arrest.

Matthew 27:12–14: Jesus refuses to defend himself through the usual adversarial confrontation before Pilate.

Mark 15:3–5: Jesus remains silent in the face of accusations.

Luke 23:34Jesus prays for the forgiveness of those responsible for his crucifixion.

1 Peter 2:21–23Jesus is described as one who did not retaliate when insulted or threaten revenge when suffering. The arrest narratives are particularly compelling. Jesus' refusal to employ violence was not merely an abstract ethical ideal. He practiced it when violence might have saved his own life.

Mark 10:42–45Jesus contrasts rulers who dominate others with his followers, who are called to serve rather than exercise power over people.

Matthew 20:25–28Greatness is measured by service and self-giving rather than coercive authority.

Luke 22:24–27Jesus rejects the model of kings who lord authority over others and identifies himself as one who serves.

John 13:1–17  Jesus washes his disciples' feet, demonstrating servant leadership rather than domination.

Matthew 23:8–12 Jesus rejects status-driven hierarchies and teaches humility.

Luke 9:46–48Jesus challenges competitive ideas of power and status.

John 6:14–15 Jesus withdraws when people attempt to make him king by force.

Matthew 4:8–10 Jesus rejects the temptation to acquire the kingdoms of the world through allegiance to Satan.

Luke 4:5–8Jesus refuses the offer of political authority obtained through compromise with evil.

Matthew 6:12–15Forgiving others is essential to the life of discipleship.

Matthew 18:21–22 Jesus calls for forgiveness beyond conventional limits.

Matthew 18:23–35 The parable of the unforgiving servant emphasizes mercy over vengeance.

Luke 17:3–4Jesus teaches repeated forgiveness of those who repent.

Matthew 9:13 Jesus emphasizes God's desire for mercy rather than sacrifice.

Matthew 12:7 Jesus again places mercy above rigid religious judgment.

Matthew 12:18–21 Matthew applies Isaiah's description of a gentle servant who does not quarrel or cry out and who brings justice without crushing the vulnerable.

Luke 9:51–56 When disciples want to call down fire on a Samaritan village that rejects Jesus, he rebukes them.

John 8:1–11Jesus prevents the stoning of a woman accused of adultery and redirects the accusers toward self-examination.

Luke 10:25–37The Good Samaritan illustrates compassionate action across hostile ethnic and religious boundaries.

Luke 23:39–43Jesus extends mercy to a condemned criminal while suffering execution himself.

Matthew 16:24–26Jesus calls followers to take up their crosses rather than secure their lives through self-preservation.

Mark 8:34–35 Following Jesus involves self-denial and willingness to suffer rather than dominate.

Luke 9:23–24 Discipleship involves taking up the cross daily.

Mark 10:45Jesus describes his mission as giving his life for others rather than exercising domination.

John 10:11–18 Jesus presents himself as the good shepherd who voluntarily lays down his life for the sheep.

John 12:23–26Jesus uses the image of a grain of wheat dying to illustrate the fruitfulness of self-giving.

John 15:12–13 The greatest expression of love is laying down one's life for others.

Matthew 27:27–44Jesus endures mockery, humiliation, and crucifixion without violent retaliation.

Mark 15:16–32Jesus refuses to save himself through a display of coercive power.

Luke 23:33–43Jesus responds to crucifixion with forgiveness and mercy.

And to respond to your comment about swords.

Matthew 10:34Jesus says he came not to bring peace but a sword. The surrounding context concerns division within families, rather than a direct command to use weapons.

Luke 22:35–38Jesus tells his disciples to purchase swords. The meaning is debated, particularly given his subsequent rejection of armed resistance.

John 2:13–17 Jesus makes a whip of cords and drives activity from the temple. The passage depicts forceful disruption, although it does not explicitly describe him striking people.

text:
A Coronary Artery Calcium (CAC) scan is a non-invasive screening tool used to detect calcified plaque in the heart's arteries. Because insurance generally does not cover routine CAC scans for screening, most health systems and imaging centers offer standard out-of-pocket self-pay rates, usually ranging between $100 and $150.
Common Facilities Offering $150 (or Less) CAC Scans
1. Major Regional Health Systems & University Hospitals
Many major medical centers provide a flat self-pay cash price of $150:
 * Duke Health (North Carolina) — Offers $150 cash pricing (physician order required).
 * Tufts Medicine (Massachusetts) — Flat out-of-pocket rate of $150.
 * WakeMed (North Carolina) — Flat rate of $150.
 * UC Davis Health & Major California Centers — $150 out-of-pocket fee.
2. Independent Outpatient Radiology & Imaging Centers
 * Independent diagnostic imaging facilities (such as RadNet, SimonMed, or local freestanding outpatient centers) routinely advertise flat self-pay rates between $99 and $150.
3. Lower-Cost Alternatives ($49–$99)
 * Kettering Health / Columbus Regional Health (Ohio area) — Offers scans for $49–$99.
 * Hackensack Meridian Health (New Jersey) — Offers scans for $99.
 * St. Louis Heart and Vascular (Missouri) — Offers scans for $99.
How to Get a $150 CAC Scan Near You
 * Ask for the "Self-Pay" or "Cash" Discount Rate:
   When calling local outpatient radiology centers or hospital imaging departments, explicitly ask for their out-of-pocket screening price rather than running it through insurance.
 * Check for a Physician Order/Referral Requirement:
   While some freestanding centers permit self-referral, most hospital systems require a prescription or electronic order from your primary care doctor or cardiologist.
 * Look for Heart Month Specials (February):
   Many cardiology practices and imaging networks offer promotional pricing (often $49–$99) during American Heart Month in February.
 * Use Direct Scheduling Tools:
   Platforms like LabFinder, MDsave, or Diagnostic Orders Direct allow you to compare cash-pay prices across local imaging facilities in your ZIP code.

text:
Grok: The ESP application is technology-neutral (using a plant parameter envelope that bounds multiple designs). It evaluates six potential reactor technologies: four small modular reactor (SMR) designs and two non-light-water designs. Large light-water reactors (like Duke’s existing fleet of 11 units) are not included in this Belews Creek ESP.

If further evaluation confirms SMRs offer the best value for customers, Duke plans to add about 600 MWe of advanced nuclear by 2037, with the first unit targeted for online in 2036 (roughly two ~300 MWe-class units). The site could potentially support more units later (the ESP remains valid for many years). The existing Belews Creek Steam Station (two units, ~2,200 MWe total, coal/natural gas co-fired, commercial since the 1970s) is scheduled for retirement in the late 2030s; the nuclear site is intended in part as a repurposing/replacement option that leverages existing water, transmission, and infrastructure.

Duke submitted the ESP application on December 30, 2025 (after roughly two years of preparation, including site studies, a meteorological tower, groundwater/core drilling, and environmental work). The NRC accepted it for review; an ESP (if issued, targeted around 2027) confirms site suitability (safety and environmental factors) but does not authorize construction or select a final design. Further permits (e.g., construction permit or combined license) would still be required. Public scoping/comment processes have been underway.

This is part of Duke’s Carolinas Resource Plan and longer-term strategy to expand nuclear capacity (alongside license renewals and uprates on the existing fleet) to meet growing demand (including data centers), support reliability, and pursue lower-carbon goals. Large light-water reactors are being evaluated separately, primarily at other sites such as the William States Lee III site in South Carolina or Shearon Harris in North Carolina. No final technology selection or construction decision has been made for Belews Creek; the ESP provides optionality while technologies mature and risks are reduced.

The site benefits from proximity to Belews Lake (cooling water), existing transmission, a skilled local workforce, available land, and community ties from the long-operating steam station. Duke emphasizes that costs, technology readiness, and customer value will drive any final decisions.

This is not a teaching moment. It is your opinion based on how you interpret the data.  

I selected a non-politically  biased website to read instead. 
TLDR

States Most Reliant On Federal Funding
The States That Are Most Reliant on Federal Aid

MoneyGeek analyzed and ranked states by their dependence on the federal government. Rankings account for political affiliation, net benefits individuals and organizations receive, state government revenue from federal sources and GDP per capita. Rankings account for political affiliation, the net benefits individuals and organizations in the state receive, state government revenue from federal sources and GDP per capita.

Key Findings:
Seven of the 10 states most dependent on the federal government were Republican-voting, with the average red state receiving $1.24 per dollar spent.
Thirty-one states sent more to the federal government than they received, slightly higher than the 29 states in 2022.
Of the states that sent more than they received, 48% were Democrat-voting, and 52% were Republican-voting.
New Mexico had the highest return on federal spending of any state ($3.42 per dollar spent), and Delaware had the lowest ($0.46 per dollar spent).

Federal Dependency Rankings by State
MoneyGeek identified the states most dependent on federal funding in 2024 by analyzing the return on taxes sent to Washington and the percentage of state revenue from federal sources. We also compared states by political affiliation and per capita GDP to learn more about the factors that contribute to federal dependency.

Chart removed due to length of post (see Money Geek)

Red States Lead With Federal Dependence
In 2022, wealthier, Democratic-leaning blue states paid more to the federal government than they received. Republican-leaning red states received more in federal funds than they contributed. By 2024, both red and blue states received more from the federal government than they paid in taxes. Red states still outpaced blue states in federal funds received per dollar paid, securing $1.24 compared to $1.14 for blue states. In the MoneyGeek rankings, seven of the 10 most dependent states are red states.

This partisan divide in fiscal dependence stems from different policy choices among states. Health care offers a clear example. MoneyGeek’s analysis of uninsured rates by state and party alignment shows that the 10 non-expansion states hold 42% of America's uninsured while making up just 28% of the population. These Republican-led states decline Medicaid expansion despite generous federal matching funds. Texas alone accounts for more than 40% of the national coverage gap. Residents in non-expansion states can compare health insurance options to find coverage.

text:
‼️ Edward Dubrovsky, co-founder of Cypfer, a Canadian firm that brokered ransomware payments, was arrested in Philadelphia on October 8. He was in Pennsylvania for the Cyber Risk Summit, where Cypfer was the lead sponsor.

He was not arrested as a negotiator caught in the middle. He was arrested as someone who, according to court records, conspired to threaten disclosure of data with intent to extort money, and interfered with commerce by threats. The complaint that charges him remains sealed, which means the public record stops at the two counts. Everything else is reported link, not proven fact.

Yet the link is reported everywhere: Dutch police arrested a ShinyHunters affiliate in September, a teenager who took over the group after that arrest and taunted the FBI over agent data stolen from its own recruitment portal. The FBI says ShinyHunters has extorted over $70 million this year. Multiple sources close to the case say the investigation is now centralized in the Eastern District of Texas, where Dubrovsky's case was moved two days after his arrest.

The scene is a conference room at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel, October 5, 7. A sponsor's stand, a book signing, a LinkedIn post a month earlier saying he was coming to offer "truly agnostic" settlement services. The same room where he would be taken into custody three days later, not as a vendor but as a defendant.

One thing he wrote that now reads differently: he described his firm as an intermediary between criminals and victims. An intermediary does not usually end up indicted for conspiracy to impair the confidentiality of information. The contradiction is not in his words alone. It is in the shape of the charges. The same role that lets a negotiator sit at the table with a victim also lets that person carry messages for the other side.

The sealed complaint decides whether this is a case about one facilitator of crime, or about a whole industry that has learned to dress as a defender while carrying the bag for extortion. The arrest is real. The connection to ShinyHunters is reported but not yet proven. The question for anyone who pays ransoms or negotiates with attackers: if the FBI can reach through the intermediary, it can reach through you.

The complaint is still sealed. This is not the end of the story. It is the first public moment of one.

Early report: these facts come from first disclosures and are not confirmed yet. Expect them to change.

Not that the scene around Oasis was exactly flourishing. By 1997, Britpop’s time was almost done, but it did have a good innings. In fact, it had a longer run at the centre than most genres ever get near. If I had to pick a moment when the starter pistol was fired, I’d say it was about 40 seconds into Blur’s 1992 single Popscene, when the horns blare out, and Britpop begins. Some might say it was the glam stomp of Suede’s The Drowners, released a few months later, that kicked things off. Either way, it began in 1992, till Pulp’s This Is Hardcore acts as the genre’s epitaph in 1998. Six years. That’s a long time in music. We think of “the 60s” as a whole, but really, that was broken up into many phases. The psychedelic era, for instance, was only about two years. But Britpop was six years of beating out the same tune. The Blur of Popscene didn’t really sound that different to the band making The Great Escape. Definitely Maybe wasn’t hugely different from Be Here Now. Even in song length, as despite the later justified accusations that their third album was bloated, their debut, magic though it is, was already rammed with songs that could do with a good bit of trimming.

But six years is a very long time, and by 1997, the music press had the good sense to see that the culture was ready for something else. Many of the bands that fell under Britpop’s Union Jack blanket had already been going for years before Oasis’ arrival. Suede, Blur, Pulp, the Charlatans, the Verve, the Manic Street Preachers. They all at some point got pulled into it. But that was the point of the press. People say now, “they weren’t really Britpop”. Well, they were at the time, because the press threw them together and told you they were part of a movement. “It was all just a lot of crap made up by the papers”. Too fucking right it was! Great. That was what they were supposed to do. Make you believe something was happening, create this moment and get you to buy into it. That’s how all the movements were canonised. It’s why there is fuck all happening now, because there’s no one to pull it all together and sell kids the wish fulfilment that they are part of something big that’s happening that belongs to their time. But it can only ever go on for so long.

So, Britpop was over, and Oasis were the sacrifice offered to the music gods in prayer for the next new. That’s what they had to do. They didn’t turn on Oasis. They still had them in the paper, on the cover; they still reviewed and interviewed them. They didn’t make out that it had all been a big mistake. But they had to find the future and make it feel important, like it was all that mattered, like this next band was what the world was waiting for. After all, the paper was called the New Musical Express. And when it was time for someone to get off, they were left at the station, no matter how big they were.

Where this backfires spectacularly is that they not only have no one decent lined up to take over, but nothing comes along anytime soon. The indie press ends up in a bit of a mess. If you look at the end-of-year lists for 1998,1999 and 2000, there’s no obvious new band to champion as the future or build a movement around. Not that nothing was happening in the late 90s. Plenty was happening. It just wasn’t necessarily NME-centric.

Electronic music was exploding. The Prodigy and The Chemical Brothers were huge, and you could clearly see a scene forming around them, with offshoots and fellow travellers appearing everywhere: Daft Punk, Propellerheads, Fatboy Slim, Basement Jaxx. Suddenly there was a thriving dance scene making its way into the charts.

You could hear Radiohead’s influence spreading too. Muse, Travis, Snow Patrol, Starsailor, Coldplay. Mostly shite, but hey, that’s not Radiohead’s fault. The point is there was a lineage there, and you could hear where it came from.

From America came the dreaded nu-metal. And Eminem and Dr Dre were massive.

text:
🔥 IF THE DEVIL WANTED TO DESTROY AMERICA, WOULD HE REALLY NEED TO CHANGE HIS STRATEGY? 🔥

SPOT 🎯N with Johnny 

🎙️ In 1965, legendary broadcaster Paul Harvey delivered a remarkable commentary titled “If I Were the Devil.”

He imagined how Satan might gradually corrupt a nation, not through an obvious invasion, but by quietly undermining its faith, families, morality, and foundational values.

More than six decades later, his warning still deserves our attention!

WHAT IF THE DEVIL'S GREATEST WEAPON ISN'T GETTING PEOPLE TO WORSHIP HIM, BUT GETTING THEM TO LIVE AS THOUGH GOD DOESN'T EXIST?

Think about it!

If I were the devil, I wouldn't begin by closing every church. I'd encourage Christians to attend on Sunday while ignoring God's Word the rest of the week.

I wouldn't immediately destroy marriages. I'd introduce temptation, pornography, selfishness, and resentment until husbands and wives became strangers beneath the same roof.

I wouldn't openly declare war on children. I'd persuade parents that everything else deserves their attention before teaching their children about Jesus Christ.

I wouldn't necessarily convince people that evil is good overnight. I'd slowly blur the distinction until standing for biblical truth became more offensive than celebrating sin.

I wouldn't need to remove every Bible. I'd simply convince people they were too busy to read one.

And perhaps most dangerously...

I'D MAKE CHRISTIANS SO BUSY FIGHTING ONE ANOTHER THAT THEY FORGOT WHO THEIR REAL ENEMY IS!

📖 EPHESIANS 6:12 (KJV)

"For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places."

Beloved, Paul Harvey's commentary wasn't Scripture or a prophecy. It was a warning about moral and spiritual compromise.

But the Bible warned us about Satan's schemes long before Paul Harvey ever approached a microphone!

📖 1 PETER 5:8 (KJV)

"Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:"

🔥 HERE'S WHAT SHOULD WAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN UP!

Satan doesn't have to convince everyone to hate Jesus.

Sometimes all he needs is for believers to become indifferent toward Him.

A neglected Bible.

A prayerless home.

A compromised conscience.

A marriage without forgiveness.

Children growing up without knowing the Gospel.

SPIRITUAL DECLINE DOESN'T ALWAYS ARRIVE WITH A ROAR. SOMETIMES IT ENTERS THROUGH THE QUIET DOOR OF COMPROMISE!

But here's the glorious news!

THE DEVIL DOES NOT GET THE FINAL WORD! JESUS CHRIST DOES!

📖 JAMES 4:7 (KJV)

"Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."

America's greatest need isn't merely better behavior, stronger institutions, or another political victory.

OUR GREATEST NEED IS GENUINE REPENTANCE, BIBLICAL TRUTH, AND HEARTS TRANSFORMED BY JESUS CHRIST!

✝️ MY FINAL THOUGHT:

Paul Harvey challenged Americans to recognize the dangers of moral decay.

But Scripture gives Christians something greater than a warning.

IT GIVES US THE ANSWER!

Open your Bible. Get on your knees. Love your family. Teach your children. Stand for truth. Share the Gospel.

And remember:

🔥 SATAN MAY BE WORKING TO DECEIVE THE WORLD, BUT HE CANNOT OVERTHROW THE KING OF KINGS!

❤️ Thank you for taking the time to read this far. Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Salvation is God's gift through faith, not works (Ephesians 2:8–9). If you've wandered far from God, turn to Jesus Christ today!

THE DEVIL WANTS YOUR DESTRUCTION. JESUS CHRIST OFFERS YOU ETERNAL LIFE!

text:
PRESSURE POINTS — PART 3

STARLINK VS INDIA: WHO CONTROLS THE DIGITAL SKY?

Elon Musk says powerful business interests are blocking Starlink. The government says security clearances remain pending. With billions at stake in India's satellite broadband market, the battle is no longer just about internet access—it is about competition, regulation and digital sovereignty.

Imagine a company capable of beaming internet from space to a remote village, a mountain outpost or a ship in the middle of the ocean. Now imagine that company has spent years preparing to enter India, obtained key licences and built infrastructure—but still cannot begin commercial operations. Who is holding up the launch?

That question exploded into public view on October 7–8, 2026, when Elon Musk accused unnamed powerful business interests of obstructing Starlink's entry into India to protect their market dominance. He described the delay as a “crime against the people of India.” The Indian government swiftly defended its regulatory process, insisting that the rules were fair and non-discriminatory.

The confrontation raises an uncomfortable question: Is India protecting its legitimate national interests—or is competition in one of its most promising technology markets being held back?

To understand the stakes, we need to look beyond the headlines.

Starlink, operated by Musk's SpaceX, uses a network of low-Earth-orbit satellites to deliver broadband connectivity. Unlike conventional broadband, which depends heavily on terrestrial cables and mobile towers, satellite internet can reach areas where laying infrastructure is difficult or uneconomical. That makes it potentially valuable for remote communities, disaster response, maritime operations and locations near India's international borders.

India is an enormous potential market. Yet commercial opportunity does not automatically confer the right to operate.

Starlink has secured key Indian authorisations, including a Global Mobile Personal Communications by Satellite (GMPCS) licence and space-sector authorisation. It has also prepared ground infrastructure and entered partnerships with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel. But final security clearances and other operational requirements remain outstanding.

Here is where the competing claims begin.

Musk argues that powerful incumbents are protecting their interests. His accusation carries weight in a market where major telecom operators have substantial commercial influence. But he has not publicly established that a particular company or individual caused the delay.

The government offers a different explanation. Starlink, Jio's satellite venture and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb are all awaiting outstanding regulatory steps, including spectrum allocation and security clearances. 
Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has emphasized that operators must meet the required security protocols before launching services.

Both commercial competition and national security deserve scrutiny. Satellite networks involve questions of spectrum management, lawful interception, gateway infrastructure, data governance and communications near sensitive locations. India has legitimate reasons to insist on enforceable safeguards.

But legitimate regulation must also be transparent, proportionate and consistently applied. Otherwise, security requirements can become difficult to distinguish from barriers to competition.

And this is where the story acquires a wider strategic dimension.

Satellite communications are becoming part of the infrastructure through which countries conduct business, deliver public services and manage security. Decisions about who operates these networks—and under what conditions—can influence both commercial competition and national autonomy.

The unresolved India–US trade negotiations add another dimension. Washington has an interest in expanding opportunities for American technology companies abroad, while India has an interest in attracting innovation without surrendering regulatory control. That creates a potential area of friction, although there is no established evidence that Starlink's delayed launch is being used to force trade concessions.

So, the questions are clear. Are the rules being applied equally? Are the remaining delays justified by specific security requirements? And can India encourage global investment while ensuring that no company, however powerful, dictates the terms?

The real test of sovereignty is not whether India admits or rejects Starlink. It is whether India can make that decision transparently, on its own terms, and under rules that apply equally to everyone.

In Part 4, we leave the technical and regulatory battlefield to examine a different question: how do powerful individuals amplify political narratives—and what evidence distinguishes public agreement from coordinated influence?

Because controlling the digital sky is one challenge. Understanding the politics unfolding beneath it is another.

text:
PRESSURE POINTS — PART 1

IS INDIA FACING A NEW BATTLE FOR STRATEGIC AUTONOMY?

Green cards on hold. A satellite internet giant challenging India’s regulator. Political leaders amplifying competing narratives. Protests targeting the Election Commission. And a trade deal that remains elusive.

What if the most consequential story unfolding around India is not any one of these controversies—but the pressure they collectively place on the country?

Consider the developments of October 2026.

On October 8, the Trump administration suspended major technology and IT services companies, including Microsoft, Adobe, TCS and Infosys, from participating in the US PERM employment-based green-card programme. Washington cited alleged abuses of the system and the need to protect American workers. The move does not amount to a blanket cancellation of H-1B visas, but it could disrupt an important route to permanent residency for affected employees.

Meanwhile, Elon Musk was publicly challenging India's regulatory process over Starlink's delayed commercial launch. His criticism escalated into a political exchange with Rahul Gandhi, bringing questions about corporate influence, competition and government accountability into the spotlight. The Indian government, however, maintained that satellite operators were awaiting security clearances rather than being singled out.

On the domestic front, the October 8 protest in Bengaluru organised by the Cockroach Janta Party brought YouTuber Dhruv Rathee and actor Prakash Raj into a mobilisation demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls. Organisers framed the demonstration around electoral transparency and alleged voter deletions. These allegations and the protesters' demands warrant examination on their own merits. The follow on protests in Delhi is planned for 10th October.

At the same time, India and the United States remain locked in difficult trade negotiations. Reuters reported on October 6 that the talks had stalled amid disagreements involving tariffs, Russian oil purchases and market access. The absence of a final agreement leaves important questions about India's exports and negotiating position unresolved.

Four pressure points. Multiple institutions and interests. One country navigating an increasingly complicated economic and political landscape.

Coincidence? Convergence? Or coordination?

That is the question—not the conclusion—with which this investigation begins.

Could immigration restrictions increase Washington's leverage over businesses dependent on American markets? 

Could competition over satellite communications become entangled with broader geopolitical interests? 
How do political narratives spread when influential business figures, opposition leaders, activists and online commentators enter the same debate? And what, if anything, connects these developments to the unresolved trade negotiations?

These are legitimate questions. But the answers cannot be manufactured from timing alone.

A trade dispute is not automatically a political weapon. A protest is not proof of a conspiracy. A public exchange between influential individuals does not establish a coordinated plan. To demonstrate a wider operation to destabilise a government, we would need credible evidence of common planning, communications, funding or intent.

That is precisely what Pressure Points will investigate.

Over the next seven instalments, we will examine the immigration restrictions, the Starlink controversy, the politics of public influence, the protest networks and the trade negotiations. We will distinguish documented connections from speculation, scrutinise competing explanations and ask whether the evidence supports a larger pattern.

The question is bigger than the fate of one government. 
It concerns India's ability to make decisions on technology, trade, security and democracy without undue external or internal pressure.

When several pressure points emerge at once, India cannot afford either blind suspicion or blind complacency. It needs evidence.

The dots are visible. The task ahead is to establish which ones actually connect.

#IndiaUSTradeDeal #Conspiracy #GreenCard #USImmigration #CJPStir #CEC #Starlink
