oil is stuck in a tug-of-war right now, & ngl that’s exactly when volatility traders start paying attention.

here’s why.

two weeks ago, Iran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if the US lifted its naval blockade & eased sanctions.

Trump rejected the offer & that matters, bcz around a fifth of the world’s oil supply used to flow through that strait. when a quick reopening starts looking less likely, the possibility of supply staying tight for longer comes back into the picture.

we’ve seen how quickly oil can react to this kind of news before. earlier this year, Brent dropped more than 9% in a day after Iran said the strait would reopen, only for prices to recover when things changed again.

basically, oil doesn’t just move on supply & demand. it moves on what traders think might happen next. one headline from Washington or Tehran can change the entire mood of the market.

& the story hasn’t gone away. Hormuz traffic is slipping again, which is why the current range matters so much.

so what is the @CoinDCX crude chart (CL-USDT, daily) actually saying?

➤ crude climbed from around ~80 in late august to nearly ~107 nearly 107 by mid-september as supply fears grew.

➤ then it faded, with lower highs & a slide back into the high 80s

➤ when the rejection hit in late september, price bounced toward the mid-90s, but sellers showed up again

➤ today it’s sitting around 90-91 in a tight range, after a bounce off 87-88 on higher volume

what stands out to me is that even with all the bullish headlines, crude hasn’t managed to get back to its previous highs.

the market is still trying to figure out what comes next. does this turn into a prolonged supply disruption, or do we get a deal that changes everything?

my thesis, in simple words: oil is coiled between ~87 & ~97. whichever side breaks first probably sets the next big move.

if momentum continues (bullish):
> price needs to hold the 87-88 zone & reclaim ~93.
> a daily close above 96-97 on strong volume opens 101-102, with the 107 high as the bigger target.
> Hormuz traffic keeps dropping, & tanker attacks or stalled talks add to supply worries.

if it reverses (bearish):
> another failed push at 96-97 means buyers are tired.
> a daily close below 87-88 puts the ~80 late-august base back in play.
> a credible phased deal or a real surge in Hormuz shipping. oil has dropped sharply on this kind of news before.

what kills the bullish thesis: a daily close below 87 with no quick recovery. if that happens, i’m wrong & i’ll accept it.

& to be clear, i’m not trying to predict the headline, i’m trying to react to it, with a clear level for being wrong.

now, how can Indian traders actually trade this on @CoinDCX?

“tokenized” just means you’re trading a crypto based contract that tracks crude oil’s price. so no overseas broker, no complicated setup. CL-USDT sits in the same Futures section of the app u already use, with both Buy/Long & Sell/Short, so u can take a view on oil going up or down.

a few things i lowkey like:
→ it’s a perpetual, so there’s no expiry to track or roll.
→ orders start from about ₹612 in notional value, so u can test a view without going all in.
→ fees are roughly 0.01% on both maker & taker.
→ the price shows in ₹ right next to the chart, & it trades 24/7, which is perfect when Middle East news drops at 2 AM IST.

my approach is pretty simple, start small and don’t go crazy with leverage. knowing when to exit if things go wrong matters way more than getting the perfect entry, fr.

so what do u think, are we breaking past 97 or dropping below 87? 👇 drop your take.

not financial advice, futures are leveraged & risky, so only trade what u can afford to lose.

text:
Well, this is quite a turn of events. Donald Trump has announced an agreement with Vladimir Putin to bring millions of tonnes of Russian diesel onto international markets, including supplies for America. Washington has even issued a temporary sanctions exemption to make it possible.

Yes, the same America that has spent years trying to restrict Russia's energy revenues is now turning to Moscow for help bringing down fuel prices. And the explanation leads us straight back to the war against Iran.

When America and Israel launched their offensive in February, Iran couldn't match them in conventional military power. But it could disrupt the movement of oil and fuel through the Gulf, particularly the Strait of Hormuz. Seven months later, the economic consequences are spreading far beyond the Middle East.

Diesel has become a particular problem because it keeps lorries, farms and much of the wider economy running. According to the International Energy Agency, combined diesel exports from Russia and the Gulf were around 1.6 million barrels a day lower in August than before the Iran war.

And this is where Ukraine complicates matters.

Ukraine has been attacking Russian refineries to undermine Moscow's ability to finance its war. The strikes have been effective too. The IEA estimates Russian diesel production has fallen by nearly 30%, forcing Russia to restrict exports to protect its own supplies.

From Ukraine's perspective, this makes perfect sense. Unfortunately for Washington, damaging Russian refineries is also making an international diesel shortage considerably worse.

So Trump is now asking Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries while negotiating with Putin to get Russian diesel flowing again.

What makes this particularly extraordinary is that American intelligence was reportedly helping Ukraine target Russian energy infrastructure last year. Washington was supporting a tactic to weaken Moscow that it now wants curtailed because of the consequences for American consumers. The Financial Times reports that US envoys have even warned Ukraine that intelligence cooperation could be at risk.

Zelenskyy has offered to halt attacks on Russian energy infrastructure if Russia reciprocates. That's rather different from expecting Ukraine to stop while Moscow continues attacking Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.

Then there's Trump's election campaign. Remember the promises about not starting new wars and cutting energy prices in half? America is now fighting a prolonged war against Iran, fuel prices have surged, and the midterms are only weeks away.

There's considerable irony in a president who promised to stop wars now trying to protect American voters from the economic consequences of one his own administration helped start.

Israel's role shouldn't be forgotten either. Netanyahu had long advocated military action against Iran, and Washington and Israel launched the offensive together. Yet their objectives haven't always remained aligned, particularly as America has become increasingly concerned about the economic damage and finding a way out.

Both have inflicted serious military damage on Iran, but Tehran has demonstrated that it can still impose enormous costs without defeating either country militarily.

Meanwhile, Britain has announced another 38 sanctions measures against Russian interests, while European governments are preparing further restrictions. Washington wants Russian diesel flowing, Ukraine wants to damage the refineries producing it, and Britain and Europe want to maintain economic pressure on Moscow.

Of course, Britain has already made limited exemptions of its own. That's the problem with economic warfare in an interconnected energy market. The consequences don't conveniently stop at your opponent's borders.

And here in Britain, with diesel hovering around £2 a litre, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been promoting petrol-price comparisons on Google Maps.

To be fair, it might save motorists a few quid, and the government has taken other measures. But there's something wonderfully British about watching global energy markets being battered by two wars while being offered a more convenient way to find the cheapest place to suffer the consequences.

Underneath the absurdity, though, there's a much more serious problem.

Ukraine's military strategy is affecting American fuel prices. The Iran war is changing Washington's calculations about Russia. Britain and Europe are continuing their sanctions policies while the economic costs of these interconnected conflicts spread.

That doesn't make a third world war inevitable, but it does create more opportunities for dangerous miscalculation between powers already involved in multiple conflicts.

And while governments struggle to reconcile their military ambitions with economic reality, ordinary people are left paying for both.

🇷🇺 Ukraine strikes major Russian oil hub in Samara again as confrontation over refinery attacks intensifies

Ukrainian forces struck the Samara oil pumping, storage and blending complex near Prosvet overnight on October 10, according to Ukraine's General Staff, marking another attack on a major component of Russia's petroleum export infrastructure.

The facility receives crude oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan and other producing regions, blending different grades into Urals crude for distribution and export. Its importance extends beyond refining: the complex connects production fields, storage facilities and major pipeline routes.

Ukraine's General Staff also confirmed that an earlier strike on October 7 destroyed four RVS-50000 storage tanks and caused a major fire at the same installation. The extent of the damage from the latest attack remains under assessment.

The renewed strike comes amid a growing dispute between Washington and Kyiv over Ukraine's campaign against Russian oil infrastructure. President Trump has authorized a temporary easing of restrictions on Russian diesel exports, while American officials have pressed Ukraine to suspend attacks on Russian refineries over concerns about global fuel prices.

Kyiv has offered to halt those operations in exchange for a reciprocal Russian suspension of strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure. No such agreement has been publicly announced.

The Samara attack demonstrates that Ukraine's campaign extends beyond refineries to the storage, blending and transportation systems underpinning Russia's oil industry. Whether the latest strike caused additional disruption to those operations remains to be established.

There’s a strong argument that @TheDemocrats lost on purpose in 2024 (slow rolling Joe Biden dropping out) because Donald Trump is actually one of them. 

Remember, the elites hover over both parties.
And Donald is friends with both the Clintons and the Emanuels @ariemanuel/@RahmEmanuel

SI: Start with a remarkable fact: Donald Trump was a registered Democrat from August 2001 until September 2009. 

New York voter registration records confirm it. 

During those years, he made political contributions to Hillary Clinton, maintained relationships with the Clintons, and operated within the same New York political, financial, and entertainment circles as many influential Democrats. 

In May 2015, Bill Clinton spoke privately with Trump, weeks before Trump announced his Republican presidential candidacy. The Washington Post reported that people familiar with the call said Clinton encouraged Trump's increasing involvement in Republican politics. Clinton's office confirmed the conversation while disputing that the presidential race was discussed. 

Here's where the chronology becomes particularly revealing.

On April 7, 2015, a strategy memorandum addressed to the Democratic National Committee identified Trump, Ted Cruz, and Ben Carson as potential Pied Piper candidates.

The memo called for elevating those candidates within the Republican field and encouraging journalists to take their candidacies seriously. The calculation was that these candidates would be easier for Hillary Clinton to defeat.

This is an actual campaign strategy documented in writing, before Trump announced his candidacy. 

Now consider the Emanuels.
Rahm Emanuel was deeply embedded in Democratic political leadership. He worked on Bill Clinton's 1992 presidential campaign, served in the Clinton White House, and became Barack Obama's first White House chief of staff. 

Yet Donald Trump donated $50,000 to Rahm's 2010 mayoral campaign.

And the connection to Ari Emanuel is even more interesting. Ari wasn't simply Trump's friend. He was his talent agent.

Ari's agency @WME represented Trump during The Apprentice. In September 2015, after Trump had entered the presidential race and NBC had severed its business relationship with him, Ari Emanuel's WME-IMG purchased the Miss Universe Organization from Trump.

In November 2016, following Trump's election, Ari visited Trump at his Bedminster golf club. Documents subsequently revealed that Trump's transition team had vetted Ari for a possible administration role. 

Think about the institutional continuity here.

Ari Emanuel was a prominent Democratic donor whose brother had served two Democratic presidents. Yet Ari maintained a professional and personal relationship with Trump that extended into his presidential transition.

Trump himself explained his contribution to Rahm by emphasizing personal loyalty across party lines. 

That is an unusually concrete example of relationships transcending political affiliation.

And now we arrive at 2024.

Joe Biden announced his reelection campaign in April 2023. Questions about the wisdom of another campaign were already being raised publicly. Yet the party continued toward his renomination.

After the June 27, 2024 debate, Biden remained in the race for another 24 days.

Reuters subsequently documented an inner circle of advisers who reinforced his determination to continue, while other Democrats worried about the consequences of replacing him. Biden ultimately withdrew on July 21, leaving Kamala Harris a radically compressed campaign.
 
The question of why powerful Democratic figures tolerated that situation for so long is entirely legitimate.

But there is a crucial distinction between an institutional failure that protects insiders and a deliberate plan to lose.

The evidence points strongly toward loyalty, personal ambition, risk aversion, and the protection of an incumbent president. Meanwhile, AP VoteCast found that inflation, economic dissatisfaction, and immigration were important drivers of Trump's actual electoral support. 

And this is where I think the most intellectually valuable part of your argument emerges:
Who benefits from maintaining the system?

The United States has two major political parties competing for votes and political authority.

Surrounding them is an enormous economy of consultants, donors, lobbyists, advertisers, media organizations, talent representatives, and political professionals.

The Federal Election Commission reports that political action committees raised approximately $15.7 billion during the 2023–2024 election cycle, while party committees raised approximately $2.7 billion. Those figures reflect enormous commercial and organizational activity around American elections. 

The incentives within that economy deserve scrutiny because the success of political institutions and the financial success of people operating around those institutions are separate questions.

An unsuccessful candidate can still generate substantial fundraising activity. An electoral defeat can still produce lucrative consulting contracts, television audiences, and new opportunities for political professionals. Networks of influence can survive changes in presidential administrations.

And a politician can campaign against an establishment while retaining longstanding relationships with influential members of that establishment.

That brings us back to your observation about the Clintons and Emanuels.

Their connections with Trump illustrate how personal loyalty, commercial relationships, and access to influential institutions can exist across partisan divisions.

The 2015 Pied Piper memorandum demonstrates that Democratic strategists were willing to influence which Republican candidates received attention.

The 2024 Biden withdrawal raises a different question about how entrenched party leadership responds when its institutional interests collide with electoral realities.

Together, those episodes raise an important question about American political power:
Are the people managing political competition always operating under the same incentives as the voters whose interests they claim to represent?

That's the problem that's keeping America from its fullest potential.
 
Because the most consequential possibility is broader than Donald Trump secretly being a Democrat.

It's that the political parties compete for control of the government while an overlapping network of influential people retains significant access, relationships, and economic opportunities across changes in power.

The Trump–Clinton–Emanuel relationships offer a documented way to begin investigating that system.

And the Biden timeline offers an opportunity to investigate what happens when the institutional preservation of political leadership comes into conflict with the electoral interests of the party itself.

text:
An analogy applicable to SI Governance:

The original U.S. Constitution remains one of the most successful governance frameworks for producing sustained positive outcomes because it solved a hard problem of power: how to enable coordination and capability without creating a single center that could dominate everyone else. Its design separated authority across three branches while recognizing three distinct interests—federal, state, and individual—and structured the system so that autonomy at one layer did not systematically destroy autonomy at the others. The result was limited government, room for local experimentation, and a strong presumption in favor of individual liberty. That structural logic offers a useful conceptual model for governing superintelligence.

The Constitution did not rely on perfect people or a single shared moral code. It relied on institutional design: separation of powers, checks and balances, enumerated powers, and residual autonomy left to states and individuals. This created durable constraints against concentrated authority while still allowing the federal government to handle issues that genuinely required common action. Over time it delivered relative liberty, innovation, and prosperity compared with more centralized alternatives, even though it required later amendments and interpretation to address its original compromises. The transferable insight is the architecture of layered sovereignty plus mutual constraint, not any particular clause.

Applied to superintelligence, the same three-interest structure maps onto the emerging landscape of AI systems:

• The individual layer preserves meaningful control for users and humans. Agents should expand capability without locking people into irreversible workflows, opaque decisions, or systems that cannot be overridden or exited. Human autonomy remains the liberty-maximizing constraint.

• The organizational or enterprise layer functions like the states. Firms and institutions retain sovereignty over their data, context, evaluation methods, and agent deployments. They can choose or substitute models, govern their own workflows, and avoid being forced into a single provider’s rigid platform. This aligns with visions of AI as an “OS for work” that organizes around existing systems and organizational control rather than requiring everyone to reorganize around one dominant model.

• The coordination layer (federal or international) handles high-stakes capabilities and risks—such as cybersecurity, biosecurity, systemic failures, or alignment problems—that affect multiple parties or the commons. Shared rules and oversight apply here without swallowing the lower layers.

Separation of powers supplies the complementary mechanism. No single lab, executive, auditor, or model family should hold unchecked authority. Recent voluntary efforts, such as the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, sketch a weak version of this idea through layered controls: internal monitoring, an internal oversight team, independent external evaluation, and board-level review. These are limited by the absence of strong enforcement or mandatory transparency, but the multi-layered checking structure is directionally consistent with constitutional design.

The analogy is useful because it prioritizes maximizing autonomy at each layer without allowing any one layer to extinguish the others. Enterprise systems that keep context, memory, evaluation, and action under organizational control, while leaving individuals with exit and override options, come closer to this ideal than fully centralized model-as-platform designs. They reduce the risk that AI agents force humans and organizations to work around the software rather than the reverse.

The model also has clear limits that any practical application must address. Human constitutional systems assume roughly comparable agents who share certain baseline interests in survival and non-domination. A superintelligent system may not. Constraints therefore need to be engineered into the technology itself through alignment techniques, capability controls, verification methods, and corrigibility, rather than depending solely on post-hoc political enforcement. 
Amendment procedures must be robust enough to resist capture yet flexible enough to adapt as capabilities evolve. And because frontier development is global, pure national frameworks must be supplemented by technical standards and coordination mechanisms that can operate across borders.

Many existing AI alignment approaches already use constitutional language—high-level principles combined with structural constraints. The distinctive contribution of the original U.S. framework is its emphasis on layered sovereignty and separation rather than a single top-down set of rules. In the context of enterprise agents and multi-model systems, this favors architectures in which organizations evaluate and govern their own stacks, individuals retain practical control, and only the highest-risk capabilities face coordinated external constraints. 
Whether current designs fully implement that principle is an open empirical question. The conceptual template itself remains one of the stronger available starting points for trying to deliver positive outcomes as capability scales.

As many of you know, I backed away from politics for good a few years ago. After the experience of Trump 1.0, COVID, Biden, and now Trump 2.0, I rarely comment publicly anymore, largely because so many people seem incapable of engaging rationally. But reading the article below, I feel compelled to offer an observation about America's increasingly absurd predicament of Team Brand vs. Team Brand.

Let's begin by acknowledging that Trump is the bull in the china shop.

And what a carefully curated china shop it is. For decades, the ruling elites have put lipstick on the pigs of propaganda, lies, plunder, and corruption, disguising their abuses beneath a veneer of respectability, civility, and institutional legitimacy.

There is, perhaps, a silver lining to Trump's rampage through the place. As the carefully constructed facade comes crashing down, the cockroaches scatter into the light, including Trump 2.0 and company as the most extraordinary king cockroaches of the current moment.

Where the old guard concealed its corruption behind polished rhetoric, political decorum, and elaborate institutional cover - e.g., pretending a dementia-addled Biden was actually in charge and not  aiding and abetting global chaos, Trump dispenses with the pretenses since 2024, plainly indicting himself in the process.

The old guard mastered the art of making imperial corruption look respectable.

Unfortunately, too many regular folks who vehemently despise Trump, often with good reason, resent him just as much for desecrating their own altars of political power and exposing the high priests and priestesses who preside over them.  Yes, they still celebrate Hillary Clinton and try to assert Harris was a respectable candidate, pretending there wasn't a deliberate goal to flood the USA with illegal immigration to turn national politics, which enraged a majority of Americans, and made the ground fertile for Trump 2.0

Rather than rejecting the corruption on both sides, they'll eagerly return to licking the hands of their preferred rulers, comforted by the familiar mythology of institutional legitimacy. Apparently, the same old pig looks beautiful again with a fresh coat of lipstick.

Which brings me to the article below.

Its central argument is that the politicization of our government-funded museums long predates Trump. The author describes a movement within these institutions that increasingly treats history less as a subject of honest inquiry and more as an instrument of social and political transformation.

I see this as part of a much broader intellectual and institutional drift away from America's founding principles of individual liberty, private property, and limitations on government power, principles deeply influenced by centuries of moral, philosophical, and Christian thought.

In my view, the consequences extend far beyond museum exhibits. Generations have increasingly been encouraged to look to political power for solutions to problems that political power itself has often created or compounded. Socialist and collectivist ideas find fertile ground among people who have little understanding of the economic and moral principles that made individual liberty -- and the unprecedented universally improved standards of living in the United State possible.

And now, predictably, we're told that Trump uniquely evil for politicizing the Smithsonian.  Well, thanks for noticing the latest round.

No doubt Trump has compounded many problems in extraordinary ways. But the institutional rot long predates him, and it will survive him unless Americans learn to distinguish principles from political personalities.  And it dooms us all for one political team to presume they are not equally responsible for creating the conditions that made Trump 2.0 viable.

Replacing one set of ruling elites with another, or one politically curated mythology with its opposite, solves nothing.

The measure of legitimate government is not which team holds power, but whether that power respects the liberty, property, and rights of the individual.  Liberty is the foundational differentiator between shared wealth, peaceful prosperity, voluntary association, and the real world reality that actions have consequences vs. poverty, mediocrity, oligarchy, imperialism, deflection, unaccountability, and massive debts and an increasingly unstable currency onto our children and grand children.

Anything less is just another pig wearing lipstick.

Hogwarts is just one of the major wizarding schools in the world. Here are some facts about the other schools you could have attended if you weren't from the UK or Ireland.

🇧🇷 Castelobruxo — Brazil
Hidden in the rainforest, the school is concealed to look like ancient ruins to Muggles. It's known for its expertise in Magizoology and Herbology. It also has pen-pal connections with Hogwarts students and offers foreign exchange programmes.

🇫🇷 Beauxbatons — France
Located in the French mountains, Beauxbatons welcomes students from France, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands and Belgium. Nicolas Flamel and his wife were among its notable attendees.

🇸🇪 Durmstrang — Northern Europe
One of Europe's three major wizarding schools alongside Hogwarts and Beauxbatons, Durmstrang accepts international students but mainly attracts those from Northern and Eastern Europe. It teaches the Dark Arts as well as Defence Against the Dark Arts. Grindelwald attended but was expelled for dangerous experiments.

🇺🇬 Uagadou — Africa
The world's largest wizarding school, Uagadou was founded before the 11th century and accepts students from across Africa. Its students learn to perform magic without wands, and acceptance comes through dream messengers. By their fourth year, students can learn to become Animagi.

🇺🇸 Ilvermorny — North America
Founded around 1627 in the mountains of Massachusetts, Ilvermorny accepts students from across North America. It has four houses: Horned Serpent, Wampus, Thunderbird and Pukwudgie.

🇯🇵 Mahoutokoro — Japan
Known as the smallest of the major wizarding schools, Mahoutokoro was attended by the Quidditch teacher featured in Hogwarts Legacy.

🇷🇺 Koldovstoretz — Russia
Students at this school are known for playing Quidditch on fully uprooted trees instead of broomsticks.

There are supposedly eleven major wizarding schools worldwide, but only eight have been identified, including Hogwarts. The identities of the others remain unknown.

Which wizarding school would you have wanted to attend?

text:
SpaceX's agreement to acquire 800 MHz spectrum for Starlink Mobile has raised some interesting discussions.

I read John Saw's article, Spectrum Alone Doesn't Make a Network. He makes several valid engineering points, but I think some of the comparisons deserve more context.

Here are my thoughts from an RF engineering perspective.

1. Spectrum and coverage

John: T-Mobile holds nearly 400 MHz of low- and mid-band spectrum, compared to SpaceX's roughly 80 MHz, some of it uplink-only. Wider channels and advanced 5G infrastructure offer a significant capacity advantage.

That's a huge capacity difference, but capacity and geographic coverage are two different problems.

Low-band spectrum (600–900 MHz) is particularly useful for wide-area coverage and building penetration. Mid-band provides higher capacity, while mmWave offers much greater bandwidth over shorter distances.

Terrestrial networks work exceptionally well in populated areas, but rural and mountainous regions still have blind spots.

Does SpaceX really need to reproduce T-Mobile's entire terrestrial footprint to provide a valuable service?

2. Satellite path loss

John: A satellite hundreds of kilometers away faces roughly 50 dB more path loss than a terrestrial tower 1 km away. Lower frequencies don't eliminate that disadvantage.

He's right about the physics.

At 550 km, free-space path loss is approximately 153 dB at 2 GHz and 145 dB at 800 MHz. That 8 dB improvement is useful, but certainly doesn't close a 50 dB gap.

However, here's what I find interesting:

SpaceX's proposed architecture uses the 800 MHz spectrum as a coverage layer, including terrestrial deployment, while its 2 GHz spectrum is positioned for capacity.

An 800 MHz signal transmitted from a ground tower doesn't face the satellite path-loss penalty.

The engineering question becomes how efficiently these two layers can work together.

3. Indoor coverage

John: Over 70% of mobile traffic occurs indoors, where terrestrial networks have a fundamental advantage.

Yes, building penetration is a real challenge for satellite signals.

But I think we should distinguish indoor cellular coverage from indoor internet access.

At home and in offices, many of us rely on Wi-Fi connected to fixed broadband. Even where I live, indoor cellular reception isn't always reliable.

Stores and crowded venues are different. That's where SpaceX's terrestrial layer would need to perform.

And for backup connectivity, not every connection needs hundreds of Mbps.

T-Mobile's own T-Satellite service, powered by Starlink, already supports messaging and selected data applications on compatible ordinary smartphones in areas without cellular coverage, generally outdoors with sky visibility.

Even a limited connection for emergency communication can be extremely valuable.

4. Network capacity

John: Satellite beams cannot match the aggregate capacity of hundreds of terrestrial cell sectors.

That's a valid comparison, but those hundreds of cell sectors are usually concentrated in densely populated areas.

In rural or mountainous regions, you might have only a handful of towers, or none at all.

So here's what I'm curious about:

For Starlink Mobile, will most of its future demand come from dense urban areas already covered by established cellular networks, or from less populated regions where terrestrial coverage is weak or nonexistent?

SpaceX may ultimately want to compete in both markets, but its initial advantage could be in underserved regions where adding terrestrial infrastructure is economically difficult.

If it's the former, John's capacity argument becomes a major challenge.

But if it's the latter, even relatively modest satellite capacity could provide tremendous value.

A reliable 1 Mbps connection in a dead zone might be more useful than another 100 Mbps where users already have 500 Mbps.

I think understanding where the actual demand comes from is just as important as comparing theoretical network capacity.

5. Network investment

John: The US wireless industry has invested over $250B in infrastructure since 2018, plus more than $200B in spectrum auctions over the past decade. Building a great network also requires time and experience.

Indeed, those investments demonstrate just how difficult it is to build and operate a nationwide network.

SpaceX will still need terrestrial sites, backhaul, permits, network optimization and operational experience.

But could a hybrid architecture change the economics?

Instead of extending terrestrial infrastructure into every remote region, satellites could cover geographic gaps while ground networks focus on population density and capacity.

That won't eliminate the infrastructure investment, but it might change where the investment makes the most sense.

Of course, the new spectrum transfer still needs FCC approval, and SpaceX's next-generation mobile satellite deployment is targeted for 2027. The proposed hybrid network hasn't demonstrated its promised nationwide performance yet.

In a nutshell:

I think John raises important technical challenges. But I'm interested in exploring how a hybrid network might solve some of them differently.

The question isn't necessarily whether SpaceX can match T-Mobile tower for tower, or Mbps for Mbps.

It's whether combining satellite and terrestrial connectivity can deliver better coverage, reliability and economics for different use cases.

Sometimes, the most important connection isn't the fastest one. It's the one that actually works.

text:
❤️ The best of humanity often shows up after the worst of Mother Nature.

I’ll never forget the aftermath of Hurricanes Frances and Jeanne in Jupiter, FL (made landfall in the same area just 3 weeks apart). Our side of the street had electricity, but the homes across from us didn’t. So what did we do? We ran extension cords across the street to share our power with our neighbors.

And it wasn’t just us. House after house, neighbors were doing the same thing. Nobody expected anything in return. We simply helped each other because that’s what neighbors do.

That’s the Florida I know and love. ❤️

One of the most beautiful things about the aftermath of a hurricane is watching communities come together. Neighbors checking on neighbors, strangers helping clear debris, people sharing food, water, supplies, and whatever else they have. In the midst of so much destruction, it’s a powerful reminder that there’s still an incredible amount of good in this world.

Unfortunately, while disasters bring out the very best in some people, they can also bring out the worst in others.

And that’s something I want every homeowner dealing with the aftermath of this hurricane to understand.

As a Floridian who has weathered more hurricanes than I’d like to count, both as a homeowner and as a licensed public adjuster, I’ve seen firsthand how overwhelming the recovery process can be. And I’ve seen how easily homeowners can be taken advantage of when they’re exhausted, stressed, and just trying to put their lives back together.

As the owner of Falcon Claims Management & Adjustment, I want to share a few things that could save you a tremendous amount of frustration, heartache, and potentially THOUSANDS of dollars.

📸 DOCUMENT EVERYTHING.

Take photos and videos of ALL damage, including your personal belongings. Document the damage before cleaning up or making repairs whenever safely possible. Don’t overlook damage that may not be immediately visible. Keep receipts for emergency repairs, temporary housing, and other storm-related expenses. Document your communications with your insurance company.

⚠️ BE VERY CAREFUL HOW YOU DESCRIBE YOUR DAMAGE.

Words like “flood” have specific meanings in the insurance industry and can significantly affect how your claim is evaluated or covered at all. Wind-driven rain, storm surge, rising water, and roof leaks are not necessarily treated the same under your policy.

Don’t assume or speculate about what caused the damage, even if you think it’s obvious. Describe exactly what you observed, be honest and thorough, and let the evidence establish the cause. If you don’t know how water entered your home, it’s perfectly acceptable to say so.

🚩 BEWARE OF STORM CHASERS AND PREDATORY COMPANIES.

PLEASE be cautious of the contractors, restoration companies, and yes, even public adjusters who descend on storm-damaged communities after a hurricane.

Unfortunately, disasters attract opportunists looking to profit from vulnerable homeowners.

Never feel pressured to sign anything on the spot. Be especially cautious of contracts involving insurance proceeds, payment authorizations, or agreements you don’t fully understand.

Verify licenses, insurance, and credentials. Ask questions. Read EVERYTHING before signing. And be extremely wary of anyone promising you a specific insurance payout before they’ve even reviewed your damage and policy.

There are plenty of reputable professionals out there who genuinely want to help, but there are also those who prey on people during their most difficult moments.

🏠 YOUR INSURANCE COMPANY’S FIRST ESTIMATE IS NOT NECESSARILY THE FINAL WORD.

Damage can be overlooked. Repair costs can be underestimated. Coverage decisions can be incorrect.

Just because an insurance company says something isn’t covered or offers a certain amount doesn’t automatically mean they’re right.

You have the right to question their findings, request explanations, provide additional documentation, and dispute decisions you believe are incorrect.

🛠️ PROTECT YOUR PROPERTY FROM FURTHER DAMAGE.

Take reasonable steps to prevent additional damage when it’s safe to do so. Document conditions beforehand whenever possible and save receipts for emergency repairs. Don’t delay necessary mitigation while waiting for an adjuster, but avoid unnecessary permanent repairs until the damage has been properly documented.

❤️ MOST IMPORTANTLY, DON’T LET ANYONE RUSH YOU INTO DECISIONS YOU DON’T FULLY UNDERSTAND.

I’ve seen firsthand how much unnecessary stress and financial hardship can result from homeowners simply not knowing their rights or understanding the claims process.

Knowledge is one of the best ways to protect yourself.

If you’re dealing with storm damage, having trouble with your insurance company, confused about coverage, or simply unsure what to do next, please feel free to reach out.

I’m always happy to answer questions, offer guidance, or help point you in the right direction, even if you never need to hire my company.

And to everyone out there checking on elderly neighbors, sharing supplies, clearing debris, opening their homes, or simply offering a helping hand…THANK YOU.

Hurricanes may tear apart our homes and communities, but they also remind us of the incredible strength of the people who call them home.

Stay safe, look out for one another, and remember that nobody should have to navigate the recovery process alone. ❤️

Falcon Claims Management & Adjustment
Licensed Florida Public Adjuster

❤️ PLEASE SHARE this with anyone impacted by the hurricane. One share could help someone avoid a costly mistake or recognize a dishonest contractor before it’s too late.

And I’d love to hear from those of you who’ve been through major hurricanes: What’s one thing you remember most about neighbors coming together after a storm?

text:
That’s useful, and rather confirms my suspicion that the weak point is distribution rather than bulk generation.

If generation and most transmission largely survived, but outages were still widespread because trees and debris took down local overhead lines, then the vulnerability is fairly prosaic: the last mile remains exposed.

The interesting question, then, is where the economic optimum lies. Full undergrounding is obviously expensive, but so are repeated outages, emergency repairs and lost economic activity. Targeted undergrounding, sectionalisation, more automated switching, local storage and microgrids sound like the sort of measures that ought to offer rather better returns than simply rebuilding the same exposed network after each storm.

Given that these weather risks are predictable and recurrent, I’d be interested in whether Florida utilities publish comparative figures for the lifetime cost of hardening versus repeated restoration. That seems the obvious place to test whether the current balance is actually rational.

text:
When Gunner Stockton was a little kid he asked his parents for cattle for Christmas.

He got a bull, five calves and five heifers.

Taking care of them became his job after school.

He is the starting quarterback for the Georgia Bulldogs, who are 4 and 0 and ranked third in the country, and today he plays at Alabama.

Here is where he comes from.

Tiger, Georgia. A little place in Rabun County up in the north Georgia mountains, near where Georgia runs into North Carolina and Tennessee. His family has been there for generations.

His name is not a nickname. His great grandfather was an aerial gunner in the Eighth Air Force in the Second World War, and a newspaper back home printed his name in a story as Gunner Stockton. The family kept it.

That man's actual name was V.D. Stockton. He was a district attorney in that part of Georgia for about 30 years. Gunner's father put it plainly. There was no way they were naming the boy V.D.

His father Rob played safety at Georgia Southern and started 48 games and later coached the defense at Rabun County High School. His mother Sherrie played basketball on scholarship at Erskine College. His older sister, whose name is Georgia, averaged 21 points a game and played at Presbyterian College.

North Carolina offered him a scholarship when he was in the eighth grade, after he threw a ball 66 yards at a camp.

He started four years at Rabun County and left holding the Georgia state high school records with 177 passing touchdowns and 77 rushing touchdowns. He broke records that belonged to Trevor Lawrence and Deshaun Watson.

He skipped the national camp circuit. He skipped the Elite 11. He never missed a practice or a workout in four years of high school.

And as a senior, he and his teammates cleaned the locker room after every practice and every game, so the custodians would have less to do.

He committed to South Carolina, and then that staff got fired. Georgia called. He said Georgia was where he was going and where he would graduate, and that he would compete for the job instead of leaving.

Then he waited.

He redshirted in 2022. In 2023 he was third on the depth chart. In 2024 he was the backup.

Then Carson Beck got hurt at halftime of the SEC Championship Game, and Gunner Stockton walked out there, and Georgia won it in overtime.

Last season he started all 14 games. In the SEC Championship Game he threw three touchdown passes against Alabama, Georgia won 28 to 7, and he was the most valuable player of it.

Today he goes back to Tuscaloosa.

Somewhere in Rabun County there is a herd of cattle that a boy asked for at Christmas, and a pickup truck, and a name a newspaper gave his great grandfather.

Lindner Center of HOPE (also known as Lindner Center of Hope) specializes in comprehensive mental health and addiction treatment.
It is a nonprofit mental health center of excellence and psychiatric hospital in Mason, Ohio (near Cincinnati), serving children, adolescents, and adults. It provides patient-centered, evidence-based care for a wide range of conditions, including:
•  Depression and bipolar/mood disorders
•  Anxiety disorders and OCD
•  Eating disorders
•  Addictive disorders and co-occurring (dual-diagnosis) conditions
•  Schizophrenia and related disorders
•  ADHD and other attention/behavioral issues
•  Trauma-related conditions, personality disorders, and more
Services span the continuum of care: inpatient hospitalization, residential programs (such as diagnostic assessment and short-term residential treatment at Sibcy House), partial hospitalization (PHP), intensive outpatient (IOP), outpatient therapy and medication management, and specialized multi-day diagnostic assessments for complex or treatment-resistant cases. It also offers advanced treatments like TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation), ECT, DBT, and others.

text:
By July 2019, Neymar was convinced that referees never protected him, while jealousy from teammates, indifference from fans and opposition from sections of the French media made life in Paris increasingly difficult.

The drawn-out speculation about his return to Barcelona added further strain to the city, until eventually talks with Barcelona broke down and he agreed to stay at PSG. When he finally took the field on 14 September for the start of the new season, the crowd greeted him with relentless booing that continued throughout the match. In the 92nd minute, he rose for a bicycle kick that secured a 1–0 victory over Strasbourg in Ligue 1.

Neymar told his family he was staying, and on Sunday, 1 September, he boarded a flight to Miami to join his international team-mates. He was ready to play, but he did not agree to make a statement that he was staying. During the following summer, reports emerged suggesting he might return to Barcelona or join Real Madrid. Kallás, who has tracked the Brazilian's ups and downs both on and off the field, remarked that in Brazil there is a saying that he is an endless promise. He was the "Menino Neymar", or Baby Neymar, yet Kallás added that he was not a boy and that he had to grow up. Despite the fact that Neymar endured another injury-plagued campaign with Paris Saint-Germain, the 2019–20 campaign stood out as one of the most productive periods of his professional journey.

The momentum carried over into the next matchday, where another late winner secured a 1–0 triumph over Lyon on 23 September, reinforcing his status as a decisive force. Neymar remained indispensable throughout the campaign, finding the net against Bordeaux and adding a goal in the comeback win over Montpellier.

During the knockout stages of the Champions League, Neymar was acclaimed as "a leader" who orchestrated the attack and found the net twice while providing two assists in victories over Borussia Dortmund, Atalanta and RB Leipzig, ultimately propelling PSG into its maiden Champions League final where it encountered Bayern Munich on 23 August before succumbing to a 1–0 defeat. Arsène Wenger, the ex-Arsenal boss, among others, lauded him as the finest player in the world. In the final, PSG lost 1–0. Neymar, visibly devastated as the clock struck full time, had been driven by the dream of steering PSG to a first-ever Champions League trophy.

When Philippe Coutinho joined Bayern Munich, a source told Barcelona that if they still wanted Neymar, they needed a new approach. Lionel Messi remained keen to see his former teammate return to the club. On Saturday, 31 August, Neymar gathered with his father and his closest representatives for a meeting in which they concluded that pinning their hopes on a transfer was futile. Neymar had offered to pay €20m in five instalments, but PSG dismissed the proposal because of French football federation regulations. With three years still remaining on his current PSG contract, the door to a new chapter stayed shut.

Neymar stood at a crossroads before agreeing to stay at Paris Saint-Germain after discussions about returning to Barcelona fell apart. With Edinson Cavani having left and Kylian Mbappé recently sidelined, the burden of the pitch now fell entirely to him. Meanwhile, his personal life had at times worn the hallmarks of a gripping telenovela, filled with intrigue and backed by an ensembled entourage.

Was this Neymar's finest hour at PSG, or would he have done more?

#Neymar #ChampionsLeague #BallinGodz

text:
11 years ago today I launched my first FB ad 

Since then i've spent millions on ads for clients & helped scale hundreds of ad accounts

Here are 10 lessons i've learned over the years:

1. If you put lip stick on a turd, it's still a turd. Great marketing with a terrible product is like trying to climb Mount Everest with a 200lb weighted vest on. Most people will lie to themselves about how good their product actually is. The market will vote with their dollars. If you've been struggling to scale, testing every creative & landing page, and getting nowhere, 9/10 it's a product issue. 

2. Stop over complicating the f*ck out of things. I used to think of the stupidest shit and think that was what was holding me back. "i need to find the perfect number of ads to put inside an adset to scale" or "I will not win with ads if I launch at 12am vs. 8am" or "I need to keep duplicating ads to try and find new pockets of people" once I stop focusing on things like this, I started to see results. 

3. Focus on what moves the needle. My personal hierarchy: Offer > product page > creatives

Offer -> Is not 20% off or buy 2 get 1 free. Look up the value equation by alex hormozi & also read 100m offers

Product page -> how we communicate that offer to people 

Creatives -> how we hook people in and communicate how our offer will help them get everything they desire 

Bonus: I put landing pages here at the bottom, because I know someone ask about it. I'm a huge fan of them but I still see soo many new people, testing landing pages while running a dog shit product page. Get your pdp dialed in first, then focus on these. 

4. Remove distractions so you can focus on what actually moves the needle. Example of this, recently I blocked out 2 days a week where I only write ads. I don't reply to emails, I don't go run around do random shit, I don't do calls, etc.. I only sit at my desk for 8 hours straight (obviously with breaks to eat) and work on writing ads. 

5. Follow the 80/20 rule. 80% of my time, energy, effort, and money, is going into things I know for a fact work for me. I want to continue to double down on those actions and go harder on them. 20% of my time, energy, effort, and money, is spent testing new things. I only move a new thing into my 80% until it's proven to be a new successful thing that works for me. Too many times we had something working really well for us and we abandoned it to chase some new trend. You still want to leave room to chase new trends, but don't make it your 80% until it's proven to be a mover for you. This comes down to creative format, messaging we use in our ads, landing pages, products, etc.. basically how we think about everything. 

6. Find mentors who are actively doing the thing that you're trying to learn. Don't work with mentors who once did it a while back or people not in a position that you want to be in. 

7. Over these 11 years, I've had soo many people come and go in this industry. 98% of the people that started with me, all have fell off over the years. Very few people I know in this industry that are still doing this thing. Others went back to a 9-5, others are still trend hopping into whatever make money online trend is next, etc.. very few will stick with it for a long period of time. Those very few people will be rewarded. 

8. There's no perfect creative. No perfect ad account structure. No perfect landing page. Everyone will be biased to what works for them. You have to adopt a "well Idk but i'll test it and see if it works for me" mentality. I know some people who are spending $50-100k a day in a single cbo within their ad account. I also know people spending that same number with 30 different campaigns all for different things. Neither one is wrong, because they found something that works for them and they went all in on it. Test everything with intentionality, review the tests, give the tests long enough to actually tests (7-30 days depending on what you're testing) and then make data driven decisions for what's best for you. 

9. All baselines / industry averages are bs. You have to break down your numbers, every step of the funnel, and then focus on improving your own numbers. "Nick's what a good cvr?" fuck if I know, What are you currently getting, let's model that out in a spreadsheet, then see the impact it has on your business depending how much we improve it. Then let's map out 2-3 tests to actually improve it. 

10. Everything will take longer than you expect it to. Fall in love with the process. As cliche as it sounds, this is very true. I genuinely love my writing days and getting to focus on new creative ways to make ads to get people's attention. The constant focus and effort of mastering my craft around this, is what allowed me to gain some success in this industry due to it. I became a millionaire in 2024 (total assets minus liabilities). I was 27. If you were to have told me at 18, back when I was just getting started, that I would hit it almost 9 years later, I would've been pissed. I wanted to be it by 21 and have a lambo etc... but in the grand scheme of things I'm still doing better than 90% of people my age and will be set for life. (i've invested a ton vs. throw it all into cars like the miami gurus.) I'm grateful for what I have accomplished but I still want more in a good way. It's like prestiging in call of duty. You simply do it for the love of the game now.

President Donald Trump has publicly called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky, saying the country needs a new leader capable of reaching a peace agreement with Russia. (video on reply)

The remarks represent a major escalation in Washington's dispute with Kyiv, coming just one day after Trump reached an agreement with Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports.

Trump also demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries, linking those strikes to rising American fuel prices and the economic pressure facing US farmers.

The confrontation follows reports from Axios and the Financial Times that Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, pressured Ukrainian negotiators in Miami to suspend attacks on Russia's petroleum infrastructure. Ukrainian sources said the possibility of restricting American intelligence sharing was raised, although a US official denied that an explicit threat had been made.

Zelensky has offered to halt Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries if Moscow reciprocates by suspending strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure. No corresponding Russian commitment has been publicly announced.

Trump's latest remarks move the dispute beyond disagreements over sanctions and military targeting. The American president is now openly questioning Ukraine's political leadership as Washington seeks an agreement with Moscow.

text:
Harvesting Grace, A Forty-Day Devotional by C.S. McDonald is a warm, reflective Christian devotional that invites readers to slow down and reconnect with God’s grace, especially during the beauty of autumn.

Inspired by the author’s love of the fall season—with its vibrant colors, crisp air, and sense of harvest and gratitude—the book offers forty days of gentle spiritual nourishment. Each entry includes a daily Bible verse, a peaceful and thought-provoking observation, and soft reflections designed to refresh faith and cultivate joy. McDonald encourages readers to pause amid life’s busyness, sit quietly or take a walk, and intentionally harvest God’s steadfast love and boundless grace. It serves as a humble, encouraging guide that can be used in autumn or anytime throughout the year. Readers looking for a calming, faith-centered companion will find it uplifting and accessible.

text:
Crystal champagne flutes clinked under glittering chandeliers as Havana’s political elite smiled through forced pleasantries, pretending their world was not collapsing around them. Shortly before midnight on December 31, 1958, inside the reception halls of Camp Columbia—the army’s fortified military headquarters outside the capital—President Fulgencio Batista raised a glass to toast the arrival of the new year. Dressed in a tailored white tuxedo, the fifty-seven-year-old dictator smiled warmly at generals, cabinet ministers, and foreign guests, wishing peace and prosperity to the Republic of Cuba. Yet just outside the banquet hall windows, four transport planes sat on the airfield with their propellers turning over in the tropical dark, their cargo holds packed with millions of dollars in cash, foreign bonds, and priceless art. Within three hours of raising his glass, the master of Cuba would slip out a side door and vanish into the night.
For a quarter of a century, Batista had treated Cuba as his personal fiefdom. The son of an impoverished sugar-cane laborer from Oriente province, he had staged the historic "Sergeants' Revolt" of 1933 as a humble military stenographer, instantly elevating himself to army chief and power broker. After serving a legitimate term as president in the early 1940s, he grew addicted to power, returning in March 1952 to stage an armed coup that extinguished Cuban constitutional democracy. Batista transformed Havana into the glittering gambling capital of the Western Hemisphere, partnering with American mafia kingpins like Meyer Lansky and Santo Trafficante to build lavish hotel casinos fueled by prostitution, rum, and narcotics. But beneath the neon facade lay an apparatus of state terror: his Military Intelligence Service (SIM) and police death squads abducted suspected dissidents off the streets, leaving their tortured, mutilated bodies hanging from lampposts in residential neighborhoods.
The facade of invincibility shattered across the final months of 1958. From the jagged peaks of the Sierra Maestra, Fidel Castro’s 26th of July Movement had waged a relentless guerrilla war that eroded the morale of the regular army. Batista’s commanders were corrupt, his conscript soldiers refused to fire on fellow countrymen, and in March 1958, Washington delivered a devastating psychological blow by imposing an arms embargo on the regime. The death knell sounded in central Cuba during the final days of December. A ragtag rebel column commanded by thirty-year-old Argentine medic Ernesto "Che" Guevara launched an assault on the strategic crossroads of Santa Clara. On December 29, Guevara’s guerrillas used a bulldozer to derail an armored train carrying four hundred government soldiers and heavy artillery, capturing its weapons and prompting the garrison to surrender. Santa Clara had fallen, bisecting the island and leaving the highway to Havana wide open.
Realizing that his military had entirely disintegrated, Batista orchestrated his exit with theatrical duplicity. He maintained the charade of the New Year’s Eve gala specifically to keep the city calm and prevent panic among the officer corps. At approximately two o'clock in the morning on January 1, 1959, Batista abruptly pulled his senior generals and ministers into a private office behind the ballroom. Visibly exhausted, he read an impromptu declaration of resignation, transferring executive authority to an elderly Supreme Court justice, Carlos Piedra. When stunned aides protested, Batista cut them off, bluntly telling them that Santa Clara had fallen and that any further resistance would result in a bloodbath. He gave those present twenty minutes to gather their wives, grab whatever luggage they had brought, and head to the runway.
At three in the morning, under heavy guard, Batista, his wife Marta, his children, and dozens of top regime officials boarded a flight of chartered Douglas DC-4 aircraft. The planes took off into the Caribbean sky heading east toward the Dominican Republic, where fellow right-wing dictator Rafael Trujillo had offered reluctant asylum. As the aircraft cleared the coast, Fulgencio Batista left behind a country he had ruled with an iron fist for seven years—and a personal fortune estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars stashed in Swiss and American bank accounts.
Dawn broke over Havana to an eerie stillness, followed by an explosion of absolute pandemonium. As radio announcers confirmed that the dictator had fled, tens of thousands of citizens flooded the boulevards in wild celebration. Angry crowds converged on the symbols of the regime’s decadence, sacking Batista’s lavish presidential palace, smashing parking meters, and storming the mafia-run casinos—smashing roulette wheels, overturning blackjack tables, and tossing slot machines out of the plate-glass windows of the Hotel Habana Libre and the Capri. Within days, Fidel Castro’s bearded rebel columns entered Havana in triumphant procession. Fulgencio Batista spent the remaining fourteen years of his life in exile between the Dominican Republic, Madeira, and Francisco Franco’s Spain, having toasted the new year as supreme ruler of Cuba and woken up as a fugitive before the sun came up.

-History After Dark

text:
Neville’s character development is one of the most underrated in Harry Potter because people often focus on the dramatic moment when he kills Nagini and forget how much it took for him to get there. In Philosopher’s Stone, Neville already shows courage when he stands up to Harry, Ron and Hermione to stop them breaking more rules, even though he knows they might fight him. Dumbledore recognises that bravery, but Neville himself struggles to see it. His real turning point comes in Order of the Phoenix: after learning more about what Bellatrix Lestrange did to his parents, he joins Dumbledore’s Army and works relentlessly to improve his defensive magic. The books show that Neville wasn’t unintelligent or incapable; he lacked confidence, struggled under pressure and needed the right environment to grow. The films capture his transformation, but they leave out some of the book’s most powerful context, including his visit to his parents at St Mungo’s and the full extent of his work with the DA. 

By Deathly Hallows, Neville has become one of the leaders of Hogwarts’ resistance against Snape and the Carrows, enduring punishment rather than surrendering to Voldemort’s supporters. Then comes the ultimate test: after Harry appears to have died, Voldemort offers Neville a place among the Death Eaters, and Neville refuses even when the situation seems hopeless. He pulls the Sword of Gryffindor from the Sorting Hat and kills Nagini, destroying Voldemort’s final remaining Horcrux. That moment is more than a heroic payoff; it brings his entire journey full circle. Neville was brave even when he was frightened, but over time he learned to trust that bravery and act on it. He didn’t suddenly become a hero at the Battle of Hogwarts. He had been becoming one since his first year; the difference is that by the end, he finally understood what he was capable of.

text:
People underestimate how much Neville Longbottom changed throughout Harry Potter.

He started as a boy who was constantly mocked, struggled with magic, and seemed terrified of everything. Yet when it mattered most, he stood up to Voldemort’s army and destroyed the final Horcrux.

Neville didn’t become brave because he stopped being afraid. He became brave because he stopped letting fear decide what he would do.

Honestly, Neville’s growth is one of the most satisfying character arcs in the entire series.

text:
Arsenal player ratings vs Leeds United: Bruno Guimaraes 8/10 inspires comeback victory.

Arsenal returned from the international break with a comeback victory over Leeds United at the Emirates Stadium, recovering from a difficult first half to secure three points. David Raya kept the hosts in contention with important saves before James Justin put Leeds ahead.

Riccardo Calafiori restored parity, while substitute Bruno Guimaraes completed the turnaround with an impressive finish. Mikel Arteta’s side showed greater urgency after the break, although several players struggled to find their rhythm before the substitutions changed the contest.

Arsenal player ratings vs Leeds United
David Raya – 8/10

Made crucial saves to deny Leeds during their strong first-half spell and kept Arsenal within reach. He could do little to prevent Justin’s goal.

Ben White – 6/10

Struggled defensively at times but redeemed himself by supplying the assist for Calafiori’s equaliser. He was withdrawn immediately afterwards.

Ezri Konsa – 8/10

Delivered an assured defensive performance, reading Leeds’ attacking movements well and making important interventions to prevent further damage.

Gabriel – 6/10

Looked slightly short of his usual sharpness and occasionally struggled to contain Leeds’ forward movement, but helped Arsenal recover after the break.

Riccardo Calafiori – 8/10

Made an intelligent run into the box to score Arsenal’s equaliser with a powerful finish. He threatened again shortly afterwards.

Declan Rice – 7/10

Provided energy and control in midfield, underlining his importance to Arsenal. His clever flick helped create Guimaraes’ decisive goal.

Myles Lewis-Skelly – 6/10

Brought intensity to Arsenal’s midfield but struggled to influence proceedings consistently as Leeds competed strongly in the middle.

Martin Odegaard – 7/10

Missed a promising opportunity in the first half but improved as the match progressed, particularly after Guimaraes entered midfield.

Noni Madueke – 6/10

Frequently found promising positions and created a couple of opportunities, although his attacking contributions lacked the consistency needed to unlock Leeds.

Kai Havertz – 5/10

Struggled to make an impact in attack, with his movement and finishing lacking sharpness. Arsenal needed considerably more from him before his withdrawal.

Bukayo Saka – 6/10

Worked hard to create attacking opportunities but found it difficult to produce his usual decisive quality against Leeds’ defence.

Substitutes
Bruno Guimaraes – 8/10

Transformed Arsenal’s midfield after coming on, adding aggression and creativity before scoring a superb winner to complete the comeback.

Viktor Gyokeres – 6/10

Provided a more physical presence up front, occupied Leeds’ defenders and offered Arsenal a greater attacking threat than Havertz had managed.

Jurrien Timber – 6/10

Performed reliably after entering the game, helping Arsenal maintain defensive stability during the closing stages.

Piero Hincapie – 6/10

Came on during the final 10 minutes and completed his defensive duties without encountering significant problems.

And I wasn't planning on explaining myself like this, I just wanted to observe them like zoo animals, but this tour was a little more personal than that, so in each of the 3  houses I visited the tour guide made me explain, over and over, Who I Am and What I'm Doing here in Lancaster County.

I can barely explain myself to baristas at Starbucks. Every family got a different story. This fat swarthy blonde on the tour with her own two pre-teen daughters clocked me instantly: are you a journalist? I just laughed. Kind of, yeah. I left out the whole "fucking girls in my van" aspect of it and just said that I travel a lot, I'm on a long road trip from Seattle to NYC. The tour guide had nothing but shit to say about NYC. All the rudest, most-ill adjusted customers come from New York City, or California. I tried to deflect the conversations away from Me and What I'm Up To but they just wouldn't stop. One woman asked for the name of my book and I just sighed... it's called "Worst Boyfriend Ever." Her two daughters laughed covering their mouths. I knew nobody would look it up after, most people don't and these people were especially offline. The other adult women on this tour seemed to be more interested in the Amish farming techniques than the people. I was high and on shrooms so I just stood stunned through most of it trying not to seem like a pedophile. 

Barbie, 11, gave us a tour of her family's milking operation. The kids grow up quick when their brains aren't fucked by screens. The cows looked sad and stared at me begging for help. I wondered if I was the only one who could see it. 

All these people have 8 kids and 40 grandkids. It's a nightmare trying to decide where to eat on the holidays. They make these totally arbitrary decisions about what Is and Is Not Allowed, no gas no electricity so they use air power for things like elevators in their homes, solar panels on every Amish roof. They're not secluded from the rest of the world here in Lancaster, they just play every game with a handicap. While driving my big heavy van with bad brakes and no insurance I am frequently acquainted with these stoic farm people wearing straw hats sitting in buggy-carriages pulled by horses waiting at intersections trying to Merge. The late-teens women are scarcely seen. On the bus I learned that "scooters are allowed... but not bicycles. it would let them get too far from home."

I deflected questions about myself all night. We were all sitting in this old widow's living room, every person dead sober except for me, as they tried to understand why I would voluntarily sleep in my van, for so long, unmarried, childless, "writing..." one of the Amish guys was sure I said "riding." It's like, fiction, I have a book, you don't understand.. The old widow offered me some delicious apple cider. They put two types of apples, and pears in it. It was thick and I had several cups. Her name was Sarah and we were instructed not to sit in that green rocking chair in the corner of the room, because that's where Ike used to sit, before he recently died. Sarah looked like Benjamin Franklin if he were a woman. Every time I said "my phone" or "online" every person in the room cringed. I'm sorry, I just can't explain my life without it. That's how I find places to eat, that's how I get money, that's how I found this. I couldn't think of the right questions to ask, I didn't want to get "too philosophical" and start dissecting these peoples' brains, prompting them to question their way of life. My own sense of reality feels increasingly fragile lately and I know philosophy is a dead end.

The old widow asked for the name of my book again, as we left. I just shook my head and smiled knowing there is no universe in which this thing actually reaches her. Worst Boyfriend Ever will never be in bookstores, and she will never use the internet. Still I yelled it out, as if warning her it would be hitting the shelves at her local library next week. 

The bus got back to the parking lot and the tour ended and I scurried out of there as quickly as I could, before anybody could ask any more questions. I drove to the only pub open in town and ate a steak salad alone. I thought about those Amish people we pay to interrogate like zoo animals and how sick they must be of that treatment. Explaining themselves over and over. I hoped they were getting paid well. I wondered if there were any whorehouses in this town. I thought it might be funny if, when I got to New York, I did another show, and charged for entry, and "Live Rapist Q&A -- Ask Me Anything!" Could be funny.

text:
Apps that help people quit bad habits are seriously powerful.

For example, Reframe, an alcohol reduction app estimated to be doing around $400K/month.

With the global movement toward drinking less getting stronger, the app has been growing rapidly along with that trend.

And apps in this “quit bad habits” category tend to have long onboarding flows.

Reframe has a whopping 50 screens.

• The first half is filled with multiple-choice questions about your drinking habits
• Every 5–10 screens or so, it reinforces the importance of reducing alcohol consumption and the value of the app
• In the second half, users rate their mindset on a 5-point scale to strengthen commitment
• They offer a money-back guarantee: if you don’t feel the effects after 30 days, they refund 2x what you paid
The long onboarding builds commitment, and then the 2x refund guarantee removes as many reasons not to pay as possible.
Insane.
With a short onboarding, you may end up with a lot of casual users who are more likely to request refunds.

But users who make it through 50 screens are probably more committed, which could mean far fewer refund requests.

Maybe that’s what makes a strategy like this possible.

You can check every onboarding screen for Reframe on Onbo Hub👇

text:
The Eucharist: A Foretaste of Heaven with St. Carlo Acutis ⤵️

✝️ A young saint who loved Jesus

Saint Carlo Acutis was born in 1991. He grew up like many other kids. He loved computers, video games, and technology, but he loved Jesus more.

From a young age, Carlo went to daily Mass and spent time praying before the Blessed Sacrament. He called the Eucharist his “highway to heaven” because he knew that Jesus was truly present.

On October 10, 2020, Carlo was beatified by the Catholic Church. Five years later, on September 7, 2025, Pope Leo XIV canonized him as a saint, making him the first millennial saint.

His feast day is October 12, the day he died.

✝️ What he taught about the Eucharist

Saint Carlo once said:

“The more Eucharist we receive, the more we will become like Jesus, so that on earth we will have a foretaste of heaven.”

Carlo understood something many people forget. The Eucharist is not just a symbol. It is truly Jesus Christ, Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity.

When we receive Holy Communion worthily, in a state of grace, we receive Jesus Himself. He strengthens our souls, helps us grow in holiness, and brings us closer to heaven.

The Catechism calls the Eucharist “the source and summit of the Christian life” (CCC 1324). In simple words, the Eucharist is at the very heart of our Catholic faith.

✝️ How he lived his faith

Carlo did not just talk about loving Jesus. He showed it through his actions.

He attended daily Mass, prayed the Rosary, and spent time in Eucharistic adoration. He even used his computer skills to create a website about Eucharistic miracles from around the world.

He wanted people to know that Jesus is truly present in the Eucharist.

In 2006, Carlo became seriously ill with leukemia. Instead of losing his faith, he offered his suffering to God for the Church and the Pope.

He died on October 12, 2006, at just 15 years old.

Today, his remains are displayed for veneration in Assisi, Italy, where many pilgrims visit and ask for his prayers. The Church has not declared his body incorrupt.

✝️ What his life teaches us today

Carlo lived in the modern world, just like us. He had hobbies, friends, and dreams. But he never forgot what mattered most.

He knew that Jesus was waiting for him in the Eucharist.

And if we truly believe that the Eucharist is Jesus Himself, shouldn't that change the way we live?

The Eucharist is more than something we receive at Mass. It is a personal encounter with Jesus, who loves us and wants to bring us closer to Him.

You do not have to be famous or do extraordinary things to become a saint. Carlo showed us that holiness begins with loving Jesus in the ordinary moments of life.

🙏 A simple prayer

Saint Carlo Acutis, pray for us. Help us love Jesus in the Eucharist, receive Him with faith, and grow closer to Him every day. Teach us to put God first and follow Him in everything we do. Amen.

💬 If you truly believed that Jesus Himself was waiting for you in the Eucharist, what would you change about your life?
